title: A 600 BC book quoting a 1611 Bible
claim: Roughly 21 chapters of Isaiah appear in the Book of Mormon. The wording is overwhelmingly identical to the King James Version of 1611 and 1769. That sits badly with the claim that the text was translated independently from sixth-century BC plates written in 'reformed Egyptian.' Royal Skousen's own critical-text work confirms the quotations match the standard later King James printings — not even the 1611 original. That points to a printed English Bible of Joseph Smith's own day rather than a fresh rendering of a Hebrew source. Where the Book of Mormon does vary from the King James, the variants rarely reflect a superior Hebrew reading.

sources.name: David P. Wright, 'Isaiah in the Book of Mormon: Or Joseph Smith in Isaiah' (American Apocrypha, Signature Books, 2002)
Royal Skousen, The History of the Text of the Book of Mormon, Part 5: The King James Quotations (2019), summarized at BYU Studies
LDS Discussions, 'The King James Bible and the Book of Mormon'

response:
FAIR and Skousen agree the translation was never word for word. Where the plates matched the Bible, the familiar King James wording was given. Two reasons are offered. Joseph may have consulted a Bible. Or, in Skousen's tight-control model, revelation supplied him with King James style English.

On that reading the King James wording is a feature of how the book was given. It is not evidence against an old source. Skousen goes further. He argues that some Isaiah variants come from Early Modern English streams of text. They are not copied from the 1611 page at all.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Isaiah and the Book of Mormon'

rationale:
Their own leading textual scholar grants the core fact. The English text comes from the King James Bible. It even carries printing habits added after 1611. Skousen does not dispute that.

So the replies explain the dependence. They do not rebut it.

plain.t: What is actually in the book
plain.d: About 21 chapters of Isaiah sit inside the Book of Mormon. They are in 1 Nephi 20-21, 2 Nephi 7-8, 2 Nephi 12-24, 2 Nephi 27, Mosiah 14 and 3 Nephi 22. The wording is almost identical to the King James Version.
The King James Version is an English translation from 1611. Lehi left Jerusalem around 600 BC. A fresh translation from his brass plates should not match one later English edition word for word.

Royal Skousen is the leading Latter-day Saint scholar of the text. His critical work found the quotations match later King James printings. Not even the 1611 original. And where the Book of Mormon does differ, the changes rarely give a better Hebrew reading.

FAIR and Skousen say the translation was never word for word. Where the plates matched the Bible, the familiar King James wording was supplied. Either Joseph consulted a Bible, or revelation gave him King James style English. Skousen adds that some variants look like older English streams rather than copying.
Strong for you. Their own leading textual scholar concedes where the English came from. The answer explains the dependence. It does not deny it.
"Why does it track a later King James printing rather than the Hebrew?"

refwhy.Isaiah 48–49: The King James text behind 1 Nephi 20-21. This is the side-by-side that starts the argument.
refwhy.Isaiah 50–51: The King James text behind 2 Nephi 7-8.
refwhy.Isaiah 2–14: The thirteen chapters copied at 2 Nephi 12-24. Skousen found the wording tracks later King James printings.
refwhy.Isaiah 29: The chapter 2 Nephi 27 rewrites. Its sealed-book language becomes a prophecy of the gold plates.
refwhy.Isaiah 53: The source for Mosiah 14. Christians read it as the suffering servant, and the wording carries over whole.
refwhy.Isaiah 54: The source for 3 Nephi 22 — 'Sing, O barren' and all that follows.
refwhy.1 Nephi 20–21: Nephi's Isaiah block. Set it beside Isaiah 48-49 and the King James wording is the same.
refwhy.2 Nephi 7–8: Jacob's block. It matches Isaiah 50-51, chapters most scholars date to the exile, long after Lehi left.
refwhy.2 Nephi 12–24: The long block: thirteen chapters of Isaiah in a row, in King James English.
refwhy.2 Nephi 27: Reworks Isaiah 29 into a prophecy about a sealed book. The clearest case of Isaiah being reshaped.
refwhy.Mosiah 14: Abinadi quotes Isaiah 53 whole. His sermon rests on it, so this block is hard to wave off.
refwhy.3 Nephi 22: The risen Jesus gives the Nephites Isaiah 54, again in King James wording.

titleLong: Isaiah chapters reproduced verbatim in King James English
responseLead: The King James wording came with the translation, not from the plates themselves.
rationaleLead: Strong for you: their own leading textual scholar grants where the English came from.

title: Isaiah edits land on words added in 1611
claim: The King James Bible prints some words in italics. Those are words the 1611 translators added to make the English read smoothly. They have no equivalent in the Hebrew, and they exist only in that printed edition. David Wright showed that a conservative 22 to 38 percent of all Book of Mormon Isaiah differences from the King James occur at or around those italic words. About 40 percent of the italic words are simply dropped. No one translating from ancient plates could know which English words a seventeenth-century committee had supplied.

sources.name: David P. Wright, 'Isaiah in the Book of Mormon: Or Joseph Smith in Isaiah' (American Apocrypha, 2002)
Dialogue: 'Joseph Smith's Interpretation of Isaiah in the Book of Mormon'

response:
Stan Spencer, of the Interpreter Foundation, accepts the pattern. He argues that Joseph Smith could see the italics on the page. An untrained reader would treat them as the weakest part of the verse. So Joseph revised around them as he dictated.

On that view a revealed translation would land on exactly those words. FAIR argues much the same. The italic words really were the softer text. A prophetic revision would be expected to correct there first.

responseSource.name: Stan Spencer, 'Missing Words: King James Bible Italics…', Interpreter

rationale:
Both sides now agree on the fact. The changes cluster on the italics. Those are a printing feature of one English Bible from 1611. That is no longer in dispute.

What the defence offers is a reframe, not a denial. And the reframe grants the thing that matters. He was working from a King James Bible.

One problem is left over. In several places, dropping the italic word hurts the sense against the Hebrew. A revision guided by God would not be expected to do that.

plain.d: Open a King James Bible. Some words are printed in italics. Those are words the 1611 translators added to make the English read smoothly. They are not in the Hebrew.
Nobody translating from ancient gold plates could know which English words a 1611 committee had added. Those words exist only in that one edition.

plain.t: What the Book of Mormon does
plain.d: It quotes long stretches of Isaiah. Where its wording differs from the King James, the changes cluster on exactly those italic words. David Wright counted it: between 22% and 38% of the differences land there. And about 40% of the italic words are simply dropped.

Stan Spencer of the Interpreter Foundation accepts the pattern. He argues Joseph Smith could see the italics on the page, treated them as suspect, and revised around them while dictating. That is a real answer, and it fits the data.
It concedes he was working from a King James Bible. That is the whole point at issue.
"Why would a translation from gold plates track the italics of one English edition?"

refwhy.Isaiah 2:16: The King James verse for comparison. It has two 'and upon all' clauses. 2 Nephi 12:16 has three.
refwhy.Isaiah 6:2: The King James verse with 'seraphims.' The double plural is the translators' English.
refwhy.Isaiah 9:1: The King James verse that italicises 'her.' Dropping that one word is what breaks the sense in 2 Nephi 19:1.
refwhy.2 Nephi 12:16: Helps their side. It adds 'the ships of the sea,' wording apologists say matches the Greek against the King James.
refwhy.2 Nephi 16:2: Cited for the double plural 'seraphims' in the early printings. That is English form, not Hebrew.
refwhy.2 Nephi 19:1: The clearest sample. It drops the King James italic 'her,' leaving the verb with nothing to act on.
refwhy.2 Nephi 12–24 (variant pattern): The whole Isaiah block, cited as the data set. Wright counted the changes across it and found the clustering.

titleLong: Book of Mormon Isaiah variants cluster on KJV italicized words
responseLead: Stan Spencer says Joseph saw the italics and revised the weakest words on purpose.
rationaleLead: Strong for you: both sides now agree the changes cluster on 1611's added words.

title: Errors made in 1611, copied word for word
claim: The Book of Mormon reproduces specific King James translation errors that a rendering from an independent Hebrew source would not contain. At 2 Nephi 14:5 it has 'and upon all the glory shall be a defence,' where the Hebrew chuppah means 'canopy.' At 2 Nephi 21:3 it has 'make him of quick understanding,' misrendering a Hebrew line that says his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. At 2 Nephi 16:2 it keeps the King James double plurals 'seraphims' and 'cherubims.' These are artifacts of the 1611 translators' English, not of any ancient text. Mosiah 14 shows the same pattern.

left.text: And the Lord will create upon every dwelling-place of mount Zion, and upon her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for upon all the glory of Zion shall be a defence.

right.text: And the LORD will create upon every dwelling place of mount Zion, and upon her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night: for upon all the glory shall be a defence.

hl: a cloud and smoke by day
shining of a flaming fire by night
comparison.note: 'Defence' is the KJV translators' misreading of Hebrew chuppah ('canopy, bridal chamber') — an error of 1611 English, reproduced on plates allegedly written centuries before English existed.

sources.name: David P. Wright, 'Isaiah in the Book of Mormon' (American Apocrypha, 2002)
Grant H. Palmer, An Insider's View of Mormon Origins (Signature Books, 2002), ch. 3
LDS Discussions, 'The King James Bible and the Book of Mormon'

response:
FAIR argues that a functional translation aimed at King James readers may keep familiar wording. That holds even where the wording is imperfect. Some of the alleged errors are also fair readings of Hebrew that is genuinely unclear.

There is a scriptural warrant too. D&C 1:24 has God speaking to people after the manner of their language. On that account the errors belong to the English layer. They do not belong to the plates.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'KJV translation errors in the Book of Mormon'

rationale:
The King James marks are conceded. The defence moves them into a translation habit given by God. It does not show that the readings are anything but King James errors.

And one thing is missing. No variant anywhere pulls the wording back toward the Hebrew. If God were correcting the 1611 committee, you would expect that somewhere.

plain.t: What a translation error looks like
plain.d: The 1611 translators got some Hebrew words wrong. Those mistakes belong to their English. They are not in the Hebrew text at all.

2 Nephi 14:5 has "upon all the glory shall be a defence." The Hebrew word there, chuppah, means canopy. 2 Nephi 21:3 has "make him of quick understanding," where the Hebrew says his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. And 2 Nephi 16:2 keeps the King James double plurals seraphims and cherubims. Hebrew already makes those words plural.
These are marks of one English committee's work in 1611. A translation made from a Hebrew source would not carry them.

FAIR says a translation aimed at King James readers may keep familiar wording even where it is imperfect. Some of the disputed lines are defensible readings of ambiguous Hebrew. And D&C 1:24 says God speaks to people after the manner of their language. So the errors sit in the English layer, not on the plates.
Strong for you. The King James artifacts are granted. The defence moves them into a translation convention. And no variant anywhere pulls the wording back toward the Hebrew.
"If the Hebrew word means canopy, why does your book say defence?"

refwhy.Isaiah 4:5: The King James source. It reads 'upon all the glory shall be a defence' — the rendering at issue.
refwhy.Isaiah 6:2: The King James verse with 'seraphims.' A 1611 English plural, not a feature of the Hebrew.
refwhy.Isaiah 11:3: The King James source of 'make him of quick understanding,' the phrase the Book of Mormon keeps.
refwhy.Isaiah 53: The chapter behind Mosiah 14. Compare the two and the King James wording runs straight through.
refwhy.2 Nephi 14:5: Has 'shall be a defence' where the Hebrew word chuppah means canopy. The King James error, carried over.
refwhy.2 Nephi 16:2: Cited for keeping the King James plural 'seraphims' in the early printings. Hebrew already makes the word plural.
refwhy.2 Nephi 21:3: Repeats 'make him of quick understanding,' which misses the Hebrew line about delight in the fear of the LORD.
refwhy.Mosiah 14: Abinadi's whole sermon is Isaiah 53 in King James English. The longest stretch showing the pattern.

titleLong: KJV mistranslations and translation artifacts reproduced verbatim
responseLead: The errors sit in the English translation layer, not on the ancient plates.
rationaleLead: Strong for you: the King James marks are granted, then moved somewhere else.

title: Lehi sails with Isaiah chapters not yet written
claim: Since the late 1700s, most scholars have held that Isaiah 40-55 had a second author. He wrote during the exile, around 545 to 539 BC. Three things point that way: the language, the history, and the theology. Those chapters treat the Babylonian exile as already happening. They also name Cyrus, a Persian king not yet born in Isaiah's day. Chapters 56-66 are dated later again. Lehi left Jerusalem around 600 BC. Yet Nephi, Jacob and Abinadi all quote those chapters at length. Abinadi builds a whole sermon on Isaiah 53.

left.text: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.

right.text: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.

hl: with his stripes we are healed
comparison.note: Abinadi's entire sermon is built on Isaiah 53 — a chapter mainstream scholarship dates decades after Lehi's party left Jerusalem with the brass plates.

sources.name: Colby Townsend, '"The Robe of Righteousness": Exilic and Post-Exilic Isaiah in the Book of Mormon,' Dialogue 55:1 (2022)
David P. Wright, 'Isaiah in the Book of Mormon' (American Apocrypha, 2002)
LDS Discussions, 'Deutero-Isaiah in the Book of Mormon'
Mormonr, 'Deutero-Isaiah' (LDS-side documentation of the problem)

response:
Two lines of answer, and they pull in opposite ways. Kevin Barney and FAIR accept the scholarly dating. They suggest the material entered during translation. Joseph rendered Nephite ideas in the King James Isaiah his readers knew.

Other defenders reject the dating instead. They argue for one author. Or they argue for an early core of Isaiah 40-55 that could have existed by 600 BC. They also note that late-dating Isaiah partly assumes prophecy cannot predict.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Deutero-Isaiah in the Book of Mormon?'

rationale:
The exile dating of Isaiah 40-55 is one of the firmest results in Hebrew Bible study. Trained Latter-day Saint scholars accept it, David Bokovoy among them.

So the defences have to pick. Reject the consensus, which is a large thing to do. Or accept it and move the material into the translation. That second route grants that the plates could not have held those chapters.

It costs a lot. Abinadi's whole sermon is built on Isaiah 53.

plain.d: Most scholars think Isaiah 40-55 had a second, unnamed author. They date it to about 545 BC, during the exile in Babylon. Two reasons. Those chapters treat the exile as already happening. And they name Cyrus, a Persian king who had not been born in Isaiah's day.

plain.t: Why that is a problem here
plain.d: Lehi left Jerusalem around 600 BC, before the exile. So those chapters could not have been on the brass plates he carried. Yet Nephi, Jacob and Abinadi all quote them at length.

Two lines. Kevin Barney and FAIR accept the late dating. They suggest the wording entered during translation — Joseph putting Nephite ideas into the King James Isaiah he knew. Others reject the dating and defend one Isaiah in the 700s BC.

Strong for you. The first answer concedes that part of the text is not ancient. The second requires overturning two centuries of scholarship — which some conservatives do attempt, and you should say so.
"If those chapters were written after Lehi left, how were they on his plates?"

refwhy.Isaiah 48–49: The chapters behind 1 Nephi 20-21. Isaiah 48 treats the exile in Babylon as already under way.
refwhy.Isaiah 50–52: The source of 2 Nephi 7-8 and of part of 3 Nephi 20.
refwhy.Isaiah 53: The servant chapter. It is the source of Mosiah 14, which is why this case bites so hard.
refwhy.Isaiah 54: The source of 3 Nephi 22, from the same block of chapters.
refwhy.Isaiah 55:1–2: The source of 2 Nephi 9:50-51. Compare them: 'come ye to the waters,' almost word for word.
refwhy.1 Nephi 20–21: Nephi quotes Isaiah 48-49. Most scholars date those chapters to the exile, well after Lehi left Jerusalem.
refwhy.2 Nephi 7–8: Jacob quotes Isaiah 50-51, also from the disputed second half of Isaiah.
refwhy.2 Nephi 9:50–51: Quotes Isaiah 55:1-2, 'come ye to the waters,' from the same exile-dated section.
refwhy.Mosiah 14: Abinadi builds a whole sermon on Isaiah 53. The costliest case for the answer that blames translation.
refwhy.3 Nephi 20:32–45: Jesus quotes Isaiah 52 to the Nephites, including 'they shall see eye to eye.'
refwhy.3 Nephi 22: Jesus gives them Isaiah 54. It sits in the same late block of chapters.

titleLong: Isaiah chapters written after Lehi left Jerusalem appear in the Book of Mormon
responseLead: Either the wording came in when it was turned into English, or the late dating is wrong.
rationaleLead: Strong for you: both answers cost them a great deal, and one gives up the plates.

title: 3 Nephi quotes a line scribes added later
claim: 3 Nephi 12-14 reproduces Matthew 5-7 in nearly verbatim King James English. Stan Larson identified eight passages where 3 Nephi follows readings of the late Greek manuscripts behind the King James — readings text-critical scholarship judges secondary. The clearest is the doxology at 3 Nephi 13:13, 'For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever,' which is absent from the earliest witnesses to Matthew 6:13. 'Openly' at 3 Nephi 13:4, 6 and 18 is the same kind of case. A genuine independent record of Jesus' New World sermon should not track scribal accretions of the fourth to sixteenth centuries.

left.ref: 3 Nephi 13:13 — Jesus in America, c. AD 34
left.text: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen.

right.text: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.

hl: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory
comparison.note: The doxology is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) — text critics judge it a later scribal addition, yet the resurrected Jesus in America speaks it in its KJV form.

sources.name: Stan Larson, 'The Historicity of the Matthean Sermon on the Mount in 3 Nephi,' in New Approaches to the Book of Mormon (Signature Books, 1993)
Grant H. Palmer, An Insider's View of Mormon Origins, ch. 3

response:
John W. Welch of BYU responded at length. Several of Larson's eight variants are uncertain rather than settled. One runs the other way. 3 Nephi 12:22 leaves out 'without a cause', agreeing with the earliest manuscripts against the King James of Matthew 5:22.

Welch also argues that the King James wording elsewhere reflects the register of the translation. It does not reflect the Nephite record. And 3 Nephi adapts the sermon to its setting on purpose. Mechanical copying would not do that.

responseSource.name: John W. Welch, Illuminating the Sermon at the Temple and Sermon on the Mount (FARMS/Maxwell Institute)

rationale:
Welch's reply engages the variants seriously. The missing 'without a cause' at 3 Nephi 12:22 is a real point for them. Hand it over before anyone asks.

The prayer ending at 3 Nephi 13:13 and the word 'openly' are still best explained by King James dependence. Scholars do argue over single cases. The King James register across the whole sermon is not in doubt.

plain.d: 3 Nephi 12-14 gives the Sermon on the Mount to the Nephites. It is near-verbatim King James English, matching Matthew 5-7.

Eight places where 3 Nephi follows late Greek manuscripts that scholars judge to be later additions. The clearest is the close of the Lord's Prayer at 3 Nephi 13:13 — "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever." That line is missing from the earliest copies of Matthew 6:13. The word openly at 3 Nephi 13:4, 6 and 18 is the same kind of case.
A record of Jesus speaking in the New World should not follow scribal additions made between the 300s and the 1500s.

John Welch of BYU answered at length. Several of Larson's eight are text-critically uncertain rather than settled. And one runs the other way. 3 Nephi 12:22 drops "without a cause," agreeing with the earliest manuscripts against the King James. Welch also points to deliberate changes for the Nephite setting, which mechanical copying would not produce.
Genuinely arguable. Welch's without a cause point is real, and you should hand it over before anyone asks. The doxology and openly are still best explained by King James dependence.
"Why does the Nephite sermon include a line the earliest copies of Matthew don't have?"

refwhy.Matthew 5–7: The King James Sermon on the Mount, which 3 Nephi 12-14 follows almost word for word.
refwhy.Matthew 6:13: The King James verse with the doxology. Modern Bibles drop it or footnote it.
refwhy.Matthew 6:4,6,18: The King James verses with 'openly.' The word is absent from the earliest Greek copies.
refwhy.Matthew 5:27: 'Ye have heard that it was said' — the King James wording 3 Nephi 12:27 changes.
refwhy.Matthew 5:44: The King James verse with the extra clauses. Set it beside 3 Nephi 12:44 and they match.
refwhy.3 Nephi 12–14: The Nephite Sermon on the Mount. Near-identical to Matthew 5-7 in King James English.
refwhy.3 Nephi 13:13: The doxology: 'For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory.' Missing from the earliest copies of Matthew.
refwhy.3 Nephi 13:4,6,18: Three verses ending 'reward thee openly.' That last word is a later addition in Matthew's manuscripts.
refwhy.3 Nephi 12:27: Reads 'it is written by them of old time' where Matthew has 'ye have heard.' Welch cites this as a real change.
refwhy.3 Nephi 12:44: Keeps 'bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you' — clauses the earliest copies of Matthew lack.

titleLong: Sermon on the Mount in 3 Nephi follows late KJV/Byzantine readings
responseLead: Welch shows one variant runs the other way, matching the earliest manuscripts against the King James.
rationaleLead: Arguable both ways: Welch's reverse case is real, but the added prayer line is not.

title: 650 New Testament phrases, centuries before Jesus
claim: Books set between 600 and 100 BC are saturated with distinctive King James New Testament phrasing. Nephi echoes Paul — 'O wretched man that I am' at 2 Nephi 4:17 is Romans 7:24, and 'to be carnally-minded is death' at 2 Nephi 9:39 is Romans 8:6. 1 Nephi 22:20 quotes Peter's Acts 3:22-23 paraphrase of Deuteronomy 18. Alma 5:52 echoes John the Baptist at Matthew 3:10. Moroni 7:45-47 tracks 1 Corinthians 13:4-8 and Moroni 10:8-17 tracks 1 Corinthians 12:4-11, nearly verbatim. The BYU professor Nicholas Frederick has catalogued roughly 650 New Testament phrases woven through the text — language that did not exist before the first-century Greek documents it comes from.

left.text: And charity suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil, and rejoiceth not in iniquity but rejoiceth in the truth, beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.

right.text: Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil; rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth; beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.

hl: beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things
comparison.note: Mormon's sermon tracks Paul's Greek epistle phrase-for-phrase in its distinctive KJV English rendering — including word choices unique to the 1611 translators.

sources.name: Nicholas J. Frederick, The Bible, Mormon Scripture, and the Rhetoric of Allusivity (Fairleigh Dickinson UP, 2016)
Frederick interview (LDS Perspectives): ~650 NT phrases in the Book of Mormon
Grant H. Palmer, An Insider's View of Mormon Origins, chs. 3–4

response:
FAIR and Frederick argue that the New Testament language belongs to the translation. It does not belong to the plates. Joseph Smith, or a revealed translation aimed at 1820s Bible readers, put Nephite ideas into the scriptural English his audience knew.

The King James New Testament itself renders ideas with shared covenant wording. Some parallels may also reflect common Old World sources. Others may reflect real parallel revelation of the same gospel to prophets before Christ.

responseSource.name: FAIR, response to An Insider's View of Mormon Origins

rationale:
The fact is granted even at BYU. Hundreds of distinctly New Testament phrases run through the text. Nicholas Frederick counts about 650.

The translation-idiom defence does not rebut that. It grants that the English text is not a literal rendering of an old record.

And it strains hardest where a New Testament passage gives a whole sermon its shape. Moroni 7 and Moroni 10 are the clearest cases.

plain.t: What is in the early books
plain.d: Books set between 600 and 100 BC are full of New Testament wording. 2 Nephi 4:17 has "O wretched man that I am," which is Romans 7:24. 2 Nephi 9:39 has "to be carnally-minded is death," which is Romans 8:6. 1 Nephi 22:20 quotes Peter's version of Deuteronomy 18 from Acts 3:22-23. Alma 5:52 echoes John the Baptist in Matthew 3:10.
Moroni 7:45-47 tracks 1 Corinthians 13:4-8 almost word for word. Moroni 10:8-17 does the same with 1 Corinthians 12:4-11.
Nicholas Frederick, a BYU professor, has catalogued roughly 650 New Testament phrases woven through the text. That number comes from inside the church.

FAIR and Frederick both say the New Testament language belongs to the translation, not the plates. Joseph, or a revealed translation aimed at 1820s Bible readers, put Nephite ideas into the scriptural English they knew. Some parallels may also come from shared Old World sources, or from the same gospel being revealed twice.

Strong for you. The fact is granted at BYU. The translation-idiom answer concedes that the English is not a literal rendering of an ancient record. And it strains hardest where a whole sermon is built on a New Testament passage.
"How does a prophet writing before Christ quote Paul?"

refwhy.Romans 7:24: Paul's cry, which Nephi uses first. Paul wrote it about 650 years later.
refwhy.Romans 8:6: Paul's contrast of the carnal and spiritual mind, which 2 Nephi 9:39 reproduces.
refwhy.Acts 3:22–23: Peter's version of Deuteronomy 18. The clause 'in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you' is Peter's, and Nephi has it.
refwhy.Matthew 3:10: John the Baptist's axe-at-the-root saying, which Alma 5:52 uses long before he said it.
refwhy.1 Corinthians 13:4–8: Paul's charity passage. Set it beside Moroni 7:45-47 and the phrases run in the same order.
refwhy.1 Corinthians 12:4–11: Paul's gifts passage, matched clause for clause by Moroni 10:8-17.
refwhy.2 Nephi 4:17: Nephi says 'O wretched man that I am' — Paul's line in Romans, spoken around 590 BC.
refwhy.2 Nephi 9:39: 'To be carnally-minded is death.' That is Romans 8:6, in a sermon dated centuries before Paul.
refwhy.1 Nephi 22:20: Quotes Moses in Peter's wording from Acts 3, not in the wording of Deuteronomy itself.
refwhy.Alma 5:52: 'The ax is laid at the root of the tree' — John the Baptist's line, about a century early.
refwhy.Moroni 7:45–47: Reads like 1 Corinthians 13, almost word for word. Same phrases, same order: 'suffereth long,' 'never faileth.'
refwhy.Moroni 10:8–17: Tracks Paul's list of spiritual gifts in 1 Corinthians 12, down to the phrase 'the same Spirit.'

titleLong: Pervasive New Testament phrasing in allegedly pre-Christian Nephite texts
responseLead: The New Testament wording came in with the English, for Bible readers of the 1820s.
rationaleLead: Strong for you: BYU grants the 650 phrases, and the answer concedes the English is not literal.

title: Alma 12–13 follows Hebrews, argument for argument
claim: David Wright showed that Alma's sermon, dated to about 82 BC, reproduces the Epistle to the Hebrews. Alma 12:9-37 and 13:1-20 follow the distinctive argument sequence, exegetical moves and King James wording of Hebrews 3:7-4:11 and 7:1-4 — priesthood 'after the order of the Son,' Melchizedek, and entering God's 'rest.' Alma 13:17-19's Melchizedek summary tracks Hebrews 7:1-4 closely. Scholars regard those elements as the author of Hebrews' own creative synthesis of Genesis 14 and Psalm 110, which no pre-Christian source contained.

sources.name: David P. Wright, '"In Plain Terms That We May Understand": Joseph Smith's Transformation of Hebrews in Alma 12–13,' in New Approaches to the Book of Mormon (Signature Books, 1994)
Book of Mormon Origins commentary on Alma 13 (documents the parallels)

response:
John W. Welch and the FARMS reviewers argue that Alma 13 and Hebrews could draw on the same older material. Melchizedek traditions are attested in Second Temple texts. 11QMelchizedek and the Genesis Apocryphon are two of them.

The shared King James wording, they say, is translation register. And Alma's treatment pulls a different way from Hebrews. Alma is about repentance and ordination. Hebrews is about Christ's superiority. Plain copying would not predict that.

responseSource.name: John W. Welch, 'The Melchizedek Material in Alma 13' (FARMS); FAIR review of New Approaches

rationale:
Wright's word-by-word case is detailed. Nobody has taken it apart.

The shared-tradition reply is a real answer. But no manuscript holds the Alma 13 argument, so it stays a guess. And it does not simply grant that Alma leans on Hebrews.

The dispute is genuine. The parallels favour Wright. They do not close it.

plain.d: A sermon dated to about 82 BC. It is about priesthood "after the order of the Son," about Melchizedek, and about entering God's "rest."

That the sermon reproduces the argument sequence, the interpretive moves and the King James wording of Hebrews 3:7-4:11 and 7:1-4. Alma 13:17-19 tracks Hebrews 7:1-4 closely. Scholars treat that Hebrews material as the author's own fusion of Genesis 14 and Psalm 110. No pre-Christian source contains it.

John Welch and the FARMS reviewers say both texts could draw on older Melchizedek traditions. Those traditions do exist: 11QMelchizedek and the Genesis Apocryphon, both from the Dead Sea Scrolls. They add that the shared wording is translation register. And Alma's emphasis differs — repentance and ordination, rather than Christ's superiority. Copying would not produce that.

Genuinely arguable. Wright's verbal case has not been taken apart. But the shared-tradition answer is a real alternative, even though no manuscript supports it directly. The parallels favour Wright. They do not close it.
"Which older source has the Melchizedek argument Alma 13 uses?"

refwhy.Hebrews 3:7–4:11: Where 'my rest' is argued out at length. Alma 12 uses the same idea in the same order.
refwhy.Hebrews 5:6–10: 'A priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec' — the phrase behind Alma's 'order of the Son.'
refwhy.Hebrews 7:1–4: The passage Alma 13:17-19 tracks. Scholars call it the author's own build from Genesis 14 and Psalm 110.
refwhy.Psalm 110:4: One of the two Old Testament sources the Hebrews author fused. Alone, it says only 'a priest for ever.'
refwhy.Genesis 14:18–20: The other source. These three verses are all the Old Testament says about Melchizedek — which is Wright's point.
refwhy.Alma 12:9–37: The first half of the sermon, on hardened hearts and entering God's 'rest.' That is the Hebrews 3-4 argument.
refwhy.Alma 13:1–20: The priesthood section, 'after the order of the Son,' following the shape of Hebrews 5 and 7.
refwhy.Alma 13:17–19: The Melchizedek summary: king of Salem, prince of peace, none greater. The tightest match with Hebrews.

titleLong: Alma 12–13 structured on the Epistle to the Hebrews
responseLead: Both texts could draw on older Melchizedek lore, and the Dead Sea Scrolls hold some.
rationaleLead: Leans your way, but their older-source answer is real and not yet ruled out.

title: The risen Jesus quotes a disputed end of Mark
claim: Mormon 9:22-24 has the resurrected Jesus commissioning the Nephite disciples in words nearly identical to Mark 16:15-18 in the King James. Ether 4:18 draws on the same material. That is the 'long ending' of Mark, which is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Mainstream textual criticism judges it a second-century scribal addition. The Book of Mormon therefore attributes to Jesus in America a saying that, on the scholarly consensus, entered Mark's text after the first century.

left.text: Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature; and he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved, but he that believeth not shall be damned; and these signs shall follow them that believe — in my name shall they cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing it shall not hurt them.

right.text: Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature. He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned. And these signs shall follow them that believe; In my name shall they cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them.

hl: Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature
believeth and is baptized shall be saved
comparison.note: The earliest manuscripts of Mark end at 16:8; most text critics judge vv. 9–20 a second-century addition.

sources.name: Grant H. Palmer, An Insider's View of Mormon Origins, ch. 3
LDS Discussions, 'The Long Ending of Mark and the Book of Mormon'

response:
Book of Mormon Central answers in KnoWhy 522, and gives two lines.

First, a minority of trained scholars outside the church defend the long ending as real. Nicholas Lunn and James Snapp argue that case from early church quotations and from the text itself.

Second, even if Mark 16:9-20 is a later addition, Moroni's source was the Nephite record of Christ's words. The King James phrasing is the register of the translation. The risen Lord could give the same charge in both hemispheres.

responseSource.name: Book of Mormon Central, KnoWhy #522

rationale:
The defence leans on a minority reading of the text. That reading does have published defenders outside the church. So whether Mark's long ending is original is genuinely disputed.

On the standard view, though, the problem stands. The risen Jesus in America quotes twelve verses that most scholars date to the second century.

plain.d: Mormon 9:22-24 has the risen Jesus commissioning the Nephite disciples. The words are nearly identical to Mark 16:15-18 in the King James. Ether 4:18 uses the same material.
Mark 16:9-20 is called the long ending. It is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Most textual scholars judge it a second-century addition.

Book of Mormon Central's KnoWhy 522 gives two lines. First, a minority of credentialed scholars outside the church defend the long ending as authentic — Nicholas Lunn and James Snapp, on patristic and internal grounds. Second, even if it is a later addition, Moroni was quoting the Nephite record. The risen Lord could give the same commission in both hemispheres.
Genuinely arguable, and the second answer is hard to disprove. Lunn and Snapp are real scholars with published defences. But they are a minority. On the majority view the problem stands.
"Do you know the story behind the last twelve verses of Mark?"

refwhy.Mark 16:15–18: The long ending of Mark. Absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and judged a later addition by most scholars.
refwhy.Mormon 9:22–24: The Nephite commission. Read it beside Mark: devils, new tongues, serpents, deadly drink, the sick recovering.
refwhy.Ether 4:18: The shorter echo — 'he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved.' Same disputed passage, used twice.

titleLong: Moroni quotes the disputed 'long ending' of Mark
responseLead: Some non-LDS scholars defend Mark's long ending, and the risen Lord could commission twice.
rationaleLead: Your case holds on the standard view, but their minority answer for Mark is real.

title: Horses pulling chariots, on a horseless continent
claim: The Book of Mormon repeatedly describes horses among Jaredites and Nephites, from about 2500 BC to AD 400, including horses harnessed to 'chariots' — 1 Nephi 18:25, Enos 1:21, Alma 18:9-12, 3 Nephi 3:22 and Ether 9:19. Equids went extinct in the Americas around 10,000 BC and were reintroduced by the Spanish in the sixteenth century. Despite extensive archaeological and paleontological sampling, no verified pre-Columbian Holocene horse remains, depictions or loanwords exist. The related Old World animals the text names — cattle, oxen, asses, swine and the elephants of Ether 9:19 — face the same null record.

sources.name: Michael D. Coe, 'Mormons and Archaeology: An Outside View,' Dialogue 8:2 (1973); Mormon Stories interviews (2011, 2018)
Mormonr, 'Anachronisms in the Book of Mormon' (documents the state of evidence)

response:
Book of Mormon Central and FAIR offer three lines.

The word 'horse' may be a loanshift. That is a familiar label placed on a native animal such as a deer or a tapir. Spaniards and native peoples did exactly that with animals they had not seen before.

Small pockets of horses may also have survived into Book of Mormon times unnoticed. Wade Miller has had candidate late-dated remains tested. And a blank record counts for little in the tropics, where bone rarely survives.

responseSource.name: Book of Mormon Central, KnoWhy: 'Why Are Horses Mentioned in the Book of Mormon?'

rationale: No verified pre-Columbian Holocene horse has ever been produced. Radiocarbon tests on candidate remains come back either Ice Age or after contact. The loanshift defence grants the core point. No actual horses were there. And the horses harnessed to chariots resist the tapir reading, because a chariot needs a draught animal. Michael Coe of Yale set the problem out in Dialogue in 1973.

plain.d: Horses among the Jaredites and Nephites, from about 2500 BC to AD 400. Some are harnessed to chariots. See 1 Nephi 18:25, Enos 1:21, Alma 18:9-12, 3 Nephi 3:22 and Ether 9:19.

Horses died out in the Americas around 10,000 BC. The Spanish brought them back in the 1500s. In between there are no verified remains, no pictures and no words for them. The same blank covers cattle, oxen, asses, swine, and the elephants of Ether 9:19.

Book of Mormon Central and FAIR give three lines. Horse may be a loanshift — a familiar word used for a native animal such as a deer or a tapir. Spaniards and native peoples did exactly that with unfamiliar animals. Small groups of horses may also have survived unnoticed; Wade Miller has had candidate remains tested. And bones rot fast in tropical soil.

No verified pre-Columbian horse has been produced. Tested candidates came back either Ice Age or after Columbus. The loanshift answer concedes that no actual horses were there. And it strains at the chariots, which need a draught animal.
Strong for you, but give the loanshift answer first and give it fairly. Michael Coe, a Yale archaeologist, laid the problem out in Dialogue in 1973.
"Has one pre-Columbian horse bone ever dated to Book of Mormon times?"

refwhy.1 Nephi 18:25: The arrival list — 'the cow and the ox, and the ass and the horse' found waiting in the promised land.
refwhy.Enos 1:21: Nephite herds, 'and also many horses.' Not one stray mention. The claim recurs.
refwhy.Alma 18:9–12: The hardest verse for the tapir answer. Ammon prepares the king's 'horses and chariots' — an animal in harness.
refwhy.3 Nephi 3:22: Whole populations moving with 'their horses, and their chariots.' Horses at scale, not as a curiosity.
refwhy.Ether 9:19: Adds elephants, and two names left as 'cureloms and cumoms.' The blank record covers the elephants too.

titleLong: Horses (and chariots) in pre-Columbian America
responseLead: The word horse may be a borrowed label for a native beast, and bone rots fast.
rationaleLead: Strong for you, but the loanshift answer is fair and belongs in your mouth first.

title: Steel swords, in a continent without iron
claim: The Book of Mormon describes New World steel and iron working. Nephi carries a 'bow of steel' from Arabia. Nephites teach the making of 'steel' and working 'in all manner of iron,' around 590 to 400 BC. Jaredites have steel swords at Ether 7:9. Archaeology finds no ferrous metallurgy anywhere in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica — no smelting sites, no slag, no tools, no iron or steel weapons. Metallurgy of any kind appears in Mesoamerica only around AD 600 to 800, and it never included iron smelting.

sources.name: Michael D. Coe, 'Mormons and Archaeology: An Outside View,' Dialogue 8:2 (1973)
Deanne G. Matheny, 'Does the Shoe Fit? A Critique of the Limited Tehuantepec Geography,' in New Approaches to the Book of Mormon (1993)

response:
On the Old World half the defence is strong. The Vered Jericho sword is carburised steel, dated about 620 BC, and held in the Israel Museum. So 'most precious steel' was real in Lehi's Jerusalem. That is a genuine vindication.

For the New World, FAIR makes three points. 'Steel' in King James English can mean any hardened metal, and the King James uses it for Hebrew bronze. Mesoamericans did work meteoric iron. And a small Nephite industry could have left little trace, with its wording a loanshift.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Book of Mormon/Metals/Steel'; Book of Mormon Central, 'Laban's Steel Sword'

rationale:
The Old World steel is genuinely answered by the Vered Jericho sword. Concede that half plainly.

The other half is not answered. A Nephite and Jaredite iron and steel industry in the Americas has no support in the ground at all. Michael Coe and Deanne Matheny have both pressed this.

The word-meaning defence grants that no real steel was there. Yet the text has people being taught to make it.

plain.d: Nephi's "bow of steel" carried from Arabia. Nephites teaching people to make steel and to work "in all manner of iron," around 590 to 400 BC. And Jaredite steel swords at Ether 7:9.
The Old World half and the New World half are different arguments. Keep them apart. One of them is answered and one is not.

plain.t: The Old World half is answered
plain.d: A carburised steel sword was dug up at Vered Jericho in Israel, dated about 620 BC. It is in the Israel Museum. So real steel existed in Lehi's Jerusalem. Concede that plainly.

Archaeology finds no iron working anywhere in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica. No smelting sites, no slag, no tools, no iron or steel weapons. Metalwork of any kind shows up only around AD 600 to 800, and it never included smelting iron.

FAIR notes that steel in King James English can mean any hardened metal; the King James uses it for Hebrew bronze. Mesoamericans did work meteoric iron. And a small Nephite industry might leave little trace. Michael Coe and Deanne Matheny have both pressed the other way.
"I'll grant you Laban's sword. What about the iron industry in America?"

refwhy.1 Nephi 4:9: Laban's sword of 'most precious steel.' This is the Old World half, and the Vered Jericho find answers it.
refwhy.1 Nephi 16:18: Nephi's bow 'made of fine steel,' broken in Arabia. Old World again, so concede it plainly.
refwhy.2 Nephi 5:15: The New World half. Nephi teaches his people to work in iron and steel, in America.
refwhy.Jarom 1:8: An industry, not a relic. Iron, copper, brass and steel worked into tools and weapons of war.
refwhy.Ether 7:9: Jaredite swords 'molten out of the hill.' That is smelting, which is what the archaeology does not find.

titleLong: Steel and an iron industry in the pre-Columbian New World
responseLead: The Vered Jericho sword proves Old World steel, and 'steel' can mean any hard metal.
rationaleLead: Split it: the Old World half is answered, the iron in America is not.

title: Wheat, barley and silkworms in ancient America
claim: The Book of Mormon describes Nephites and Jaredites cultivating wheat and barley and producing silk — Mosiah 9:9, Alma 1:29, Ether 9:17 and Ether 10:24. Old World wheat (Triticum), barley (Hordeum vulgare) and silkworm sericulture are absent from the pre-Columbian archaeological and botanical record. New World agriculture centred on maize, beans and squash. Barley is also embedded in the text's Mosaic-law economy at Alma 11:7 and 11:15 — a system of weights, not coins. The 'coins' chapter heading was a twentieth-century editorial addition, since corrected.

sources.name: Michael D. Coe, Dialogue 8:2 (1973) and subsequent interviews
Debunking-CES-Letter (apologetic) and CES Letter exchange documenting the dispute

response: Apologists point to little barley, Hordeum pusillum. It is now confirmed as a farmed grain in pre-Columbian North America. Nobody knew that in 1830. So barley is no longer a clean anachronism. FAIR defends wheat and silk as loanshifts. A familiar label could stand for a like native grain such as amaranth. It could also stand for fine local fibres, like kapok, and the wild-silk cloth attested in Mesoamerica.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Principles for assessing anachronisms'

rationale: The little-barley find gives their case real traction, even though the species has shifted. Wild-silk cloth is genuinely attested too. Hand both over. Old World wheat is still unattested anywhere. And the loanshift answer again grants that the named plant was absent. The dispute is real, but lopsided. Michael Coe set out the first form of the problem in Dialogue in 1973.

plain.d: Nephites and Jaredites growing wheat and barley, and producing silk. See Mosiah 9:9, Alma 1:29, Ether 9:17 and Ether 10:24.
Old World wheat, barley and silkworm farming are absent from the pre-Columbian record. Farming in the Americas ran on maize, beans and squash.

plain.t: One point in their favour first
plain.d: Barley is built into the measures at Alma 11:7 and 11:15. Those are weights, not coins. The word coins was a twentieth-century chapter heading, and the church has since corrected it. Do not repeat the coins version.

Domesticated little barley, Hordeum pusillum, has since been confirmed as a cultivated grain in pre-Columbian North America. Nobody knew that in 1830. So barley is no longer a clean anachronism. FAIR defends wheat and silk as loanshifts too. A familiar word could stand for a native grain such as amaranth. Or for fine local fibres like kapok, and the wild-silk cloth attested in Mesoamerica.

Genuinely arguable, and lopsided. The little-barley find is a real point for them, and wild silk is attested. Old World wheat is still unattested anywhere. And the loanshift answer again grants that the named thing was not there. Michael Coe set out the original problem.
"The barley one has a real answer. Where does the wheat come from?"

refwhy.Mosiah 9:9: The seed list: 'corn, and of wheat, and of barley,' plus neas and sheum. Wheat is the unanswered one.
refwhy.Alma 11:7,15: Partly helps them. Barley runs the Nephite weights, and little barley was in fact farmed in ancient North America.
refwhy.Alma 1:29: Nephites with 'abundance of silk and fine-twined linen.' This is the silk half of the claim.
refwhy.Ether 9:17: Jaredite 'silks' and fine linen. The wild-silk answer has to stretch back this far too.
refwhy.Ether 10:24: Jaredites weaving 'silks, and fine-twined linen.' The second silk text, so one answer must cover both peoples.

titleLong: Old World crops and fabrics: wheat, barley, silk
responseLead: Little barley was farmed here before Columbus, and wheat and silk may be borrowed labels.
rationaleLead: Arguable and lopsided: barley is a real win for them, Old World wheat is not.

title: Timothy and Jonas, Greek names in a Hebrew colony
claim: The Book of Mormon has Greek names in a Hebrew colony. Timothy and Jonas appear at 3 Nephi 19:4. Lachoneus appears at 3 Nephi 1:1; the name means 'the Laconian.' At 3 Nephi 9:18 the risen Jesus calls himself 'Alpha and Omega.' Those are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. The phrase is drawn from Revelation 1:8. But Lehi's people left Jerusalem in 600 BC and wrote in 'reformed Egyptian.' They had no Greek contact.

sources.name: Ricks/Nibley exchange records (B.H. Roberts Foundation)
Grant H. Palmer, An Insider's View of Mormon Origins

response:
Hugh Nibley and Stephen Ricks argue that Greeks were already in Lehi's world. From the mid-600s BC, Ionian and Carian soldiers and traders served Egypt. They fought in the army of Necho II and worked across the Levant.

So a Greek name could reach Lehi's people, and more easily the Mulekites. There is a second line too. 'Timothy', 'Jonas' and 'Alpha and Omega' may be the translator's English stand-ins for Nephite names and sayings.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'What is known about the name Lachoneus in the Book of Mormon?'

rationale:
The mercenary reply rests on real history. Greeks were in Egypt and the Levant in the 600s BC. And the stand-in reading works well for 'Alpha and Omega'.

Two things still fit an 1829 writer better. One is 'Lachoneus' as a personal name. The other is wording that matches Revelation exactly. Grant Palmer made that case.

Neither side has a decisive case here, and this is a small point.

plain.d: Greek personal names in a Hebrew colony. Timothy and Jonas at 3 Nephi 19:4. Lachoneus at 3 Nephi 1:1, a name meaning the Laconian. And the risen Jesus calling himself "Alpha and Omega" at 3 Nephi 9:18.
Alpha and omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. The phrase comes from Revelation 1:8. A colony that left Jerusalem in 600 BC and wrote in reformed Egyptian had no Greek contact.

Hugh Nibley and Stephen Ricks point to real history. From the mid-600s BC, Ionian and Carian mercenaries and traders served in Egypt, including in Necho II's army, and moved across the Levant. Greek names could reach Lehi's people, or more easily the Mulekites. They add that Timothy, Jonas and "Alpha and Omega" may be the translator's English stand-ins for Nephite equivalents.

Genuinely arguable, and this is a small case. The mercenary history is real. Substitution works well for "Alpha and Omega." Lachoneus as a personal name, and the exact match with Revelation, still fit an 1829 writer more easily. Grant Palmer made that case.
"Where would a Nephite have picked up the Greek alphabet?"

refwhy.Revelation 1:8: Where the phrase comes from. The wording matches, which is the point: John's Greek in a Nephite mouth.
refwhy.3 Nephi 1:1: Names Lachoneus as chief judge. The name looks like Greek for 'the Laconian,' a Spartan.
refwhy.3 Nephi 19:4: The list of twelve disciples. Timothy and Jonas are Greek names, in a list of Nephite ones.
refwhy.3 Nephi 9:18: The risen Jesus says 'I am Alpha and Omega' — Greek letters, to a people with no Greek.

titleLong: Greek names and Greek-alphabet expressions in a Hebrew-Egyptian colony
responseLead: Greek soldiers served Egypt from the 600s BC, so Greek names could reach Lehi's world.
rationaleLead: A small case, and the Greek trade history is real; Lachoneus still fits 1829 better.

title: The word 'Bible' on Nephi's lips, centuries too early
claim: The text uses institutional terms that postdate its setting. 'Church' describes Jerusalem in 600 BC at 1 Nephi 4:26, and formal Nephite institutions before Christ. 'Synagogues' appear at 2 Nephi 26:26, Alma 16:13 and Alma 21:4-6, before the institution developed after the exile. And Nephi uses the word 'Bible' at 2 Nephi 29:3-10 — a term from the Greek biblia, first applied to the scriptural codex centuries after Christ. That passage anticipates and rebuts a nineteenth-century objection: 'A Bible! A Bible! We have got a Bible.'

sources.name: Documented criticism (Fraser, Whalen et al.) via B.H. Roberts Foundation records
MormonThink, 'Book of Mormon Difficulties'

response:
FAIR responds that 'church' and 'synagogue' are the translator's English words for whatever gatherings the Nephites had. The King James is loose with 'church' in the same way.

Lee Levine, who studies synagogues, allows for shared worship before the exile, in settings such as the gate chambers.

And 'Bible' appears inside an open prophecy of the latter days. Naming a future thing is exactly the point of such a prophecy.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Book of Mormon/Anachronisms/Buildings' and 'Book of Mormon/Synagogues'

rationale:
Take 'church' and 'synagogue' as words only. Any theory of translation handles them. Translators always use their own words for groups and buildings. So do not press those two.

That answer does sit oddly beside Skousen's tight-control evidence.

2 Nephi 29 is different. Its 'Bible' passage answers critics of the 1830s in their own words. That reads better as 1830s writing than as prophecy.

plain.d: Church, used of Jerusalem in 600 BC at 1 Nephi 4:26. It is used of formal Nephite bodies too. Synagogues, at 2 Nephi 26:26 and Alma 16:13. Those did not exist until after the exile. And the word Bible, on Nephi's lips at 2 Nephi 29:3-10.

plain.t: Why the third one is different
plain.d: The word Bible comes from the Greek biblia. It was first used for the bound book long after Christ. And that passage answers an 1830s objection in its own words: "A Bible! A Bible! We have got a Bible."

FAIR says the first two are just the translator's English. He had to call Nephite meetings something. The King James is loose with church too. Lee Levine, who studies synagogues, allows for shared worship before the exile in the gate chambers. And Bible sits inside a prophecy about the last days. Knowing a future thing is the point of it.

Weak on the first two words. Worth a look on the third. Any translator uses his own words for groups and buildings. So do not press those two. 2 Nephi 29 is different. It argues with critics who were not yet born.
"Who is Nephi arguing with in 2 Nephi 29?"

refwhy.1 Nephi 4:26: 'The brethren of the church' in Jerusalem, 600 BC. The weakest of the three. Any translator needs some word here.
refwhy.2 Nephi 26:26: 'Out of the synagogues,' long before there were any. Also weak. This is likely just the translator's word.
refwhy.Alma 16:13: Synagogues 'built after the manner of the Jews.' Harder than bare vocabulary, but still arguable.
refwhy.Alma 21:4–6: Synagogues built by a rival sect. Here the word names a real institution, not just a loose label.
refwhy.2 Nephi 29:3–10: The strong one. Nephi answers 'A Bible! A Bible! We have got a Bible' — an argument of the 1820s.

titleLong: Anachronistic institutional terms: 'church,' 'synagogue,' 'Bible'
responseLead: Those first two words are the translator's own, and the Bible line sits in a prophecy.
rationaleLead: Weak on the first two words; 2 Nephi 29 is the only part worth pressing.

title: Galatians 1:8 versus the angel Moroni
claim: Two arguments get made together, and only one of them works. The first says the Book of Mormon is "another gospel" under Paul's warning in Galatians 1:8, where even an angel from heaven preaching a different gospel is accursed — which critics apply straight to the angel Moroni. The second says adding to scripture breaks the closing warnings of Revelation 22:18-19 and Deuteronomy 4:2. Whether the first lands depends entirely on whether the gospel content actually differs, which is what the doctrinal cases on this site examine.
bom: Introduction ('the fulness of the everlasting gospel')

sources.name: CARM, 'The Gospel According to Mormonism'
Mormonism Research Ministry, 'Does Revelation 22:18 Condemn the Book of Mormon?'
pursueGOD, 'Mormonism Exposed by the Book of Galatians'

response: Three replies, and the first two are strong. Revelation 22:18 warns against tampering with 'the words of the prophecy of this book'. That means Revelation itself. It was a standard closing curse on a single ancient scroll. Revelation was not even the last book written. And the same logic applied to Deuteronomy 4:2 would cancel everything after Deuteronomy. Many evangelical scholars agree. Second, the warning is about men adding to scripture. It is not about God speaking again. Third, Galatians 1:8 condemns a different gospel. Latter-day Saints hold that the Book of Mormon teaches the same Christ crucified. On their reading the argument assumes what it is trying to prove.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Latter-day Saint scripture and the closed canon'

rationale:
The Revelation 22:18 version is the weakest form of this argument. Christians should stop using it. Most textual scholars agree the curse is scoped to Revelation, and the Deuteronomy comparison lands.

The Galatians 1:8 form survives that reply. But it settles nothing on its own. It turns on whether the gospel content actually matches. That sends you to the doctrinal cases, on grace and on exaltation.

Not a standalone argument. Not answered either.

plain.t: The two verses Christians reach for
plain.d: Galatians 1:8 — "though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you… let him be accursed" — applied to the angel Moroni. And Revelation 22:18, warning against adding to the book.

plain.t: Be careful with the second one
plain.d: Revelation 22:18 says "the words of the prophecy of this book." That means Revelation itself. It is a standard closing curse for one ancient scroll. Revelation was not even the last book of the New Testament written. Using it to shut the whole Bible is bad reading, and your friend will say so.

plain.t: Where the first verse does work
plain.d: Galatians 1:8 is different. It does not say an angel cannot appear. It grants the possibility and removes its authority: the message is tested by the gospel already delivered. And Paul includes himself — though we — which makes it a test rather than a weapon.
Arguable both ways. The canon half fails. The Galatians half holds — and it holds against us too.
"I'd have to reject an angel with a new gospel too. Paul puts himself under that rule."

refwhy.Galatians 1:6–9: The verse that works. Paul puts himself and an angel alike under the test of the gospel already given.
refwhy.Revelation 22:18–19: Does not prove what people think. The warning is about 'this book,' meaning Revelation, not the whole Bible.
refwhy.Deuteronomy 4:2: Shows why that argument fails. The same warning sits here, and nobody thinks it closed the Old Testament.
refwhy.Jude 3: 'The faith which was once delivered unto the saints.' Cited for a closed canon, but it is about teaching, not a book list.
refwhy.Hebrews 1:1–2: God 'hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.' Used to argue the last word has been given.
refwhy.Introduction ('the fulness of the everla: The book's own claim to hold the fulness of the gospel. That claim is what Galatians is being used to test.
refwhy.1 Nephi 13:34–40: Their frame: plain and precious parts were 'kept back,' so a further book was needed.
refwhy.3 Nephi 27:13–21: Cuts against you. Jesus here defines the gospel as the cross, repentance, baptism and enduring — which sounds familiar.

titleLong: The 'another gospel' / closed-canon argument
responseLead: The closing curse seals one scroll only, and the Galatians point assumes what it must prove.
rationaleLead: Drop the canon half; the Galatians half holds, and it tests us too.

title: Salvation by grace, 'after all we can do'
claim: 2 Nephi 25:23 says "it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do." Moroni 10:32 adds that you must deny yourself of all ungodliness, and then his grace is sufficient. Critics read both as making grace conditional on human effort first. The Bible says the opposite in Ephesians 2:8-9 — saved by grace through faith, and not of works, so that no one can boast. The disagreement is not about whether obedience matters. It is about whether it is the ground of salvation or the fruit of it.

left.text: For we labor diligently to write, to persuade our children, and also our brethren, to believe in Christ, and to be reconciled to God; for we know that it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.

right.text: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.

comparison.note: The whole dispute lives in two phrases: the Bible's 'not of works' against the Book of Mormon's 'after all we can do.'

sources.name: Mormonism Research Ministry, 'How Has 2 Nephi 25:23 Been Interpreted?'
Mormonism Research Ministry, 'Saved by Grace "In Spite Of" All We Can Do?'
LDS Fact Check, 'Why 2 Nephi 25:23 and Ephesians 2:8 Can't Both Be True'

response: Four replies. Stephen Robinson of BYU and Royal Skousen read 'after all we can do' as an old turn of phrase. It means in spite of all we can do. Grace saves despite our failure, not after our success. In 2015 Dieter Uchtdorf of the First Presidency preached that 'after' does not mean 'because'. Salvation is not earned by hitting a quota. Third, in context Nephi's point is that the law of Moses is dead and only grace saves. Fourth, John Welch reads the verse against the covenant framing of Mosiah 4.

responseSource.name: BYU ScholarsArchive, '"After All We Can Do" (2 Nephi 25:23)'

rationale: The 'in spite of' reading is possible in English, and after Uchtdorf it is close to official. That genuinely narrows the gap. Christians who ignore it are arguing with a position the church no longer holds. Two things keep the criticism alive. The new reading is late. From Joseph Fielding Smith through Kimball and McConkie, the standard reading was conditional. And Moroni 10:32 sets a condition in its grammar that no idiom removes. Deny yourselves of all ungodliness, then is his grace sufficient. Neither side lands a knockout.

plain.d: 2 Nephi 25:23 — "it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do." Moroni 10:32 adds: deny yourselves of all ungodliness, then is his grace sufficient.
It reads like a condition. Your own maximum effort first, then God covers the gap. Ephesians 2:8-9 says the opposite — saved by grace through faith, "not of works, lest any man should boast."

Stephen Robinson of BYU says "after all we can do" is an old turn of phrase. He reads it as in spite of all we can do. And in 2015 Dieter Uchtdorf, of the First Presidency, preached grace in words most evangelicals would recognise.

Arguable both ways. The old-phrase reading is fair. The modern preaching is real. But ask what the system asks of a member in practice. Temple worthiness. Interviews. Ordinances. Then see if that matches the sermon.
"When you stand before God, what are you resting on?"

refwhy.Ephesians 2:8–9: The reply text: saved by grace through faith, 'not of works, lest any man should boast.'
refwhy.Romans 11:6: Paul's either/or. If by grace, 'then is it no more of works.' The two do not blend.
refwhy.Romans 4:4–5: Wages against gift. God 'justifieth the ungodly,' which is the opposite of paying for a finished effort.
refwhy.Titus 3:5: 'Not by works of righteousness which we have done' — saved by mercy instead.
refwhy.Galatians 2:21: The stake. If righteousness comes by law, 'then Christ is dead in vain.'
refwhy.2 Nephi 25:23: The verse the case turns on: 'it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.'
refwhy.Moroni 10:32–33: The harder verse. Deny yourselves of all ungodliness, and 'then is his grace sufficient.' No idiom removes that.
refwhy.Alma 11:37: Amulek says God 'cannot save them in their sins.' Read as a limit on grace, though Christians say much the same.

titleLong: Salvation by grace 'after all we can do' vs. grace apart from works
responseLead: Robinson and Uchtdorf read the verse as grace in spite of all we can do.
rationaleLead: A draw: their newer reading is fair, but Moroni 10:32 still sets a test first.

title: 'A skin of blackness' — 2 Nephi 5:21
claim: The Book of Mormon teaches that God cursed the Lamanites with 'a skin of blackness' so they would not be enticing to the righteous Nephites (2 Nephi 5:21-23). Alma 3:6-9 marks their descendants the same way, and 3 Nephi 2:14-15 describes converted Lamanites' skin becoming white. Jacob 3:8-9 and Mormon 5:15 belong with these. That contradicts the biblical teaching that God made all nations of one blood (Acts 17:26). It contradicts Acts 10:34-35, where he shows no partiality, and 1 Samuel 16:7, where he looks on the heart rather than the outward appearance. Galatians 3:28, John 7:24 and Revelation 7:9 point the same way. The church's own edits are cited as tacit admission that the racial reading is the natural one. In 1981, 'white and delightsome' became 'pure and delightsome' at 2 Nephi 30:6. In 2010, racial language was removed from the chapter headings of 2 Nephi 5 and Mormon 5.

left.text: And he had caused the cursing to come upon them, yea, even a sore cursing, because of their iniquity… wherefore, as they were white, and exceedingly fair and delightsome, that they might not be enticing unto my people the Lord God did cause a skin of blackness to come upon them.

right.text: And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation.

comparison.note: No biblical passage ties skin color to covenant standing; the church's 2013 'Race and the Priesthood' essay disavows the theory the verse plainly states.

sources.name: Salt Lake Tribune, 'Church removes racial references in Book of Mormon headings' (2010)
Rational Faiths, '"White and Delightsome": Racism in the Book of Mormon'
CES Letter (Jeremy Runnells), Book of Mormon section

response:
Scripture Central and recent BYU work argue that 'skin of blackness' may be a figure of speech. Ethan Sproat and Gerrit Steenblik read it as garments and marks the Lamanites took on. On that reading the curse itself is being cut off from the Lord at 2 Nephi 5:20. The mark is a separate thing.

FAIR notes that the book itself condemns Nephite racism. Jacob 3:5-9 calls the Lamanites more righteous. In some scenes the two peoples cannot be told apart, which a stark skin difference would prevent.

The heading edits fixed 1981 study helps by Bruce R. McConkie, not the revealed text. And the 2013 Gospel Topics essay 'Race and the Priesthood' disavows the idea that dark skin marks God's disfavour.

responseSource.name: Scripture Central, 'What Is the "Skin of Blackness" in the Book of Mormon?'

rationale:
The figure-of-speech and garment reading is a late development. It cuts against nearly two centuries of the church's own teaching. Brigham Young taught the plain reading. So did Spencer W. Kimball, who reported Lamanite converts growing lighter.

The text's own chain resists it too. Cursed because of iniquity, therefore a skin of blackness, so they would not be enticing. 3 Nephi 2:15 has the curse and the skin change together.

The 2013 disavowal grants the criticism against the plain sense. It does not refute it.

plain.d: 2 Nephi 5:21 says God cursed the Lamanites with "a skin of blackness," so they would not be "enticing" to the Nephites. Alma 3:6-9 marks their descendants. 3 Nephi 2:14-15 has converted Lamanites becoming white. Jacob 3:8-9 and Mormon 5:15 belong with these.

Acts 17:26 says God made all nations "of one blood." Acts 10:34-35 says he shows no partiality. 1 Samuel 16:7 says he looks on the heart. Galatians 3:28, John 7:24 and Revelation 7:9 point the same way.

plain.t: What the church itself has changed
plain.d: In 1981, "white and delightsome" became "pure and delightsome" at 2 Nephi 30:6. In 2010, racial wording came out of the chapter headings of 2 Nephi 5 and Mormon 5. In 2013 the Gospel Topics essay Race and the Priesthood disavowed the idea that dark skin marks God's disfavour.

Scripture Central, with the BYU scholars Ethan Sproat and Gerrit Steenblik, argue that "skin of blackness" may be a metaphor, or may mean garments and marks the Lamanites took on. On that reading the curse is separation from the Lord in 2 Nephi 5:20, and the mark is a separate thing. FAIR adds that the book itself condemns Nephite racism — Jacob 3:5-9 calls the Lamanites more righteous. In some episodes the two peoples cannot be told apart, which a stark skin difference would prevent. And the headings were 1981 study helps by Bruce R. McConkie, not scripture.

Strong for you, and this is one to make gently. The garment reading is recent. It cuts against nearly two centuries of the church's own teaching, from Brigham Young to Spencer W. Kimball, who reported Lamanite converts growing lighter. And the text's own chain resists it: cursed for iniquity, therefore a skin of blackness, so they would not be enticing.
"Read me 2 Nephi 5:21. What does it say the curse actually was?"

refwhy.Acts 17:26: God 'hath made of one blood all nations.' The clearest biblical answer to a curse marked on skin.
refwhy.Acts 10:34–35: Peter says God 'is no respecter of persons,' and accepts people in every nation.
refwhy.1 Samuel 16:7: God 'looketh on the heart,' not the outward appearance. The exact opposite of skin as a mark.
refwhy.Galatians 3:28: 'Neither Jew nor Greek… ye are all one in Christ Jesus.' The gospel erases the line this curse draws.
refwhy.John 7:24: 'Judge not according to the appearance.' Short, and it lands right on this.
refwhy.Revelation 7:9: The end of the story. Every nation and tongue stands before the throne, all in white robes.
refwhy.2 Nephi 5:21–23: The verse the case rests on. A 'skin of blackness' comes 'because of their iniquity,' so they would not be 'enticing.'
refwhy.Alma 3:6–9: Ties dark skin to a 'mark' set on the fathers. It puts the same curse on anyone who marries in.
refwhy.3 Nephi 2:14–15: The reverse. 'Their curse was taken from them, and their skin became white.' Curse and colour move together.
refwhy.Jacob 3:8–9: Cuts partly against you. Jacob rebukes Nephite racism, and says Lamanite skins may be whiter at the judgment.
refwhy.2 Nephi 30:6 (1830/1981 variants): The 1981 edit. 'White and delightsome' became 'pure and delightsome.' The church changed the wording itself.
refwhy.Mormon 5:15: 'A dark, a filthy, and a loathsome people.' The same link runs to the end of the book.

titleLong: Dark skin as a divine curse (and the modern text and heading edits)
responseLead: The mark may mean garments, and the church disavowed the racial reading in 2013.
rationaleLead: Strong for you, but make it gently: the garment reading is recent, the old teaching plain.

title: The Fall as a blessing, not a disaster
claim: 2 Nephi 2:22-25 teaches that Adam's fall was necessary and good. Without it Adam and Eve 'would have had no children,' and 'Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy.' Alma 12:22-26 follows the same line. Critics argue this contradicts the Bible, which presents the fall as sin bringing death and condemnation (Romans 5:12-19, Romans 8:20-22), never as the enabling condition of procreation. God commanded 'be fruitful, and multiply' at Genesis 1:28, before the fall. That makes the Book of Mormon's premise a direct contradiction, and makes God the author of a transgression he forbade in the same breath. 1 Timothy 2:14 and 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 point the same way.

sources.name: Christian Research Institute, '2 Nephi 2 in the Book of Mormon'
Creation Ministries International, 'The Fall: a "glorious necessity"?!'
Mormonism Research Ministry, 'Citations on the Fall'

response: The BYU Religious Studies Center, in 'The Fortunate Fall of Adam and Eve', places this doctrine inside the old Christian felix culpa tradition, the happy fault. Ambrose taught it. Augustine wrote 'O felix culpa'. The Easter Exsultet still sings it. On that tradition the fall makes room for a greater good, the Incarnation. So a fall inside God's plan is not foreign to Christian faith. Scripture Central adds that Lehi's point is structural. Mortal life, choice and the capacity for joy all need a world built on opposition. 2 Nephi 2:11 says exactly that. They also call the fall a transgression of a lesser law rather than sin in the fullest sense. Some Christian theologians draw the same line. And Eve is honoured here rather than blamed.

responseSource.name: BYU Religious Studies Center, 'The Fortunate Fall of Adam and Eve'

rationale: The felix culpa parallel is a genuine steelman. Christians have long held that God brings a greater good out of the fall. Concede that at once. It does not reach the claim actually made here. 2 Nephi 2 says the fall was needed for children to be born. Genesis 1:28 has God command 'be fruitful, and multiply' before the fall. The text also says Adam and Eve would have stayed in innocence, having no joy. So the old tradition celebrates rescue in spite of the fall. 2 Nephi 2 makes the fall itself necessary. That is a different claim, and Genesis 1:28 still has no strong published answer.

plain.d: 2 Nephi 2:22-25 says Adam's fall was necessary and good. Without it, Adam and Eve "would have had no children." And "Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy." Alma 12:22-26 takes the same line.
Romans 5:12-19 treats the fall as sin. It brought death and condemnation, not joy. Romans 8:20-22 says creation was subjected to futility by it.

plain.t: The verse that does the work
plain.d: Genesis 1:28. God told Adam and Eve to "be fruitful, and multiply" before the fall. So the premise that there could be no children without the fall runs straight into that command.

And it is a real one. The BYU Religious Studies Center points to the felix culpa tradition — the happy fault. Ambrose taught it. Augustine wrote "O felix culpa." The Easter Exsultet sings it. Christians have long said God brings a greater good out of the fall. Scripture Central adds 2 Nephi 2:11: agency and joy need a world with opposition in it. And Eve is honoured here rather than blamed.

Genuinely arguable, and narrower than critics usually make it. Concede the felix culpa point at once. But notice the difference. That tradition celebrates redemption despite the fall. 2 Nephi 2 makes the fall itself necessary. Genesis 1:28 still has no strong published answer.
"God says be fruitful in Genesis 1:28. That's before the fall, isn't it?"

refwhy.Genesis 1:28: The verse that does the work. 'Be fruitful, and multiply' is spoken before the fall, not after.
refwhy.Genesis 2:17: The command Adam broke. It frames the fall as disobedience, with death as the penalty.
refwhy.Romans 5:12–19: Paul's account. Sin and death entered by one man, and judgment came 'to condemnation.' Not a happy event.
refwhy.Romans 8:20–22: Creation 'made subject to vanity,' and groaning. The fall as damage, not as a needed step.
refwhy.1 Timothy 2:14: Paul calls the fall a transgression, brought on by deception. Nothing here treats it as a blessing.
refwhy.1 Corinthians 15:21–22: 'By man came death.' Paul makes the fall the problem Christ answers, not part of the plan.
refwhy.2 Nephi 2:22–25: The core text. Without the fall they 'would have had no children,' and 'Adam fell that men might be.'
refwhy.Alma 12:22–26: Alma takes the same line. The fall made this life a 'probationary state,' so it had to happen.

titleLong: The Fall as necessary blessing vs. the Fall as catastrophe
responseLead: Christians have long taught the happy fault, and Augustine wrote 'O felix culpa' himself.
rationaleLead: Their happy fault point is real, but the Genesis 1:28 command still has no answer.

title: Moroni 8: infant baptism is 'solemn mockery'
claim: Moroni 8 declares that little children 'are not capable of committing sin.' It calls infant baptism 'solemn mockery before God.' And it says that anyone who supposes children need baptism 'must go down to hell' if he dies in that thought (Moroni 8:8-23). Mosiah 3:16-21 and 2 Nephi 2:25 support it. Critics set this against the Bible. Psalm 51:5 says we are sinful from conception. Ephesians 2:3 calls us 'by nature the children of wrath.' Romans 5:12 and 18-19 say we are condemned in Adam, and so do Genesis 8:21, Psalm 58:3 and 1 Corinthians 15:22. Critics add two points. The position mirrors the Pelagian controversy settled in AD 418. And damning most of historic Christendom, which practised infant baptism, goes far past any biblical warrant.

sources.name: Department of Christian Defense, Book of Mormon theology analyses
LDS Scripture Teachings, 'Moroni 8, Pelagius, and Questions about Infant Baptism'
Improvement Era (critical analysis), 'When Rhetoric Overpowers Revelation: Moroni 8'

response: FAIR makes three points, and they land. First, the Bible never commands infant baptism and never shows one. Baptists and most evangelicals agree with Moroni's practical result. So this is not simply Bible against Book of Mormon. It tracks a fight among Christians. Second, treating original sin as inherited guilt comes from Augustine. Eastern Orthodoxy rejects inherited guilt and keeps only a fallen nature and death. Psalm 51:5 is David's poetry about how deep sin runs, not a rule about infant guilt. Third, Latter-day Saints teach that Christ's atonement covers Adam's fall for children with no conditions. Moroni 8:8 says the curse of Adam is taken from them in him. So children are redeemed, not merely innocent.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Plan of salvation/Original sin'

rationale:
As a proof-text fight the critics overreach. Infant baptism is disputed among Bible-believing Christians. So is inherited guilt. The Latter-day Saint reply finds real allies for parts of its case.

What survives is narrower but real. Moroni 8 sends infant-baptisers to hell. That condemns nearly all Christians before the Reformation, with a harshness no Bible text allows.

And the chapter argues a fight that came after the Bible, inside a text set in fourth-century America. The fight is Pelagius against Augustine, plus revival preaching in the 1800s. That shades into a question about where the text came from.

plain.d: That little children "are not capable of committing sin." That infant baptism is "solemn mockery before God." And that anyone who thinks children need baptism "must go down to hell" if he dies in that thought. See Moroni 8:8-23.
