plain.t: What the Bible is usually quoted back
plain.d: Psalm 51:5 says we are sinful from conception. Ephesians 2:3 calls us "by nature the children of wrath." Romans 5:12 and 18-19 say we are condemned in Adam.

FAIR makes three points, and they land. The Bible never commands infant baptism and never shows one. Baptists and most evangelicals end up where Moroni does. Second, the idea that we inherit Adam's guilt — and not just a fallen nature — comes from Augustine. The Eastern Orthodox reject it to this day. Third, Latter-day Saints teach that Christ covers Adam's fall for children, with no conditions. Moroni 8:8 says the curse of Adam is taken from them in him.

Not on infant baptism. Christians have argued that one among themselves for centuries. It stands on two narrower points. Moroni 8 sends almost every Christian before the Reformation to hell. No verse in the Bible allows that. And a record set in the fourth century is arguing a fight that belongs to Pelagius, to Augustine, and to revival preaching in the 1800s.
Do not use the simple version. If you argue Bible against Book of Mormon here, you will be arguing against a lot of Christians too. Use the narrow version or leave it.
"I don't baptise babies either. But why does Moroni send everyone who does to hell?"

refwhy.Psalm 51:5: 'In sin did my mother conceive me.' The usual proof-text. It is a psalm of confession, not a doctrine of infant guilt.
refwhy.Ephesians 2:3: 'By nature the children of wrath.' The strongest of the inherited-nature verses.
refwhy.Romans 5:12, 18–19: Condemnation came 'by one man's disobedience.' The verse the whole original-sin case leans on.
refwhy.Genesis 8:21: 'The imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth.' Note 'from his youth' — not from conception.
refwhy.Psalm 58:3: 'The wicked are estranged from the womb.' Poetry about the wicked, not a claim about every baby.
refwhy.1 Corinthians 15:22: 'As in Adam all die.' Cited for inherited death, which their side grants, so it settles little.
refwhy.Moroni 8:8–23: The passage at issue. Infant baptism is 'solemn mockery before God,' and those who teach it 'must go down to hell.'
refwhy.Mosiah 3:16–21: The same doctrine, put gently. Children are covered by 'the blood of Christ,' not by baptism.
refwhy.2 Nephi 2:25: 'Adam fell that men might be.' Supplies the frame in which children are born innocent, not guilty.

titleLong: Denial of original sin and damnation of infant-baptizers (Moroni 8)
responseLead: The Bible never commands infant baptism, and Baptists land where Moroni does.
rationaleLead: Do not use the simple version, or you will be arguing against many Christians too.

title: One God in 1830, many gods by 1844
claim: The Book of Mormon teaches strict monotheism, and its Father-Son unity is so tight that it reads as trinitarian or even modalist. Mosiah 15:1-5 says Christ is "the Father, because he was conceived by the power of God" and is "the Father and the Son… one God." Alma 11:26-29 states there is one God and no other. Alma 11:38-39 calls Christ the very Eternal Father. None of the doctrines that define later Mormonism appear anywhere in it — no plurality of gods, no eternal progression, no God with a body, no exaltation of humans.

sources.name: Mormonism Research Ministry, 'Modalism in the Book of Mormon'
Grant Palmer, An Insider's View of Mormon Origins, ch. 4
CES Letter (Jeremy Runnells), Book of Mormon section
James K. Walker, 'Re-imagining Elohim' (CESNUR 2004)

response:
David Paulsen and Ari Bruening of BYU argue the 1830 text is not modalist when read whole. It does tell Father and Son apart. The Father's voice introduces the Son in 3 Nephi 11, and Christ prays to the Father.

So its 'one God' language describes a unity of distinct persons. That is no further from later teaching than the New Testament's own 'one God' texts are from Nicaea.

Mosiah 15 is explained by divine investiture. Christ acts as Father by creation and covenant, and as Son in the flesh. The First Presidency set that out in 1916. Brant Gardner adds that the modalist ring may come from the limits of translation language.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Monotheism, Messiah, and Mormon's Book' (2003 FAIR Conference); Paulsen scholarship

rationale:
The narrow charge of modalism is genuinely arguable. Critics do sometimes overstate it. Paulsen really does find Father and Son told apart in the text.

The broader point survives anyway. The Book of Mormon insists on one eternal God. It says nothing at all about many gods, about eternal progression, about God having a body, or about people becoming gods. Those doctrines define mature Mormonism, and the 1830 book is silent on every one.

The 1916 divine-investiture framing exists because the plain text does not teach the later doctrine.

plain.t: What the Book of Mormon says about God
plain.d: It is strictly monotheistic, and the Father-Son unity is so tight it reads almost as one person in two roles. Mosiah 15:1-5 has Christ as "the Father and the Son… one God." Alma 11:26-29 says there is one God and no other.
That the Father, Son and Holy Ghost are three separate beings. That the Father has a body of flesh and bone. And that faithful people may become gods themselves.

David Paulsen of BYU says the 1830 text read whole is not modalist. It does tell Father and Son apart in other places. He adds that early Christian writers were loose with words too, before the councils tightened them.
Arguable on any one verse. Harder to argue with is the direction of travel. The 1830 book sounds much more like ordinary Christianity than 1844 does.
"Read me Alma 11:26-29 in your own book. How many Gods does it say there are?"

refwhy.Deuteronomy 6:4: 'The LORD our God is one LORD.' Israel's basic confession, and the standard being applied here.
refwhy.Isaiah 43:10: 'Before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.' It rules out gods who became gods.
refwhy.Isaiah 44:6–8: 'Beside me there is no God… I know not any.' The flattest denial of many gods in the Bible.
refwhy.John 10:30: 'I and my Father are one.' Cited because 3 Nephi 11:27 says the same thing in the same words.
refwhy.1 Timothy 2:5: 'There is one God, and one mediator.' New Testament monotheism, as plain as Alma 11.
refwhy.Mosiah 15:1–5: Abinadi says Christ is 'the Father and the Son… one God.' As tight a unity as anything in the Bible.
refwhy.Mosiah 16:15: Calls Christ 'the very Eternal Father.' Apologists use it too, to show the wording is not a slip.
refwhy.Alma 11:26–29, 38–39: The plainest exchange in the book. Zeezrom asks 'Is there more than one God?' Amulek answers 'No.'
refwhy.2 Nephi 31:21: Ends 'which is one God, without end.' It ties the one-God claim to the way of salvation.
refwhy.Mormon 7:7: Father, Son and Holy Ghost 'are one God.' The same formula near the close of the book.
refwhy.3 Nephi 11:27: Jesus gives the baptism words: 'the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost are one.'
refwhy.Testimony of Three Witnesses ('one God'): Printed at the front of every copy. It gives praise to Father, Son and Holy Ghost, 'which is one God.'

titleLong: The Book of Mormon's monotheism vs. later LDS plurality of gods
responseLead: Read whole, the 1830 text does tell Father and Son apart, as the New Testament does.
rationaleLead: Arguable on that one charge, but the 1830 book says nothing of the later teaching.

title: 1837: Mary is no longer 'the mother of God'
claim: In the 1830 first edition, 1 Nephi called Jesus God outright. Verse 11:18 called Mary "the mother of God." Verse 11:21 called him "the Lamb of God, yea, even the Eternal Father." Verse 11:32 said "the everlasting God, was judged of the world." And 13:40 said "the Lamb of God is the Eternal Father." In the 1837 Kirtland edition Joseph Smith added the words the Son of to each one. The change is small and deliberate. It lands in the same years his teaching about God was shifting.

left.text: And he said unto me: Behold, the virgin which thou seest is the mother of God, after the manner of the flesh.

right.text: And he said unto me: Behold, the virgin whom thou seest is the mother of the Son of God, after the manner of the flesh.

hl: the mother of the Son of God
comparison.note: Four verses received the same 'the Son of' insertion in 1837 — the same period Smith's godhead doctrine was shifting.

sources.name: Mormonism Research Ministry, 'First Nephi and the Son of God'
1830 first edition text of 1 Nephi (primary source)
CES Letter (Jeremy Runnells), Book of Mormon changes section

response:
Three replies. FAIR says a translator may clarify his own work. Royal Skousen treats the change as clarifying rather than correcting. Christ is still called Eternal Father elsewhere in the book, at Mosiah 16:15. Other verses of that kind were left alone, which a systematic cover-up would not do.

Second, the phrase 'mother of God' drew Catholic-sounding objections from Alexander Campbell. Taking it out removed a stumbling block without changing doctrine.

Third, thousands of changes across the editions are simply typographical. These four are printed openly in Skousen's variant lists. Nothing was hidden.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Book of Mormon/Textual changes/"the Son of"'

rationale:
Nobody disputes the facts. FAIR grants the four insertions and grants that Joseph Smith made them. Only the meaning is argued. The point that similar wording survives elsewhere is fair, and it does weaken a cover-up framing.

One thing is not explained well by any Latter-day Saint source. Why would a translation given by God need a fix about Christ? And why at exactly the verses a critic had attacked, in exactly the years his teaching about God was shifting?

As evidence of a text that changed with its author, this stands. As proof of wholesale rewriting, it overreaches.

plain.d: 1 Nephi 11:18 called Mary "the mother of God." 11:21 called Jesus "the Lamb of God, yea, even the Eternal Father." 13:40 said "the Lamb of God is the Eternal Father."
Joseph Smith inserted the words the Son of. Mary became the mother of the Son of God. The Lamb became the Son of the Eternal Father. The change is small and it is not accidental.
FAIR says a translator may clarify his own work. Royal Skousen treats the change as clarifying, not correcting. Both readings work, they say, since Christ is called Eternal Father in the book anyway.
Arguable. But watch the timing. The edits land just as the teaching about God moves from one being to three separate ones.
"Why did those four verses need the words 'the Son of' added in 1837?"

refwhy.John 1:1, 14: Cuts against the easy version of this argument. The Word 'was God' and became flesh, so the 1830 wording was not strange.
refwhy.Colossians 2:9: 'In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.' More reason the first edition read as normal Christianity.
refwhy.Isaiah 9:6: Calls the child 'The mighty God, The everlasting Father.' The Bible does the very thing the 1830 text did.
refwhy.Titus 2:13: 'The great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ.' Another place the Bible calls Jesus God outright.
refwhy.1 Nephi 11:18 (1830 vs 1837): The 1830 text called Mary 'the mother of God.' In 1837 she became mother of the Son of God.
refwhy.1 Nephi 11:21 (1830 vs 1837): 1830 read 'the Lamb of God, yea, even the Eternal Father.' The 1837 edition inserts 'the Son of.'
refwhy.1 Nephi 11:32 (1830 vs 1837): 1830 had 'the everlasting God, was judged of the world.' The same three words were added here.
refwhy.1 Nephi 13:40 (1830 vs 1837): 1830 read 'the Lamb of God is the Eternal Father.' The fourth and last of the four edits.

titleLong: The 1837 'the Son of' edits to 1 Nephi (Christology revisions)
responseLead: Joseph was free to make his own work clearer, and Mosiah 16:15 still reads that way.
rationaleLead: Arguable, but watch the timing: the four edits land as his teaching about God moved.

title: Jacob bans polygamy; D&C 132 commands it
claim: Jacob 2:24-27 says the many wives and concubines of David and Solomon were "abominable before me, saith the Lord," and commands that no man among you have more than one wife, and no concubines. Doctrine and Covenants 132:38-39 says the opposite. David's wives and concubines "were given unto him of me," and he sinned only in the case of Uriah. Solomon is listed among those who sinned not. The Bible agrees with the Book of Mormon here, and D&C 132 stands against both.

sources.name: 'The Scriptures vs. D&C Section 132' (aggregating the standard critical case)
Richard Packham, 'Major Contradictions in Mormonism'
Mormonr, 'Doctrine and Covenants 132 and Polygamy' (documents both sides)

response:
FAIR reads Jacob 2:30 as an exception clause. Monogamy is the rule. But 'if I will, saith the Lord of Hosts, raise up seed unto me, I will command my people.' On that reading D&C 132 is the commanded exception, and the two texts state one policy.

On David and Solomon they draw a line. Jacob condemns the excess that was never authorised, the Bathsheba affair and the foreign wives who brought their idols. D&C 132:38-39 says David sinned only in the case of Uriah.

So the wives 'given of me' were the authorised ones. And 2 Samuel 12:8 does have Nathan say God gave David his master's wives.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Contradiction between Jacob and D&C 132'

rationale:
The harmony is available in the text. 2 Samuel 12:8 really does say that. And Jacob 2:30 can be read as an exception, though some scholars, Latter-day Saints among them, argue its grammar means the opposite.

The strain shows at Solomon. No text anywhere authorises Solomon's wives. Jacob condemns them and so does 1 Kings 11. Yet D&C 132:38 lists Solomon among those who sinned not.

The rule-plus-exception reading keeps the texts formally consistent. The price is that an 'abominable' practice becomes something God can grant. Narrowed, not removed.

plain.t: What the Book of Mormon says
plain.d: Jacob 2:24 says David's and Solomon's many wives were "abominable before me, saith the Lord." Verse 27 commands: "there shall not any man among you have save it be one wife; and concubines he shall have none."
That David's wives and concubines "were given unto him of me." The same practice, from the same God, with the opposite verdict.
FAIR points to Jacob 2:30, which they read as an exception clause: monogamy is the rule, unless God commands otherwise to raise up seed. That reading is available in the text.
Here the Bible and the Book of Mormon agree with each other, and D&C 132 stands alone against both. That is worth pointing out gently.
"Your own scripture calls it abominable. What changed?"

refwhy.Deuteronomy 17:17: The law given to kings: 'Neither shall he multiply wives to himself.' The Bible agrees with Jacob here.
refwhy.1 Kings 11:1–11: Solomon's wives 'turned away his heart,' and God takes the kingdom from him. D&C 132 lists him among those who sinned not.
refwhy.Matthew 19:4–6: Jesus goes back to the start: 'they twain shall be one flesh.' Two, not more.
refwhy.1 Timothy 3:2: A church leader must be 'the husband of one wife.'
refwhy.Genesis 2:24: The pattern set before any law. A man and 'his wife,' one flesh.
refwhy.Jacob 2:24–30: The core text. David's and Solomon's wives were 'abominable,' and no man may 'have save it be one wife.'
refwhy.Jacob 3:5: Repeats the rule as a standing command. One wife, no concubines. Jacob adds that the Lamanites kept it better.
refwhy.Mosiah 11:2: King Noah's many wives mark him out as wicked. The book uses the practice as a sign of a bad king.
refwhy.Ether 10:5: Riplakish, the same pattern among the Jaredites. Two peoples, one verdict on the practice.

titleLong: Jacob's condemnation of polygamy vs. D&C 132 (the Bible agrees with the Book of Mormon)
responseLead: Jacob 2:30 is an exception clause, and 2 Samuel 12:8 says God gave David those wives.
rationaleLead: It is narrowed, not removed, and the strain shows the moment you reach Solomon.

title: God never changes, yet once was a man
claim: Moroni 8:18 says God is "not a partial God, neither a changeable being; but he is unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity." Mormon 9:9-10 and 9:19 say the same. That agrees with the Bible — Psalm 90:2, Malachi 3:6, and Isaiah 43:10, where God says "before me there was no God formed." It contradicts Joseph Smith's King Follett discourse of 1844, which taught that God was once a man like us and dwelt on an earth, and that men may become gods in turn.

left.text: For I know that God is not a partial God, neither a changeable being; but he is unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity.

right.text: We have imagined and supposed that God was God from all eternity. I will refute that idea… He was once a man like us; yea, God himself, the Father of us all, dwelt on an earth, the same as Jesus Christ himself did.

hl: unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity
God was God from all eternity
comparison.note: Smith's 1844 sermon explicitly sets out to refute the doctrine his own 1829 scripture teaches — and the Bible sides with the 1829 text (Psalm 90:2: 'from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God').

sources.name: Institute for Religious Research, 'The Mormon God Has Not Always Been God'
Robert M. Bowman Jr., 'Answers to Mormon Answers on Moroni 8:18'
Richard Packham, 'Major Contradictions in Mormonism'

response:
Three replies. Blake Ostler and FAIR argue that Moroni 8:18 is about God's moral character. He is not partial or fickle. It is not about his history. The verses around it concern God's fairness to children, so reading a claim about his being into it is proof-texting.

Second, 'from all eternity to all eternity' can be a Hebrew way of saying throughout all the ages of this creation. That fits a being who always existed and was exalted before this creation began.

Third, since attaining godhood he is unchanging in everything that bears on salvation. That is all Mormon 9 needs for its argument about miracles.

responseSource.name: FAIR / Blake Ostler, 'Mormonism and the nature of God'

rationale:
The character-only reading is hard to sustain. Moroni 8:18 and Mormon 9:9 use the language of time and being. It is the same formula the Bible uses of God in Psalm 90:2.

The Book of Mormon nowhere hints that God was once a mortal man. And the King Follett sermon frames the 1844 teaching as overturning the older view. That older view is exactly what the 1829 text holds.

The idiom-and-cycles reply is speculative and comes after the fact. No Latter-day Saint scripture supports it. Here the Book of Mormon sides with the Bible against later Mormonism, and that has not been answered.

plain.t: What the Book of Mormon says
plain.d: Moroni 8:18 — God is "unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity." That matches the Bible: Psalm 90:2, Malachi 3:6, and Isaiah 43:10, where God says "before me there was no God formed."
In 1844 he preached at a funeral for a man named King Follett. He taught that God "was once as we are now" — a man who rose to become God. And that we may do the same.

Blake Ostler and FAIR argue Moroni 8:18 is about God's character — he is not fickle or partial — rather than his history. The surrounding verses are about God's fairness to children, which supports that reading.
Strong for you. The character reading is fair for Moroni 8:18 on its own. It does not help with Isaiah 43:10, which is about existence, not temperament.
"Read me Isaiah 43:10. Was there ever a God before this one?"

refwhy.Psalm 90:2: 'From everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.' The Bible uses the same formula Moroni 8:18 uses.
refwhy.Malachi 3:6: 'I am the LORD, I change not.' The source of the line quoted at 3 Nephi 24:6.
refwhy.Isaiah 43:10: The sharpest one. 'Before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.' That is about being, not mood.
refwhy.Isaiah 44:6: 'I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God.'
refwhy.James 1:17: 'No variableness, neither shadow of turning.' Mormon 9:9 uses that phrase almost word for word.
refwhy.Numbers 23:19: 'God is not a man.' Blunt, and the plainest reply to a God who was once a man.
refwhy.Moroni 8:18: The verse it turns on. God is 'unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity,' in their own scripture.
refwhy.Mormon 9:9–11, 19: God 'the same yesterday, today, and forever.' Mormon argues that a God who changed would 'cease to be God.'
refwhy.Moroni 7:22: God 'being from everlasting to everlasting.' A third witness in the book to the same idea.
refwhy.3 Nephi 24:6: 'I am the Lord, I change not.' Jesus gives the Nephites the line from Malachi.

titleLong: God 'unchangeable from all eternity' vs. God as exalted man
responseLead: That verse is about God's character, not his past, and the ones around it fit that.
rationaleLead: Strong for you: the Book of Mormon here sides with the Bible against later Mormon teaching.

title: Alma 34: no second chance after death
claim: Alma 34:32-35 teaches that "this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God," and that after it comes "the night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed." Those who put off repentance are sealed to the devil, and "this is the final state of the wicked." That agrees with the Bible in Hebrews 9:27 and with the fixed gulf of Luke 16:26. Later teaching added the spirit world, the preaching of the gospel to the dead, and baptism performed by proxy for them.

sources.name: Richard Packham, 'Major Contradictions in Mormonism'
Grant Palmer, An Insider's View of Mormon Origins
CES Letter (aggregates the doctrinal-evolution case)

response:
Three replies. Amulek is addressing the Zoramites, people who had the gospel and turned it down. His warning applies to them, not to the billions who never heard. D&C 138:32-34 limits acceptance after death to 'those who died without a knowledge of this gospel'. So the two texts divide humanity with no overlap.

Second, Latter-day Saints teach that character carries over after death. So this is no easy second chance, and Amulek's urgency still stands.

Third, 1 Peter 3:19 and 4:6 have Christ preaching to spirits in prison. 1 Corinthians 15:29 mentions baptism for the dead. So the later doctrine has biblical footing.

responseSource.name: LDS D&C 138 Student Manual

rationale:
The audience answer is coherent, and it is the church's actual teaching. Critics who ignore it are overclaiming.

It does strain the text. Amulek's words are universal in form. This life is the time for men to prepare. This is the final state of the wicked. The Book of Mormon repeats that scheme elsewhere without the carve-out.

And the whole apparatus of spirit prison, proxy ordinances and three degrees of glory is missing from a book whose next life is simply heaven or hell. As evidence of doctrine growing between 1829 and Nauvoo it holds. As a flat contradiction it can be answered.

plain.t: What the Book of Mormon says
plain.d: Alma 34:32-35: "this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God," and after it comes "the night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed." Those who put off repentance are sealed to the devil — "this is the final state of the wicked."
The spirit world, where the gospel is preached to the dead, and baptism performed by proxy for them by the living.

That Amulek is addressing the Zoramites — people who had already received the gospel and rejected it. His warning applies to them, not to the billions who never heard. D&C 138 makes that distinction explicit.
Genuinely arguable. The Zoramite context is real. But Alma's language is sweeping, and the Bible says the same thing in Hebrews 9:27.
"Alma says there's no labour after this life. How does that fit with baptism for the dead?"

refwhy.Hebrews 9:27: 'Appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment.' The Bible agreeing with Alma.
refwhy.Luke 16:26: The 'great gulf fixed' after death. Nobody crosses it in either direction.
refwhy.2 Corinthians 6:2: 'Now is the day of salvation.' The urgency is for now, not later.
refwhy.John 8:24: 'Ye shall die in your sins' if you do not believe. Death set as the deadline.
refwhy.Alma 34:32–35: The passage. 'This life is the time for men to prepare to meet God,' then comes 'the night of darkness.'
refwhy.2 Nephi 9:38: 'Wo unto all those who die in their sins… and remain in their sins.' No second chance in view.
refwhy.Mosiah 2:36–39: Ends in 'a never-ending torment' for the man who dies an enemy to God. The same two outcomes.
refwhy.Mosiah 26:25–27: At the last trump, those who 'never knew me' are sent away. No spirit-world preaching appears here.

titleLong: No repentance after death (Alma 34) vs. postmortem salvation and baptism for the dead
responseLead: Alma 34 warns those who had the gospel and threw it away, not those who never heard.
rationaleLead: Their reading of Alma 34 is what the church teaches, but his words are sweeping.

title: Alma 7:10 says Jesus was born at Jerusalem
claim: Alma 7:10 prophesies that Jesus "shall be born of Mary, at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers." The Bible's prophecy in Micah 5:2 and its fulfilment in Matthew 2:1 and Luke 2:4-7 place the birth in Bethlehem. Critics call it a plain geographical error by Joseph Smith, and note that the Bible he knew made Bethlehem famous. This is one of the weaker criticisms on the site, and the Latter-day Saint reply to it is unusually strong.

left.text: And behold, he shall be born of Mary, at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers, she being a virgin, a precious and chosen vessel.

right.text: But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel.

hl: at Jerusalem which is the land
comparison.note: The LDS defense turns on the apposition 'which is the land' — a regional reading with genuinely ancient parallels (Amarna letters; 4Q385a).

sources.name: Mormonism Research Ministry, 'Was Jesus Born "at Jerusalem"?'
MRM, '"The Land of Jerusalem" and the Dead Sea Scrolls' (rebuttal of the LDS reply)
MRM, 'Do the Amarna Letters support Alma 7:10?'

response:
Three replies, and this is one of the better sets. The verse says 'at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers'. Land, not city. The Book of Mormon uses 'land of Jerusalem' more than forty times for the whole region Lehi left. Its writers were six centuries and an ocean away from Judean village geography.

Second, that phrasing is genuinely ancient. Amarna letter EA 287, from the fourteenth century BC, speaks of towns of the land of Jerusalem. A Dead Sea Scroll fragment says Jeremiah was taken captive from the land of Jerusalem. Neither was knowable in 1829.

Third, Bethlehem is five miles away, well inside any such land.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Born at Jerusalem, the land of our forefathers'

rationale:
This is among the strongest Latter-day Saint replies in the whole section, and Christians should say so plainly. The verse's own wording, the steady land-versus-city usage, and the genuinely ancient parallels give it real footing.

The counters keep some bite. The parallels are regional usages in other settings. And a nineteenth-century writer being loose explains the same data. Neither side closes it.

Note too that even on the critical reading this is an imprecision, not a clash of doctrine. That is why it is graded low.

plain.d: Alma 7:10 prophesies that Jesus "shall be born of Mary, at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers." The Bible says Bethlehem — Micah 5:2 predicts it, Matthew 2 and Luke 2 report it.

And this one is good. The verse says the land of our fathers, not the city. The Book of Mormon uses "the land of Jerusalem" more than forty times for the whole region. Bethlehem is five miles away. An Egyptian letter from the 1300s BC even calls Bethlehem part of the land of Jerusalem.
Genuinely arguable, and this is one where the Latter-day Saint answer is stronger than most critics admit. Do not lead with it.
Give away a weak argument openly and you earn a hearing on the strong ones. The papyri. The italics. The Isaiah dating.
"I've heard this one used against you and I don't think it works. Can I ask about something that does?"

refwhy.Micah 5:2: The Bethlehem prophecy. It is what Alma 7:10 is accused of getting wrong.
refwhy.Matthew 2:1–6: The fulfilment, with the priests quoting Micah. Bethlehem is five miles from Jerusalem.
refwhy.Luke 2:4–7: The birth in Bethlehem. It does not settle the case, since a 'land of Jerusalem' could take it in.
refwhy.Alma 7:10: The verse. Read the exact words: 'at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers.' Land, not city.

titleLong: Jesus born 'at Jerusalem' (Alma 7:10) vs. Bethlehem (Micah 5:2)
responseLead: The verse says the land, not the city, and Amarna letter EA 287 uses it the same way.
rationaleLead: One of their strongest replies: say so plainly, and do not lead with this case.

title: 'Plain and precious' parts cut from the Bible
claim: 1 Nephi 13:26-29 and 13:40 claim that a "great and abominable church" deliberately took from the gospel "many parts which are plain and most precious, and also many covenants," corrupting the Bible after the apostles. That claim is the foundation of the case for a Restoration. It is also testable. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied around 125 BC, matches the medieval Hebrew text with roughly 95 percent verbal identity. The New Testament survives in thousands of copies from too early, too many places, and too many languages for a coordinated removal to go unrecorded.

sources.name: CARM, 'Mormonism and the Corruption of the Bible'
MRM, 'The Dead Sea Scrolls' (on LDS use of the scrolls)
Probe Ministries, 'The Dead Sea Scrolls Shed Light on the Accuracy of our Bible'

response: Three replies. Scripture Central and FAIR move the loss earlier, into the first and second centuries. That is before our earliest substantial manuscripts, since most complete New Testament codices are fourth century. If it happened then, uniform later copies cannot rule it out. They cite Bart Ehrman on early changes made for doctrinal reasons. Second, the loss need not be deletion at all. 1 Nephi 13 mentions covenants as well as plain and precious things. So it could mean lost books the Bible itself names, or lost ordinances, or lost keys to reading. Third, the Dead Sea Scrolls show real fluidity in copying. Jeremiah and Samuel survive there in variant editions.

responseSource.name: Scripture Central KnoWhy, 'Were Plain and Precious Doctrines Lost?'

rationale:
The manuscripts settle the popular form of this claim. There was no purge of doctrines out of the Bible after the apostles. The Dead Sea Scrolls close the Old Testament gap. The Great Isaiah Scroll, copied about 125 BC, matches the medieval Hebrew text about 95 percent word for word.

New Testament copying is too early, too spread out and too widely attested for a coordinated cut to leave no trace.

The careful version survives. But it survives only by retreating to where evidence is thinnest, and by becoming untestable. It also gives up the natural reading of 1 Nephi 13, and puts nothing positive in its place.

plain.t: The claim that makes a restoration necessary
plain.d: 1 Nephi 13 says a "great and abominable church" deliberately took from the gospel "many parts which are plain and most precious, and also many covenants." If the Bible was gutted, something has to replace it.
Because we have the copies. Thousands of them, from before and across that whole span. In Greek, Latin, Syriac and Coptic. Made in places that never spoke to each other.
No sign of a coordinated removal. Variants exist and are catalogued, but they are spelling, word order, and a handful of footnoted passages. Nothing doctrine rests on.

FAIR and Scripture Central move the loss earlier — to the first or second century, before our oldest full copies. If it happened then, the copies could not show it. That is a real answer. It is also one that no evidence could ever count against.
"If it was removed before our oldest copies, what evidence could ever count either way?"

refwhy.Isaiah 40:8: 'The word of our God shall stand for ever.' The promise a wholesale gutting would break.
refwhy.Matthew 24:35: Jesus says 'my words shall not pass away.' The same promise, from him.
refwhy.1 Peter 1:24–25: 'The word of the Lord endureth for ever,' applied by Peter to the gospel that was preached.
refwhy.1 Nephi 13:26–29, 34, 40: The charge itself. A 'great and abominable church' took 'many parts which are plain and most precious' from the Bible.
refwhy.1 Nephi 14:20–26: Says the apostle John's book was 'plain and pure' when it left him. So the loss must come after.

titleLong: 'Plain and precious things' removed from the Bible vs. the manuscript evidence
responseLead: If it happened before our oldest copies, then no copy we have could ever show it.
rationaleLead: Strong for you on the popular version, but their retreat cannot be tested at all.

title: 190 years of digging, no Nephite city found
claim: The Book of Mormon describes large civilizations in the Americas before Columbus. They read and write. They work metal. They build cities. They number in the millions, and they fight battles with hundreds of thousands of dead. Archaeologists have worked the Americas for about 190 years. Not one city, battlefield, road, temple, artifact or skeleton has been tied to the book. No inscription in any related script has been authenticated. And the church itself takes no official position on where any of it happened.

sources.name: Michael D. Coe, 'Mormons and Archaeology: An Outside View,' Dialogue 8/2 (1973) — 'nothing, absolutely nothing, has ever shown up in any New World excavation which would suggest to a dispassionate observer that the Book of Mormon… is a historical document'
Michael D. Coe, Mormon Stories interview transcript (2011) — reaffirms the 1973 verdict after 38 more years of Maya epigraphy
Dee F. Green (LDS archaeologist), 'Book of Mormon Archaeology: The Myths and the Alternatives,' Dialogue 4/2 (1969) — 'no Book of Mormon location is known with reference to modern topography'
Smithsonian Institution, 'Statement Regarding the Book of Mormon' (rev. 1998)
National Geographic Society letter (1998)

response:
Five replies, and one is a genuine hit.

John Sorenson's limited-geography model keeps the story inside a corridor of about 500 miles in Mesoamerica. On that model a hemisphere-wide blank is beside the point. He lists over 400 claimed matches.

Second, identifying a site may be impossible in principle. Only Maya script can be read with confidence, and the conquest erased most old place-names. Third, John Clark counts about 60 concrete things the text asserts. He reckons support for them rose from 13% in 1842 to 75% by 2005.

Fourth, and this is the strong one, the NHM altars from Yemen date to the seventh or sixth century BC. They sit on the right bearing for Lehi's route. Fifth, FAIR notes the famous Smithsonian statement was a form letter to cut down mail, not a research finding.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Archaeological Evidence and the Book of Mormon'; Sorenson, Mormon's Codex

rationale:
The reply explains why no signpost says Zarahemla. It does not answer the harder version. The text asserts a literate people with Old World crops, metalwork and writing. No remains of that kind exist anywhere in the Americas, and finding them would not require reading a place-name.

Clark's tally is generic. Warfare, thrones and cities are true of almost any complex society. NHM is a real hit, but it is in Arabia, where the story overlaps documented geography. It says nothing about the two-thirds of the book set in the New World.

And the small map is a retreat from the hemispheric reading Joseph Smith and every nineteenth-century leader held.

plain.d: Cities. Temples. Roads. Coins. Steel swords and armour. Civilizations in the millions. And a final battle with hundreds of thousands of dead.
After about 190 years of digging in the Americas: not one city. Not one battlefield, road, temple or skeleton tied to the book. No inscription. And no site the church itself points to.

John Sorenson keeps the whole story inside a corridor of about 500 miles in Central America. If that is right, an empty hemisphere proves nothing. He lists hundreds of claimed matches with Maya culture.

The church takes no official position on where it happened. And the small-map idea is a long way from what was taught for a century. Back then, the Lamanites were the ancestors of all American Indians.
"Where did it happen? I'd genuinely like to read the church's position on that."

refwhy.Mormon 6:10–15: The final battle. Ten thousand at a time, and no burial ground has ever been found.
refwhy.Ether 15:2: 'Nearly two millions' of Jaredites slain. That scale is what makes an empty record surprising.
refwhy.Alma 2:19: Exact figures — 12,532 and 6,562 dead in one day. The text is precise, which invites a test.
refwhy.Helaman 3:7–11: Cities and temples 'of cement,' plus shipping. These are concrete claims about building, not vague ones.
refwhy.Mosiah 11:8–10: King Noah's palace and temple, in gold, silver, iron, brass and copper. A named material culture.
refwhy.2 Nephi 5:15–16: A temple built 'after the manner of the temple of Solomon,' plus iron and steel work.

titleLong: No archaeological trace of Nephite civilization; no Book of Mormon site ever identified
responseLead: Sorenson's 500-mile map, and the NHM altars in Yemen sit right on Lehi's route.
rationaleLead: Strong for you: NHM is in Arabia, and says nothing about the New World two-thirds.

title: 'Reformed Egyptian', a script no Egyptologist knows
claim: The Book of Mormon describes a thousand years of continuous record-keeping. Scribes write Hebrew and a modified Egyptian script on metal plates and stone — Mormon 9:32-34, 1 Nephi 1:2, Omni 1:20-22, Mosiah 8:11-13, Jacob 4:1-3. No pre-Columbian inscription in Hebrew, Egyptian or any Semitic-derived script has ever been authenticated in the Americas. No script called 'reformed Egyptian' is attested in Egyptology. The writing systems we can read there are Maya, Zapotec and Epi-Olmec. None is related to Afro-Asiatic writing in structure or in sign inventory. Four objects are periodically advanced as exceptions. They are the Bat Creek Stone, the Los Lunas Decalogue Stone, the Newark Holy Stones and the Michigan Relics. All four are documented or strongly suspected forgeries.

sources.name: Michael D. Coe (Yale Mayanist), Mormon Stories interview (2011)
Survey of the scholarly position and forgery history of claimed exceptions ('Reformed Egyptian')
Criticism of the Book of Mormon (survey with primary citations)

response:
Three replies. First, 'reformed Egyptian' is the text's own phrase for its script, 'altered by us, according to our manner of speech', at Mormon 9:32. It is not a claim that Egyptologists should know the name. Egyptian really was reformed over time, from hieroglyphic to hieratic to demotic. Hugh Nibley noted real cases of Semitic languages written in Egyptian characters.

Second, the record was a small elite tradition on metal plates. A few men kept it, and then it was buried. It was never public monument writing, so we would not expect to find it.

Third, Brian Stubbs, a specialist in Uto-Aztecan, argues for about 1,500 proposed Semitic and Egyptian matches. He claims regular sound correspondences. That is the kind of evidence historical linguistics accepts.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Reformed Egyptian and the Book of Mormon'; Brian D. Stubbs

rationale:
The small-corpus argument hangs together. It also grants that the claim cannot be tested.

Stubbs's work is the only positive evidence offered. No historical linguist outside the church has accepted it or engaged it seriously. The standard criticism is that his method searches a large word list for sound resemblances. Given enough candidates, that can turn up matches between unrelated families.

Meanwhile the null result stands. A whole field of decipherment has found no Afro-Asiatic link in any Mesoamerican script. Michael Coe of Yale has said so.

plain.d: A thousand years of continuous writing. Hebrew, and a modified Egyptian script, cut into metal plates and stone. See Mormon 9:32-34, 1 Nephi 1:2, Omni 1:20-22, Mosiah 8:11-13 and Jacob 4:1-3.

Nothing. No writing in Hebrew or Egyptian has ever been dug up in the Americas and proved real. Nor in any related script. No script called "reformed Egyptian" is known to Egyptologists. And the scripts we can read there — Maya, Zapotec, Epi-Olmec — are built on other lines. The signs are not the same.

Four objects come up. The Bat Creek Stone. The Los Lunas Decalogue Stone. The Newark Holy Stones. The Michigan Relics. Each one is a known fake, or is strongly suspected of being one. Do not lean on any of them.

Three lines. First, "reformed Egyptian" is the book's own phrase for a script "altered by us, according to our manner of speech." It is not a claim that Egyptologists should know the name. Egyptian really was reformed over time. It went from hieroglyphic to hieratic to demotic. And Hugh Nibley noted Semitic languages written in Egyptian letters. Second, this was a small record. A few men kept it on plates, and then it was buried. It was never public writing on walls. Third, Brian Stubbs works on Uto-Aztecan. He argues for about 1,500 matches with Semitic and Egyptian, and claims regular sound rules.

Strong for you. The small-record answer hangs together. But notice what it grants: there is now no way to test the claim. Stubbs is the one piece of evidence on the other side. No linguist outside the church has taken it up. Michael Coe, the Yale Maya scholar, said the field has found nothing.
"Has any inscription in the Americas ever been read as Hebrew or Egyptian?"

refwhy.Mormon 9:32–34: The 'reformed Egyptian' verse. It also holds their best answer: the script was 'altered by us,' so no outsider knows it.
refwhy.1 Nephi 1:2: The starting claim. A record in 'the learning of the Jews and the language of the Egyptians.'
refwhy.Omni 1:20–22: A stone with engravings, brought to a king and read. Writing on stone, not just on plates.
refwhy.Mosiah 8:11–13: Plates found in the ground with rusted swords, and nobody able to read them.
refwhy.Jacob 4:1–3: Helps their side. Jacob says writing on anything but plates 'must perish,' which is why nothing else would survive.

titleLong: No Hebrew or Egyptian inscriptions — no 'reformed Egyptian' — in pre-Columbian America
responseLead: Reformed Egyptian is the book's own phrase, and Stubbs claims 1,500 matches in Uto-Aztecan.
rationaleLead: Strong for you: the small-record answer works, but it grants the claim cannot be tested.

title: Native American DNA points to Siberia, not Israel
claim: Mitochondrial, Y-chromosome and autosomal studies place essentially all pre-Columbian Native American ancestry in Siberian and East Asian source populations entering via Beringia more than 15,000 years ago. No Middle Eastern founding lineage from about 600 BC has been identified. Two Latter-day Saint scientists published this as a direct falsification of the Lamanite claim in 2002 and 2003 — Thomas Murphy, an anthropologist, and Simon Southerton, a geneticist and former bishop. Murphy faced a disciplinary council, postponed 24 hours before it convened, and Southerton was disciplined. In 2006 the church silently changed the Book of Mormon introduction: the Lamanites went from 'the principal ancestors of the American Indians' to 'among the ancestors.' The Title Page, 1 Nephi 13:30, 2 Nephi 30:4-6, Alma 10:3, Helaman 15:11-13 and 3 Nephi 21:2-7 are the texts at issue.

sources.name: Thomas W. Murphy, 'Lamanite Genesis, Genealogy, and Genetics,' in American Apocrypha (Signature Books, 2002)
Simon G. Southerton, 'Simply Implausible: DNA and a Mesoamerican Setting for the Book of Mormon,' Dialogue 36/4 (2003)
Documentation of the 2002 Murphy disciplinary council
MormonR, 'DNA and the Book of Mormon' — sourced documentation of the 1981 vs. 2006 introduction wording

response:
The church's own Gospel Topics essay grants that 'the majority of Native Americans carry largely Asian DNA'. It then answers on five fronts.

Nothing in the text says Lehi's party was the only population. The introduction was a 1981 editorial addition, not scripture, and 2006 corrected an over-reading.

A founding party of about 30 joining an already-large population would leave a signal below detection after 2,600 years. That is standard population genetics, not special pleading. Founder effect, drift and the bottleneck after contact each erase small founding lines. And we do not know the ancient Israelite genetic profile to look for.

Ugo Perego, a population geneticist, notes that the Asian ancestor of haplogroup X2a is itself undetected in modern Asia. Real founding lines do go missing. The essay's own bottom line is that DNA studies 'cannot be used decisively to either affirm or reject' the book.

responseSource.name: Gospel Topics Essay, 'Book of Mormon and DNA Studies'

rationale:
The population-genetics reply is technically sound. Drift, founder effects and the bottleneck genuinely can erase a small founding line. Critics who say DNA disproves the book overstate what a blank result can do.

The concession is still enormous. The defence works only by shrinking the Book of Mormon peoples into a marginal group inside a continent already full of Asians. That cuts against the text itself. 2 Nephi 1:8-9 has the land 'kept as yet from the knowledge of other nations'. It also cuts against 150 years of prophetic teaching.

And it took an unannounced edit to the printed introduction. That is the most concrete institutional concession in this whole list.

plain.d: Three kinds of test have been run on Native American DNA. The mother line, called mitochondrial. The father line, from the Y chromosome. And the whole genome. All three point the same way: to Siberia and East Asia. People crossed at Beringia more than 15,000 years ago. No Middle Eastern founding line from about 600 BC has been found.

Two Latter-day Saint scientists. Thomas Murphy, an anthropologist, and Simon Southerton, a geneticist and former bishop. They published in 2002 and 2003. Murphy faced a disciplinary council, postponed 24 hours before it met. Southerton was disciplined.
The introduction to the Book of Mormon was quietly reworded. The Lamanites had been "the principal ancestors of the American Indians." They became "among the ancestors."

The church's own Gospel Topics essay grants that most Native Americans carry largely Asian DNA. Then it makes real points. The text never says Lehi's party was alone. A group of about 30 joining a large population leaves no detectable signal after 2,600 years. Founder effect, genetic drift and the bottleneck after contact each erase small lines. Ugo Perego notes the Asian ancestor of haplogroup X2a is itself missing from modern Asia. And the essay's own bottom line is that DNA "cannot be used decisively to either affirm or reject" the book.

Genuinely arguable, and be careful. The population genetics is sound, and anyone who says DNA disproves the book has overstated it. But look at the price. The answer works only by shrinking the Nephites into a small group inside a continent already full of Asians. 2 Nephi 1:8-9 says the land was "kept as yet from the knowledge of other nations." And it took an unannounced edit to the printed introduction.
"Why did the introduction change from 'principal ancestors' to 'among the ancestors'?"

refwhy.Title Page: Says the book is written to the Lamanites, 'a remnant of the house of Israel.' The identity claim at issue.
refwhy.1 Nephi 13:30: Promises the Gentiles will not 'utterly destroy the mixture of thy seed.' Lehi's line lives on here.
refwhy.2 Nephi 30:4–6: The remnant will learn 'that they are descendants of the Jews.' A direct claim about American peoples.
refwhy.Alma 10:3: Traces Lehi to Manasseh, son of Joseph. The book's own family line, which the DNA question tests.
refwhy.Helaman 15:11–13: Prophesies the Lamanites brought back 'in the latter times.' Missionary work to Native Americans was built on this.
refwhy.3 Nephi 21:2–7: Jesus ties the last days to 'a remnant of the house of Jacob' in this land. The same claim, from him.

titleLong: Native American genetics show Asian, not Israelite, ancestry — and the 2006 introduction change
responseLead: A party of 30 joining a large population leaves no trace after 2,600 years.
rationaleLead: Take care: the science is sound, but their fix shrinks the Nephites to a tiny group.

title: Lehi's 30 settlers become armies of 230,000
claim: A founding party of roughly 20 to 30 people arrives about 589 BC. It splits almost at once into Nephites and Lamanites. Within about 500 years the text reports 19,094 Lamanites slain in a single battle (Alma 2:19). Armies of tens of thousands appear throughout Alma, and 230,000 Nephites are killed at Cumorah (Mormon 6:10-15). The Jaredites reach 'two millions' (Ether 15:2). John Kunich showed that reaching these figures from the stated founders needs sustained growth rates far above anything seen in pre-modern populations. The text also has the Nephites building temples, and fielding kings and standing armies, within two generations of a landing party of a couple of dozen — 1 Nephi 18:23, 2 Nephi 5:6-16, Jarom 1:8, Alma 28:2.

sources.name: John C. Kunich, 'Multiply Exceedingly: Book of Mormon Population Sizes,' Sunstone (1990), repr. in New Approaches to the Book of Mormon (1993)
Deseret News, 'The genetics of the Book of Mormon' (2008)

response:
James E. Smith is a trained historical demographer. He wrote in FARMS Review 6/1 in 1994. Kunich, he says, applies long-run averages to a young colony. That is the wrong yardstick. A frontier people with land to spare can hold 2 to 3% a year for centuries. Colonial New England did it. So did Pitcairn. Smith's own model runs reach Book of Mormon numbers on fair assumptions. Plural marriage among Lamanites and early Nephites would help too.

The strongest point is in the text itself. The book never says the land was empty. Sherem walks in from nowhere in Jacob 7. The Mulekites are found already numerous in Omni 1. And 'Lamanite' can work as a label for a side, not a bloodline. If Lehi's party joined peoples already there, no huge growth rate is needed.

Last, war dead in old records are famously inflated. That is true of the Bible, of Greece and Rome, and of the Maya. Reading those figures as a census is a mistake about what they are.

responseSource.name: James E. Smith, 'Nephi's Descendants?' (FARMS Review 6/1); FAIR, 'Adding Up the Book of Mormon Peoples'

rationale:
This is the criticism the Latter-day Saint side has answered best on its own terms. Smith is a credentialed demographer. His frontier-growth objection to Kunich is technically right, and the others-in-the-land reading is defensible from the text.

But the fix is costly, and it creates a squeeze. The more others you import to solve the demography and the DNA, the less the book is what its own narrators thought it was. Its nineteenth-century readers thought the same. And the text's total silence about a surrounding native majority becomes strange in itself.

On its own this does not sink the text. It works as a force multiplier on the DNA and archaeology entries.

plain.d: A founding party of about 20 to 30 lands around 589 BC. It splits almost at once. Within roughly 500 years the text reports 19,094 Lamanites killed in one battle at Alma 2:19. Later, 230,000 Nephites die at Cumorah in Mormon 6:10-15. The Jaredites reach "two millions" at Ether 15:2.

That reaching those figures from those founders needs growth rates far above anything measured in pre-modern populations. And the text has temples, kings and standing armies within two generations of a landing party of a couple of dozen.

This is one they answer well. James E. Smith is a professional historical demographer. He argues Kunich applied long-run averages to a frontier colony, where 2 to 3% a year is normal for centuries — colonial New England did it, and so did Pitcairn. His simulations produce Book of Mormon numbers. Polygamy is attested among Lamanites and early Nephites. Ancient casualty figures are notoriously inflated everywhere. And the book never says the land was empty: Sherem appears from nowhere in Jacob 7, and the Mulekites are found already numerous in Omni 1.

The fix and the DNA fix are the same fix. The more other people you put in the land, the less the book is what its own narrators thought it was. And the silence about a surrounding native majority becomes strange in itself.
Genuinely arguable, and weak on its own. Smith is right against Kunich on the demography. Use this one only alongside the DNA and archaeology cases, where it adds weight.
"If there were already people there, why does nobody in the book mention them?"

refwhy.1 Nephi 18:23: The landing. A party of roughly twenty to thirty people, and the clock starts here.
refwhy.2 Nephi 5:6–16: The split, naming who went with Nephi. Then a temple and metal work, inside one generation.
refwhy.Jarom 1:8: 'We multiplied exceedingly,' says Jarom. Buildings, tools and a full set of weapons, only a few generations in.
refwhy.Alma 2:19: The precise figure: 12,532 Amlicites and 6,562 Nephites dead in a day, about 500 years after the landing.
refwhy.Alma 28:2: 'Tens of thousands of the Lamanites were slain' in one battle. Armies on a national scale.
refwhy.Mormon 6:10–15: Cumorah. Ten thousand under each commander, and about 230,000 Nephite dead.
refwhy.Ether 15:2: 'Nearly two millions' of Jaredites already slain. The largest number the book gives.

titleLong: Population growth from Lehi's party to the reported armies is demographically implausible
responseLead: Smith answers Kunich well: a new colony with land to spare grows far faster.
rationaleLead: Weak on its own: Smith wins against Kunich, so use this only with DNA.

title: The seer stone in a hat, now openly taught
claim: The best-attested account comes from insiders, not critics. Emma Smith, David Whitmer and Martin Harris all describe the same thing. Joseph Smith put a seer stone in his hat. He buried his face in it to block the light. Then he read out the English he saw there. The gold plates were often covered, in another room, or not present at all. It was the same stone he had used to hunt for treasure in the 1820s. That practice is what brought him before a court in 1826. For about 150 years, church manuals and paintings showed him reading from the plates instead.

sources.name: Gospel Topics Essay, 'Book of Mormon Translation' — official acknowledgment of the stone-in-hat method
Emma Smith, 'Last Testimony of Sister Emma,' Saints' Herald (1879) — 'sitting with his face buried in his hat, with the stone in it'
MRM annotated analysis of the translation essay (documenting the curriculum gap)

response:
Four replies, and the first is decisive. The church now teaches this openly. It is in the Gospel Topics essay, the Joseph Smith Papers, the Saints volumes, and the 2015 photographs in the Ensign. The sources were published in the nineteenth century and discussed in BYU Studies long before the internet found them. There was no suppression.

Second, 'Urim and Thummim' was used loosely at the time. It covered both the Nephite interpreters and the single stone. That makes the older telling imprecise rather than false.

Third, the method is beside the point in theology. If revelation is real, the instrument is incidental, and the Bible has comparable objects. Fourth, Skousen and Carmack argue the dictation was tightly controlled, which the seer-stone account supports.

responseSource.name: Interpreter Foundation, 'Seeing with a Hat'; Gospel Topics Essay, 'Book of Mormon Translation'

rationale:
On the history, the church has conceded fully. The concession is in official curriculum now. Nobody disputes the facts.

Two things remain, and both are matters of meaning rather than evidence. The plates were not needed for the translation. That sits oddly beside the long story of digging them up and guarding them. And the stone that produced scripture is the stone he had used to hunt treasure.

The criticism as it is usually told, that the method was hidden, has been answered.

plain.d: Joseph Smith reading from gold plates, perhaps with a curtain, writing down what he read. That is what church manuals and paintings showed for about 150 years.

Something different. He put a brown stone into his hat, buried his face in it to block the light, and dictated. The plates were often covered, or in another room, or not there at all. That comes from Emma Smith, David Whitmer and Martin Harris — insiders, not critics.
He had used the same stone earlier for treasure-seeking, which is what brought him before a court in 1826.

This one has a clear answer — the church now teaches it openly. The Gospel Topics essay says so, the Joseph Smith Papers document it, and the church published photographs of the stone in 2015. The scandal was the silence, not the stone.
"Have you seen the church's photos of the seer stone? What did you picture before that?"

refwhy.Mosiah 8:13–18: The book's own picture of a seer: a man who 'can look' into interpreters and translate. It describes its own method.
refwhy.Mosiah 28:11–16: Mosiah translates 'by the means of those two stones which were fastened into the two rims of a bow.'
refwhy.Ether 3:23–28: Where the two stones come from. God gives them so the sealed writing can be read later.

titleLong: Translation method: a seer stone in a hat, plates often not present — vs. the narrative taught for 150 years
responseLead: The church now teaches the seer stone openly, in essays, Saints, and 2015 photographs.
rationaleLead: This one is answered: the church teaches it openly now, so do not lead with it.

title: The lost 116 pages, never retranslated
claim: Martin Harris lost the first 116 manuscript pages, the Book of Lehi, in the summer of 1828. Joseph Smith did not retranslate them. Instead a revelation, now D&C 10, explained that wicked men had altered the lost pages, and would publish the altered version to discredit him. It directed him to translate the 'small plates of Nephi' instead — a second record, covering the same period, which Mormon says he included 'for a wise purpose… I know not' (Words of Mormon 1:3-7). Critics argue this is the signature of a human author who cannot reproduce a lost draft word for word. It is a test that would have been trivially passable for a text delivered word for word on a seer stone. 1 Nephi 9:2-6 and 19:1-6 are the internal references.

sources.name: Dan Vogel, Joseph Smith: The Making of a Prophet (Signature Books, 2004); Fawn Brodie, No Man Knows My History (1945)
Doctrine and Covenants 10 (primary revelation text)
LDS Discussions, 'The Lost 116 Pages'

response:
Three replies. First, the stated reason is guarding against forgery, not dodging. If enemies held the only other copy, a fresh translation differing in any wording, as dictated translation always would, could be paraded as proof of fraud. Declining the trap is the rational move.

Second, the convenient-replacement framing ignores the text. The small plates are foreshadowed inside it, at 1 Nephi 9 and 19, as a second record made by Nephi. Mormon's plain 'I know not' why he included them reads like an old editor noting a prompting he did not understand. That is a strange thing for a forger to invent.

Third, believers read this as God providing ahead of a failure he foresaw. The episode is also the origin of a lasting lesson about Joseph's fallibility, in D&C 3.

responseSource.name: BYU Religious Studies Center, 'The Lost 116 Pages Story'

rationale:
This turns entirely on what you think likely to begin with. Both sides agree on every fact. Their reading hangs together, and the point about wording is genuinely right about how translation works.

The ordinary reading is still the simpler one, and it has one specific edge. The seer-stone method as the church now describes it has fixed English words appearing on the stone. That is a tight-control model, and under it a second try should have matched. So the wording objection loses its force.

Their defence and the church's own translation essay sit in mild tension. Nothing here can be settled either way.

plain.d: In 1828 Martin Harris borrowed the first 116 pages of the translation and lost them. They were never recovered.

They were not retranslated. A revelation, now D&C 10, said wicked men had altered the lost pages and would publish the altered version to discredit him. So he was told to translate a different set of plates covering the same period instead.

That this is guarding against forgery, not dodging. Dictated translation never comes out word for word the same twice. If enemies held the only other copy, any difference would be paraded as proof he made it up.
Arguable. The forgery worry is reasonable. What is worth noticing is that a replacement text already existed, covering the same years. And no altered version was ever published.
"Did the altered pages ever actually appear?"

refwhy.Words of Mormon 1:3–7: Mormon says he added the small plates 'for a wise purpose' he does not know. The replacement text, flagged in advance.
refwhy.1 Nephi 9:2–6: Nephi is told to make a second set of plates 'for a wise purpose in him, which purpose I know not.'
refwhy.1 Nephi 19:1–6: Supports their side. The second record is set up early in the book, not improvised in 1828.

titleLong: The lost 116 pages and the convenient pre-existing replacement text
responseLead: Doing it again would never match word for word, and enemies held the only copy.
rationaleLead: The forgery worry is fair, but no altered pages were ever published.

title: The eleven witnesses were all family or backers
claim: The Eleven Witnesses were all Smith family, Whitmer family, or Martin Harris. There were no disinterested observers, and they shared a documented folk-magic worldview that included 'second sight.' Harris and Whitmer later described the experience in visionary terms; Harris spoke of 'the eyes of faith' and 'spiritual eyes,' and Stephen Burnett's 1838 letter reports Harris saying the witnesses saw the plates only in vision. All Three left or were excommunicated by 1838. Whitmer's 1887 pamphlet declared that God told him by voice to leave the church — the same evidentiary channel he claimed for the plates. Harris subsequently endorsed the Shaker 'Sacred Roll,' which also carried multi-witness testimony of angelic visitation. And no witness ever claimed to view the uncovered plates in a mundane, non-visionary setting. Deuteronomy 19:15 and 2 Corinthians 13:1 set the standard for witnesses; Ether 5:2-4 and 2 Nephi 27:12-13 promise them.

sources.name: Dan Vogel, 'The Validity of the Witnesses' Testimonies,' in American Apocrypha (Signature Books, 2002)
David Whitmer, An Address to All Believers in Christ (1887) — primary text
Martin Harris, collected primary statements (LDS-produced archive printing the 'spiritual eyes' statements alongside affirmations)

response: Four replies, and the first is the strongest fact on that side. Not one of the eleven ever took it back. That includes Cowdery, Harris and Whitmer, after bitter church trials threw them out. Taking it back then would have cost nothing and won them vindication. Whitmer never returned. Yet he restated it to hostile interviewers for 50 years, and had it carved on his gravestone. Second, the Eight Witnesses' account is plain and in daylight. They 'hefted' and 'handled' the plates. No angel was involved. That is a different kind of evidence, and the 'spiritual eyes' point does not touch it. Third, Richard Lloyd Anderson wrote Investigating the Book of Mormon Witnesses in 1981. He shows that 'spiritual eyes' in that century often meant real sight granted by the Spirit, as at 2 Kings 6:17. Most such quotes are late, secondhand, or hostile paraphrase. Fourth, the Whitmer point cuts the other way. A man who denounced Smith and never came back is the hardest witness of all to explain by social pressure.

responseSource.name: Richard Lloyd Anderson, Investigating the Book of Mormon Witnesses (Deseret Book, 1981); FAIR

rationale:
This one is genuinely two-sided. It is the strongest surviving Latter-day Saint position in this list. The record of never taking it back is real and not easily brushed off. Whitmer above all.

Against that, the witnesses were not outsiders. They were kin and business partners in one venture. Their view of knowing counted a vision as seeing. And Harris later gave the same kind of backing to the Shaker 'Sacred Roll'. That costs his word some of its value as a test.

Be wary of any source that calls this settled. The criticism is weaker than critics claim, and the answer stronger. But sincere men prove sincerity, not what was there.

plain.d: Eleven men signed statements printed in the front of every Book of Mormon. Three describe an angel and a voice; eight describe handling the plates. It is the strongest evidence the book has, and it deserves serious treatment.

plain.t: What is worth knowing about them
plain.d: All eleven were Smith family, Whitmer family, or Martin Harris. None was an outsider. And all of them lived in a world where seeing by "second sight" was normal.

plain.t: How some of them described it
plain.d: Harris spoke of seeing "with the eyes of faith" and "spiritual eyes." Stephen Burnett's 1838 letter reports Harris saying so publicly.

plain.t: Their answer, and it is strong
plain.d: Not one of the eleven ever took it back. Not Cowdery. Not Harris. Not Whitmer — even after being thrown out of the church, when taking it back would have cost nothing. Whitmer never came back to the church, and reaffirmed it as he was dying.
Genuinely arguable, and this is the best card the other side holds. Treat it with respect.
"What do you make of the 'spiritual eyes' language? I'm asking honestly."

refwhy.Deuteronomy 19:15: 'At the mouth of two or three witnesses.' The biblical rule the whole arrangement copies.
refwhy.2 Corinthians 13:1: Paul repeating that rule. Together these show the format was chosen, not stumbled into.
refwhy.Testimony of Three Witnesses: The statement at the front of every copy. An angel and a voice — the visionary half of the evidence.
refwhy.Testimony of Eight Witnesses: The other statement, and the stronger one for them. Plain daylight handling, with no angel in it.
refwhy.Ether 5:2–4: The book predicts its own witnesses: 'unto three shall they be shown by the power of God.'
refwhy.2 Nephi 27:12–13: The same promise again. Three witnesses, and no one else shall view it. The plan was in the text first.

titleLong: The Three and Eight Witnesses: visionary 'spiritual eyes' language and later religious careers
responseLead: Not one of the eleven ever took it back, even when it would have cost nothing.
rationaleLead: The best card they hold: treat it with respect, and do not call it settled.

title: No outsider ever examined the gold plates
claim: The plates were reportedly kept covered or hidden. They were shown only to insiders Smith chose — family, financial backers, early believers. The Three Witnesses saw them in vision. The Eight saw them in a private setting. Then they were returned to the angel. So no scholar, no scientist and no neutral third party ever inspected them. Weight estimates from those who hefted the covered object cluster around 40 to 60 pounds. A solid gold block of the described size would weigh well over 100 to 200 pounds. The object at the centre of the founding claim is gone for good, and cannot be checked.

sources.name: Mormonr, 'The weight of the plates' (Q&A with primary quotes)
FAIR, 'Weight and size of the gold plates'
Scripture Central, 'Composition of the plates' (tumbaga argument)
Mormon Stories, 'Book of Mormon Witnesses' (critical analysis)

response:
Apologists argue that the reported weight fits a real ancient object. Tumbaga is a copper-gold alloy, gilded at the surface, and it was used in Mesoamerica. Plates of the size described, made of tumbaga, would weigh roughly 53 to 58 pounds. They would look like gold. A forger guessing at 'gold plates' would be unlikely to land there.

The return to the angel is explained from scripture. The record was not meant to convince by proof. Ether 5 says witnesses were appointed instead. And Richard Lloyd Anderson's work shows those witnesses held to it for life.

responseSource.name: Scripture Central, 'Composition of the plates'

rationale:
The core fact is conceded on all sides. No independent examination ever happened, and none is possible now.

The tumbaga answer makes the reported weight of 40 to 60 pounds add up, where solid gold that size would run well past 100. It still cannot stand in for the missing object.

What is left in dispute is only how much the insider witnesses can carry instead.

plain.d: The plates were shown only to people Joseph Smith chose. Family. Money backers. Early believers. Then they were returned to the angel. No scholar or neutral party ever saw them, and none ever can.

plain.t: What that does and does not mean
plain.d: It is not proof of anything on its own. Plenty of genuine ancient objects are lost. But it does mean the central physical evidence for the book is permanently unavailable for testing.

An interesting one. Witnesses put the plates at 40 to 60 pounds. Solid gold that size would weigh about 200. But tumbaga is different — a copper-gold mix used in Central America, gilded on the surface. Plates that size in tumbaga would weigh about 53 to 58 pounds, and look like gold. That fits a real object better than a forger would have guessed.
Strong for you on the main point, but give them the tumbaga argument first. It is a good one, and pretending otherwise costs you.
"Is there anything that could be examined today, either way?"

refwhy.Testimony of Eight Witnesses: The only claim of ordinary handling of the plates. It is also the nearest thing to an examination that ever happened.

titleLong: The gold plates were never examined by any independent party
responseLead: Tumbaga is a copper-gold mix, and plates of that size would weigh what they said.
rationaleLead: Strong for you, but hand them the tumbaga point first, because it is a good one.

title: The Kinderhook forgery, and what Smith actually said
claim: In 1843 three men made six bell-shaped brass plates, cut fake 'ancient' characters into them, and planted them in an Illinois mound. They then delivered them to Joseph Smith, to test whether he would translate them. Smith's clerk William Clayton recorded that Smith said the plates held 'the history of the person with whom they were found… a descendant of Ham through the loins of Pharaoh.' That statement entered the official History of the Church in the first person: 'I have translated a portion of them.' Wilbur Fugate confessed the hoax in 1879. Testing in 1980 destroyed part of a plate and confirmed a nineteenth-century brass fake.

sources.name: Stanley B. Kimball, 'Kinderhook Plates… Appear to Be a Nineteenth-Century Hoax,' Ensign (August 1981) — the church's own publication of the testing results
William Clayton journal, 1 May 1843 (primary)
Utah Lighthouse Ministry (Tanner), 'The Kinderhook Plates' — documentation of the History of the Church first-person conversion

response:
This is the church's own current published position. Joseph Smith never claimed a revealed translation, and never produced a translated text.

Don Bradley and Mark Ashurst-McGee, in 'President Joseph Has Translated a Portion' (2011), identify a specific character match against Smith's Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar. That makes the identification a plain comparison, not a revelation. Smith took the matter no further and dropped the subject. That is the opposite of a con artist walking into a baited trap.

The first-person wording is a known artifact of the History of the Church, which turned clerks' journals into Smith's voice. And the church published the forgery finding itself, in the Ensign in 1981.

responseSource.name: Church History Topics: 'Kinderhook Plates'

rationale:
The Bradley and Ashurst-McGee work is decisive, and it is good scholarship rather than spin. The 'descendant of Ham' line traces to a character match against Smith's own Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar. So it was a plain comparison, not a revealed reading. And the church made the forgery finding public itself.

What is left is narrower than critics present. The match was still wrong, because the characters mean nothing at all. That bears on how far the Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar can be trusted.

And that leads straight to the Book of Abraham case, where the same papers are the problem. Treat Kinderhook as answered on its own terms.

plain.d: In 1843 three men in Illinois made six small brass plates. They covered them in made-up "ancient" writing, buried them in a mound, and brought them to Joseph Smith. The point was to see whether he would translate them.

His clerk William Clayton recorded that Smith said the plates contained the history of a descendant of Ham. The plates were later proved a hoax; one of the makers admitted it, and metal testing in 1980 confirmed a nineteenth-century origin.

And the church's own published position agrees with much of it. Smith never produced a translation. He never claimed revelation about them. Don Bradley and Mark Ashurst-McGee argue he was trying a scholarly comparison, using his Egyptian alphabet papers.
This one has a clear answer, and the answer goes largely their way. Clayton's entry is secondhand, and no translation exists. Use it as evidence about method, not as a knockout.
"What do you make of the Kinderhook episode? I've read the church's account of it."

titleLong: The Kinderhook plates: Joseph Smith and a known 19th-century forgery
responseLead: He made no translation at all, and the church itself published the hoax finding.
rationaleLead: This one is answered: use it about method, not as a knockout.

title: 'View of the Hebrews', studied privately by Roberts
claim: Two books from the 1800s are offered as sources. First, Ethan Smith's View of the Hebrews, of 1823 and 1825. It argued that American Indians came from the lost tribes, and it was printed in the town where Oliver Cowdery's family lived. B. H. Roberts, a General Authority, privately compiled a 291-page study of it. He listed about 26 structural likenesses: a divided people, a buried ancient record, the Urim and Thummim, Egyptian writing. It was printed after his death, in 1985. Second, a 2013 computer study compared over 100,000 books printed before 1830. It found a strong word-string match with The Late War, by Gilbert Hunt, from 1816 — a school book about the War of 1812, written on purpose in King James style. Shared items include 'curious workmanship' and the shape of the battle scenes. Critics offer both as evidence that the Book of Mormon came out of its own time and place. Alma 46:12-13, 3 Nephi 24-25 and the shape of Ether are the passages cited, against Ezekiel 37:15-20 and Isaiah 18.

sources.name: B. H. Roberts, Studies of the Book of Mormon (University of Illinois Press, 1985)
Chris and Duane Johnson, 'The Late War and the Book of Mormon' (n-gram corpus study, 2013)
Ryan Thomas, 'The Book of Mormon and The Late War: Direct Literary Dependence?' — a non-apologist critic's negative methodological assessment
MRM, 'The Late War and the Book of Mormon'

response: Three replies. Roberts drew no conclusion of dependence. He framed the work as questions a believer must be able to answer, and he died affirming the Book of Mormon. Using him for the prosecution misstates what he said. There is also no evidence Joseph Smith saw View of the Hebrews before 1830, and he cited it warmly in 1842 as support. That is how a man behaves who found it later. Second, the likenesses are generic to a whole genre of the 1820s about Hebrew origins for the Indians. The books differ on nearly every point. View of the Hebrews has no Christ, no story and no named people. And the Book of Mormon flatly denies the lost-ten-tribes idea it is built on. Third, on The Late War, 75 of the 'significant' matches come from the boilerplate copyright pages. The rest is mostly the King James register both books set out to imitate. The method detects 'wrote in biblical English'. The sharpest attack on it came from Ryan Thomas, who does not accept Book of Mormon historicity either.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'View of the Hebrews theory' and 'The Late War theory'

rationale:
The direct-source claims are among the weakest material critics use. Hunting parallels across a huge body of books is unreliable. The copyright-page problem in the Johnson study is a real defect. And a critic himself rejects direct literary dependence. Roberts is routinely misused.

What survives is the modest version, and it is well supported. The Book of Mormon is at home in the religious culture of New England in the 1820s. Hebrew origins for the Indians. Anti-Masonic language. The fights over grace and universal salvation behind Alma 40-42.

That shows the ideas were in the air. It does not show copying. The King James and Isaiah dating entries are the strong textual case.

plain.t: Two books that were around before 1830
plain.d: Ethan Smith's View of the Hebrews (1823) argued American Indians descended from the lost tribes of Israel. It was published in the town where Oliver Cowdery's family lived. And Gilbert Hunt's The Late War (1816) retold the War of 1812 in King James English for schoolchildren.

B. H. Roberts, a senior Latter-day Saint leader and historian, privately compiled a 291-page study listing about 26 structural similarities with View of the Hebrews — a divided people, a buried record, and more.

Roberts drew no conclusion of dependence. He framed the work as questions a believer must be able to answer, and he died affirming the Book of Mormon. Using him as a witness for the prosecution misrepresents what he said.
Genuinely arguable. Parallels are easy to find and easy to overstate. The honest version is narrow: these ideas were in the air, in that region, in that decade.
"Have you read what B. H. Roberts actually wrote? He was one of yours."

refwhy.Ezekiel 37:15–20: The two sticks, Judah and Joseph. The Bible verse both Ethan Smith and Latter-day Saints build on.
refwhy.Isaiah 18: 'A nation scattered and peeled.' Ethan Smith read that as America — the sort of reading in the air then.
refwhy.Alma 46:12–13: The title of liberty. Offered as a match for the battle scenes in The Late War, and one of the weaker parallels.
refwhy.3 Nephi 24–25: Malachi given to the Nephites. It turns up in the parallel lists, but the King James cases cover it better.
refwhy.Ether 1–15 (structure): The Jaredite story, cited for its shape. A people crossing water, a buried record, a nation wiped out.

titleLong: Claimed 19th-century sources: View of the Hebrews and The Late War
responseLead: Roberts drew no such conclusion, and 75 of the Late War matches are boilerplate.
rationaleLead: Weak as stated: the ideas were in the air, but copying is not shown.

title: Abraham's papyrus was a Theban priest's funeral text
claim: Unlike the gold plates, the source documents for the Book of Abraham exist. Smith bought Egyptian papyri in 1835. He declared one roll 'the writings of Abraham while he was in Egypt,' and published the Book of Abraham in 1842. Fragments were rediscovered in 1966. Egyptologists identified them, definitively in Robert Ritner's complete edition of 2011. They are the Breathing Permit of the priest Hor, and portions of the Book of the Dead.
