Those are standard Ptolemaic funeral texts, about 1,500 years after Abraham. They contain no reference to Abraham at all. Smith's own Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar maps single characters from the surviving Hor fragment onto long English paragraphs of the published book. And his printed readings of the three facsimiles do not match what Egyptologists read; the female figures in Facsimile 3 are called male kings. This is the only outside, controlled test of Joseph Smith's ability to translate an ancient document. It fails. Abraham 1:1-3 and Genesis 11-12 are the texts at issue.

sources.name: Robert K. Ritner (University of Chicago Oriental Institute), The Joseph Smith Egyptian Papyri: A Complete Edition (Signature Books, 2011)
Robert K. Ritner, 'The "Breathing Permit of Hor" Thirty-four Years Later,' Dialogue 33/4 (2000)
Institute for Religious Research, 'Translation and Historicity of the Book of Abraham — A Response'
Gospel Topics Essay — official concession: 'the characters on the fragments do not match the translation given in the book of Abraham'

response:
Two defences, both backed in the church's own essay.

The first is the missing-scroll theory, from John Gee and Kerry Muhlestein at BYU. The fragments we have are a small remnant. Eyewitnesses describe a long roll. Gee works out that about 314 centimetres of the Hor roll are missing. And much of the collection is thought to have burned in the Chicago fire of 1871. On that view the Abraham text sat on papyrus we do not have.

The second is the catalyst theory. Joseph's study of the papyri 'provided an occasion for meditation, reflection, and revelation'. God then gave him a revelation about Abraham 'even if that revelation did not directly correlate to the characters'.

Two supports follow. The Kirtland Egyptian Papers may be a later attempt by scribes to work backwards from a text already given. And apologists point to old parallels for content not in Genesis. Abraham nearly sacrificed. Abraham teaching the stars. And the name 'Olishem', which may match the attested place-name Ulisum. Those sit in traditions outside the Bible that Smith is unlikely to have known.

responseSource.name: Gospel Topics Essay, 'Translation and Historicity of the Book of Abraham'; Gee and Muhlestein (BYU Studies)

rationale:
This is the strongest outside test in the whole corpus. The source document exists, and Egyptology is a mature science with no Latter-day Saint stake in it. The church has conceded the core fact in an official essay. Robert Ritner's complete edition of 2011 settled the reading.

The two defences each make sense alone. Together they are telling, because they contradict each other. Either the Abraham text was on a lost papyrus, which makes the translation real and the fragments beside the point. Or the papyri were only a prompt, which makes the lost scroll beside the point.

The missing-scroll theory has one problem it has not overcome. Smith's own Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar lines up characters from the surviving fragment against verses of the Book of Abraham. That puts his working source in documents we hold.

The catalyst theory cannot be tested. And it dissolves the word 'translation' as the church used it for 130 years, which drains force from the Book of Mormon claim too. Parallels such as Olishem are of the weak type flagged elsewhere, and cannot offset a direct mismatch in decipherment.

plain.t: Why this case is different from all the others
plain.d: The source document survives. For the Book of Mormon the plates are gone. Here, we have the papyri.

In 1835 Joseph Smith bought Egyptian papyri from a travelling mummy exhibition. He declared one roll to be "the writings of Abraham while he was in Egypt" and published the Book of Abraham in 1842. The papyri were thought lost, then rediscovered in 1966.

plain.t: What they turned out to be
plain.d: Ordinary Egyptian funeral texts. A Book of Breathings, made for a Theban priest named Hor, from about the second century BC. That is roughly 1,500 years after Abraham. Every Egyptologist who has looked at them agrees, including Latter-day Saint ones.

Two defences, both in the church's own essay. The missing-scroll idea says the surviving pieces are a small remnant. The Abraham text was on a part now lost. The catalyst idea says the papyri only prompted revelation. On that view the words were never on them at all.
Strong for you — this is the single most testable claim in the whole section. But note what the catalyst theory concedes: that the words are not on the papyri at all.
"The church says Egyptologists read these differently than he did. What do you make of that?"

refwhy.Genesis 11–12: The Bible's own Abraham story. The Book of Abraham adds material not found here, which is what needs a source.
refwhy.Abraham 1:1–3 (Pearl of Great Price): The opening of the published text. These English words were said to come from a papyrus we can now read.

titleLong: The Book of Abraham papyri: the one case where Joseph Smith's source text survives
responseLead: Either the long roll is lost, or the papyri only prompted what God gave him.
rationaleLead: Strong for you: the two defences are each fair, and they cancel each other.

title: Word-print studies settle nothing, BYU or Rigdon
claim: Two opposed bodies of computer work on authorship exist. On the pro-historicity side, Larsen, Rencher and Layton in BYU Studies in 1980, and Hilton in BYU Studies in 1990. They reported that the Book of Mormon's internal narrators can be told apart, from each other and from Joseph Smith. On the other side, Jockers, Witten and Criddle, in Literary and Linguistic Computing in 2008. They applied a method called nearest-shrunken-centroid, and concluded that the chapters point most strongly to Solomon Spalding and Sidney Rigdon. That would support the Spalding-Rigdon theory of how the book was written.

sources.name: Jockers, Witten, Criddle, 'Reassessing authorship of the Book of Mormon…,' Literary and Linguistic Computing 23/4 (2008)
Larsen, Rencher, Layton, 'Who Wrote the Book of Mormon? An Analysis of Wordprints,' BYU Studies 20/3 (1980)
Hilton, 'On Verifying Wordprint Studies,' BYU Studies 30/3 (1990)
Roper, Fields, Schaalje, 'Stylometric Analyses of the Book of Mormon: A Short History,' JBMS 21/1 (2012)

response:
G. Bruce Schaalje, a BYU statistician, and his colleagues found the decisive flaw. The method is a closed-set classifier. Its own maths obliges it to assign every chapter to one of the candidates you give it. Joseph Smith's own writings were largely left out of the pool, while Rigdon and Spalding were put in.

Schaalje extended the method so it could return 'author not in the set', and reran it on the same data. Rigdon and Spalding each scored 0%. The chance of an author outside the set came out at 93%.

Separately, the Spalding-Rigdon theory is rejected by nearly all historians of Mormonism, believers and non-believers alike. Fawn Brodie and Dan Vogel both reject it. The documents give Rigdon no traceable contact with Smith before late 1830, after the book was printed.

responseSource.name: Schaalje, Fields, Roper, 'Examining a Misapplication of NSC Classification' (Mormon Studies Review)

rationale:
This one is lopsided, and worth using as a lesson in method. The critical study is the weaker one. Schaalje's closed-set objection is correct, and mainstream historians reject Spalding-Rigdon on other grounds. Treat that study as answered.

But the studies on the other side do not therefore win. Telling several voices apart does not tell an ancient author from one writer making distinct characters. That is a known limit of the method on fiction. And the same 'author not in the set' logic cuts against any positive ancient attribution.

Stylometry as now practised cannot settle who wrote the Book of Mormon, in either direction. Discount confident claims from either camp.

plain.d: Writers have measurable habits — how often they use small words like of and and. Statisticians have tried to use those fingerprints to work out who wrote the Book of Mormon.

BYU studies by Larsen, Rencher and Layton (1980) and Hilton (1990) found the book's internal narrators are statistically distinguishable from each other and from Joseph Smith. Jockers, Witten and Criddle (2008) pointed instead toward Sidney Rigdon and Solomon Spalding.

BYU statistician Bruce Schaalje identified it. The Jockers method is a closed-set classifier: it is mathematically obliged to assign every chapter to one of the candidates you feed it. If the real author is not on the list, it will still return a confident answer.
Genuinely arguable, and honestly neither side settles anything. Do not cite either study as proof — the method is contested enough that both results should be held loosely.
Nothing. This is a case to know about so you don't get caught using it.

titleLong: Stylometry: the Spalding–Rigdon study vs. the BYU wordprints — why neither settles authorship
responseLead: Schaalje showed the method must pick from your list; Rigdon and Spalding scored 0%.
rationaleLead: Neither side settles this: do not cite either study as proof.

title: Joseph Smith adds a prophecy of himself to Genesis
claim: Joseph Smith's revision of the Bible, made between 1830 and 1833, expands Genesis 50 with roughly 14 verses. In JST Genesis 50:24-38 the patriarch Joseph prophesies a latter-day 'choice seer' named Joseph, whose father is also named Joseph. That matches Joseph Smith Jr., son of Joseph Smith Sr. The same prophecy appears at 2 Nephi 3:6-18 and 4:1-2, which quote the 'lost' Genesis material. No ancient version contains this passage. Not a Hebrew manuscript. Not the Septuagint. Not a Dead Sea Scroll, the Samaritan Pentateuch, or any targum. The entire known textual tradition of Genesis ends chapter 50 without it.

left.text: And his name shall be called after me; and it shall be after the name of his father. And he shall be like unto me; for the thing, which the Lord shall bring forth by his hand, by the power of the Lord shall bring my people unto salvation.

right.ref: Genesis 50:24 (KJV) — how every known manuscript ends
right.text: And Joseph said unto his brethren, I die: and God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land unto the land which he sware to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.

hl: his name shall be called after me
after the name of his father
comparison.note: A prophecy naming the revelator himself — 'Joseph, son of Joseph' — appears in zero ancient witnesses: not the Masoretic text, not the Septuagint, not the Dead Sea Scrolls, not the Samaritan Pentateuch.

sources.name: JST Genesis 50 (official LDS scripture text)
FAIR: Relationship between the JST and biblical manuscripts
BYU Religious Studies Center: The Contribution of the JST
2026 LDS Seminary manual lesson on JST Genesis 50 (current official use)

response:
Latter-day Saint scholars grant that no ancient copy has the passage. Robert Matthews and Kent Jackson say so, and FAIR follows them.

Their argument is that the revision was never meant only to restore lost words. It can be restored content. It can be inspired comment. It can be a bringing together of texts, or a prophetic expansion shaped for a latter-day audience.

On that view, JST Genesis 50 may restore a real prophecy kept on the brass plates. That is why it also stands at 2 Nephi 3. It would have dropped out of the Hebrew line very early. Or it may be new content that was never in the Bible at all. Either way it rests on revelation, not on old copies.

responseSource.name: FAIR: The JST as a restoration of the original Bible text

rationale:
The textual fact is conceded on all sides. No ancient witness contains the passage. Not the Hebrew, not the Septuagint, not a Dead Sea Scroll, not the Samaritan Pentateuch, not a targum. And the prophecy names the man who produced it.

The reply does not rebut the evidence. It reclassifies the revision so that missing manuscript support cannot count against it. That is untestable rather than a refutation.

plain.t: What Joseph Smith added to Genesis
plain.d: He made his own version of the whole Bible. In it, Genesis 50 gains about fourteen new verses. In them the dying Joseph of Egypt foretells a "choice seer" who will be named Joseph. That seer's father will be called Joseph too.
Joseph Smith Jr. His father was Joseph Smith Sr.
Nothing like it. Not the Hebrew. Not the Dead Sea Scrolls. Not the Greek. Not the Samaritan text. No ancient copy of Genesis has these verses.
Robert Matthews and Kent Jackson agree no old copy has it. They argue the revision was never meant to restore lost words only. It could be new revelation, or added comment.
Strong for you. That answer is honest, and it gives the point away. A prophecy naming the translator was put into Genesis by the translator.
"Which ancient manuscript has those verses in Genesis 50?"

refwhy.Genesis 50:22–26 (KJV): How Genesis really ends. Joseph dies, and no seer is foretold. Read it and the addition stands out.
refwhy.JST Genesis 50:24–38: The added verses themselves. About fourteen of them, and no ancient copy of Genesis has any.
refwhy.2 Nephi 3:6–18: The same prophecy inside the Book of Mormon. 'A choice seer will I raise up out of the fruit of thy loins.'
refwhy.2 Nephi 4:1–2: Nephi says Joseph's prophecies 'are written upon the plates of brass.' The claimed source for the missing Genesis text.

titleLong: JST Genesis 50: Joseph Smith inserts a prophecy of himself with no manuscript support
responseLead: The added verses need not be lost text; they can be given by God.
rationaleLead: Strong for you: the answer is honest, and it gives the point away.

title: The angel was named Nephi, then Moroni
claim: Joseph Smith's official manuscript history of 1838 and 1839 names the angel of the gold plates 'Nephi,' not Moroni. It was published that way under his own editorship, in the Times and Seasons of 15 April 1842. The 'Nephi' reading was reprinted in the Millennial Star in 1842, in the first edition of the Pearl of Great Price in 1851, and in Lucy Mack Smith's history of 1853. Smith lived two years after the 1842 printing and published no correction. Later editions silently emended the name to Moroni.

sources.name: Joseph Smith Papers, History 1838–1856 vol. A-1 (manuscript showing 'Nephi')
MormonThink: Did Joseph Smith see Nephi or Moroni?
FAIR: Moroni's visit — Nephi or Moroni

response:
FAIR and church historians call the 'Nephi' reading a slip by a clerk or an editor. It came in when clerks put the history together in 1838 and 1839.

Sources before 1842 already name the messenger Moroni. Oliver Cowdery's 1835 letters in the Messenger and Advocate do. So does D&C 27:5, also from 1835. So Moroni comes first in the record.

Joseph Smith did not read the proofs of every instalment of the serialised history. And the church fixed the name to match the earlier, better-attested one. Nothing was covered up.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Moroni's visit — Nephi or Moroni

rationale:
The print history is undisputed. It comes from the sources themselves. 'Nephi' stood in print from 1842 to 1853, and was later changed.

Their point that 1835 sources name Moroni first is also solid. That makes a clerk's slip quite likely.

What is left unexplained is why the slip ran on uncorrected through several official printings. It stood while Smith was alive, and after.

plain.d: Every Latter-day Saint knows him as Moroni — the last Nephite, who buried the plates and returned as an angel to reveal them.

Joseph Smith's official history, published in the Times and Seasons in April 1842 under his own editorship, names the angel Nephi. So does the Millennial Star the same year, the first edition of the Pearl of Great Price in 1851, and Lucy Mack Smith's 1853 history.

FAIR and church historians call it a copying slip. They say clerks introduced it while compiling the 1838-39 history. And they point to earlier sources that already say Moroni — Oliver Cowdery's letters from 1835.
Genuinely arguable. A clerical error is entirely possible. What makes it worth knowing is that the error survived into published scripture and stood for years.
"Have you seen the 1842 Times and Seasons? It names the angel Nephi."

titleLong: Early published accounts name the angel 'Nephi,' later changed to Moroni
responseLead: It was a clerk's slip, and sources from 1835 already name the angel Moroni.
rationaleLead: Arguable: a slip is likely, but that name stood in print from 1842 to 1853.

title: First Vision: one person in 1832, two in 1838
claim: Joseph Smith left at least four firsthand accounts of his First Vision, and they differ on core details. The 1832 account, in his own hand, describes one personage, 'the Lord.' It gives his age as about 15 or 16. It says he had already concluded that all the churches were wrong before he prayed. And it does not mention a revival. The 1835 account describes one personage followed by another, plus 'many angels.' The canonized 1838 account describes two personages, the Father and the Son, gives his age as 14, and makes an 1820 revival the trigger. The 1842 Wentworth letter describes 'two glorious personages.' The 1832 account was unpublished, and effectively unknown to members until the 1960s.

sources.name: Joseph Smith Papers: Primary accounts of the First Vision
LDS Discussions: Overview of First Vision accounts
Dialogue: 'The First Vision Controversy — A Critique and Reconciliation'
Gospel Topics essay: First Vision Accounts (church acknowledgment of the differences)

response:
The church's Gospel Topics essay acknowledges all the accounts. It argues that the differences reflect audience, purpose and memory, rather than invention.

The 1832 account stresses personal forgiveness. The 1838 account stresses the founding of the church. Retellings that grow in detail are normal when a person tells his own story many times.

Historians such as Milton Backman and James Allen argue that the accounts fit together. 'The Lord' in 1832 can cover two persons. And several tellings with shifting emphasis point to a real core experience, rather than a story being built up.

responseSource.name: Gospel Topics essay: First Vision Accounts

rationale:
The accounts and their differences are plain fact from the sources. The church itself now prints them.

What is argued is whether the differences are ordinary shifts of memory, or a story that grew. The sharpest of them are one person against two. And a search for forgiveness against a question about which church is true.

Trained historians argue both readings.

plain.d: God the Father and Jesus Christ appearing to Joseph Smith in a grove of trees. Everything else rests on it.

plain.t: He told it more than once
plain.d: At least four times in his own lifetime, and the accounts differ. The 1832 one is in his own handwriting. It describes one person, not two. It gives his age as about fifteen or sixteen. And it says he had already decided the churches were wrong before he prayed. The 1838 account — the one now in scripture — has two persons and a different order of events.

The church's own Gospel Topics essay acknowledges all the accounts. It argues the differences reflect audience, purpose and memory rather than invention: the 1832 telling is about personal forgiveness, the 1838 about which church to join.

Genuinely arguable. People do retell formative experiences differently. What is harder is that the number of persons present changes, and that most members never heard there was more than one account.
"Have you read the 1832 account in his own hand? The church published it."

titleLong: First Vision: four differing firsthand accounts (1832, 1835, 1838, 1842)
responseLead: Retellings shift with audience and purpose, and the church now publishes all four accounts.
rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. The sharp point is that one person in 1832 became two.

title: The Palmyra revival records point to 1824
claim: The canonized 1838 account ties the First Vision to an 'unusual excitement on the subject of religion' in the Palmyra area in 1820, which added 'great multitudes' to the churches. Wesley Walters examined Presbyterian, Methodist and Baptist records, in work published in 1967 and 1969. He found no significant revival or membership surge in the Palmyra area in 1819 or 1820. What he found was a large, well-documented revival in 1824 and 1825 — after Moroni's claimed visit of 1823. That suggests Smith projected the later revival back into the 1820 narrative.

sources.name: Wesley P. Walters, 'New Light on Mormon Origins from the Palmyra Revival,' Dialogue 4:1 (1969)
Walters' original 1967 article (Bulletin of the Evangelical Theological Society)
Dialogue roundtable: The Question of the Palmyra Revival (Bushman/Walters exchange, 1969)

response:
Milton Backman answered directly. He wrote 'Awakenings in the Burned-over District' in BYU Studies in 1969. He set out Methodist camp meetings near Palmyra in 1819 and 1820. He also found revival work across the wider Genesee region.

His point is that Smith described a stirring across a whole region. He did not describe a formal Palmyra revival with counted new members. The Gospel Topics essay takes that reading.

Smith was recalling his teenage years. He wrote of religious excitement in 'the whole district of country'. A Palmyra camp meeting in 1818, and an 1819 Methodist conference at nearby Vienna, fit that.

responseSource.name: Gospel Topics essay: First Vision Accounts

rationale:
Walters's blank finding stands largely unanswered in the church records. There was no 1820 Palmyra revival that added 'great multitudes' to the churches.

But Backman's camp meetings across the region in 1819 and 1820 give the 1838 account a fair looser reading.

It turns on how tightly you must read 'great multitudes' joining churches.

plain.d: That there was an "unusual excitement on the subject of religion" in the Palmyra area in 1820, which added "great multitudes" to the churches, and that this is what sent him to pray.

Wesley Walters went looking in 1967. He examined Presbyterian, Methodist and Baptist records for Palmyra and found no significant revival in 1820. The major local revival was in 1824-25 — after the date given.

Milton Backman replied in 1969, documenting Methodist camp meetings near Palmyra in 1819-20 and revival activity across the wider Genesee region. "In that region of country" is a loose phrase and need not mean Palmyra alone.
Genuinely arguable. Backman's reply is real and should be given. But the account describes multitudes joining churches locally, and the membership numbers for those years do not show it.
"When was the big revival in Palmyra? It's worth checking the church records."

titleLong: No documented 1820 Palmyra revival; the documented revival was 1824–25
responseLead: Backman found camp meetings near Palmyra in 1819 and 1820, across the wider region.
rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. The Palmyra records came back blank, but the wider reading is fair.

title: 150,000 members used a lawyer to resign
claim: To resign your membership you normally go through your bishop, and then the stake president. There are waiting periods. Leaders reach out to you. Many people who resign say the visits and calls went on, even after they asked to be left alone. Mark Naugle, a Utah lawyer, set up a free service called QuitMormon.com. It sends the demand as a lawyer, so the church has to deal with him rather than with the member. It has handled on the order of 150,000 resignations since 2015. In 2019 the church said those submissions must be notarized, citing fake requests. That added one more step.

sources.name: Salt Lake Tribune: 'LDS Church adds a new step for members using QuitMormon.com' (Aug 2019)
QuitMormon.com (the service itself)
Mormon Stories #1414: Mark Naugle — QuitMormon.com
NPR: 'More than 1,000 Mormons resign in protest' (Nov 2015)

response:
The General Handbook already sets out a free official path. A member writes to the bishop and asks that the record be removed. The request is to be honoured.

Leaders are told to check who the person is, and to make sure they know what follows. The church says those steps guard against fake or rushed removals. It says the 2019 notary rule came after real fake requests, including pranks that resigned other people.

Follow-up contact is care from lay leaders, who are taught to answer with love and not to pester. And any member may simply stop coming, with no penalty at all.

responseSource.name: General Handbook ch. 32 (membership record removal provisions)

rationale:
The facts hold up. The scale of QuitMormon, on the order of 150,000 resignations since 2015, has been reported in the mainstream press. Both sides confirm the 2019 notary rule. And the reports of contact after leaving are many.

A legal buffer is the whole point of Mark Naugle's service, and it exists because of those reports.

What is argued here is motive: care for the member, or pressure to keep them.

plain.d: You write to your bishop. The request goes on to the stake president. There are waiting periods. Leaders reach out to you. Many people who resign say the visits and calls went on. They went on even after they had asked to be left alone.

A Utah attorney named Mark Naugle set up a free service, QuitMormon.com. It sends the resignation as legal representation. The church then deals with a lawyer, not with the member. Since 2015 it has processed on the order of 150,000 resignations.
The church added a notarisation requirement for QuitMormon submissions. It cited fraudulent requests. That added a step, and friction, to resigning through a third party.

The General Handbook already sets out a free official path. A member writes to the bishop and asks that the record be removed. The request is to be honoured. Leaders are told to check who the person is. They are told to make sure the person knows what follows. The church says those steps guard against fake or rushed removals. It says the 2019 rule came after real fake requests. Some were pranks that resigned other people. Follow-up contact is care from lay leaders, who are taught to answer with love. And any member may simply stop coming, with no penalty at all.

Strong for you, and keep it factual. The scale of QuitMormon has been reported in the mainstream press. Both sides confirm the 2019 rule. And the reports of contact after leaving are many. A legal buffer is the whole point of the service. What is argued here is motive, not fact.
"If leaving is simple, why do a hundred and fifty thousand people need a lawyer to do it?"

titleLong: Formal resignation is burdensome enough that 150,000+ members have used a pro bono lawyer
responseLead: There is a free path in the Handbook, and real fake requests came first.
rationaleLead: Strong for you, and keep it factual: what is argued here is motive, not fact.

title: A parent waiting outside their child's wedding
claim: Only members holding a current temple recommend may attend a temple sealing. So family who are not members, or who have resigned, or who do not hold a recommend, must wait outside during the wedding. That includes a bride's or groom's own parents. Until May 2019, couples in the United States who held a civil ceremony first — so that excluded family could attend — were penalized with a one-year wait before sealing. That pressured couples to choose the temple over excluded relatives. The First Presidency removed the one-year penalty in 2019, explicitly citing families feeling excluded. The recommend requirement for attending sealings is unchanged.

sources.name: Religion News Service: 'Mormon leaders change policy on temple weddings' (May 2019, quotes First Presidency letter)
Mormonism Research Ministry: 'The exclusion of non-Mormons at temple weddings'
General Handbook ch. 27: Temple ordinances for the living (current policy)

response:
The church holds that the temple is a sacred space, and that its ordinances ask for covenant worthiness. That is the same standard applied to everyone for any temple ordinance. It is not aimed at wedding guests.

The 2019 First Presidency change was made expressly so that 'when a temple marriage would cause parents or immediate family members to feel excluded, a civil marriage followed by a temple sealing is authorized'.

So couples may now hold a fully inclusive civil wedding first and be sealed straight after. The church presents that as solving the family problem while keeping the temple holy.

responseSource.name: First Presidency policy change as reported with full quotation (RNS)

rationale:
The rule and the old one-year wait are church policy, set down in writing.

The church's own 2019 letter names the harm it was easing. That change is a real improvement, and you should say so.

It also confirms the underlying claim rather than answering it. The recommend rule for a sealing has not changed. A parent without one still waits outside.

plain.d: Only members with a current temple recommend may attend a sealing. So a parent who is not a member, or has resigned, or does not hold a recommend, waits outside while their child is married.

In the United States, a couple could hold a civil ceremony first, so that the excluded family could be there. If they did, they then had to wait a year to be sealed. That pushed couples to choose the temple over the people who could not come in.
The First Presidency removed the one-year wait in May 2019. Their letter gave the reason plainly: families were feeling excluded. The recommend rule for attending a sealing is unchanged.

That the temple is a sacred place, and its ordinances ask for covenant worthiness. The same bar applies to everyone, for every temple rite. It is not aimed at wedding guests. And the 2019 letter says its own reason: "when a temple marriage would cause parents or immediate family members to feel excluded, a civil marriage followed by a temple sealing is authorized." So a couple may now hold a wedding that no one is shut out of, and be sealed right after.

They admit this themselves. The rule and the old one-year penalty are documented church policy. The 2019 letter names the harm it was fixing. That change is a real improvement, and you should say so. It also confirms the underlying facts rather than answering them.
"Would your parents be able to come in?"

titleLong: Temple weddings exclude family without recommends — including parents of the couple
responseLead: The temple asks the same of everyone, and the one-year wait went in 2019.
rationaleLead: They admit this: the 2019 letter names the very harm it was fixing.

title: Leave the church, lose your BYU degree
claim: BYU asks every student for a yearly sign-off from a church leader. It calls this an ecclesiastical endorsement. BYU's own written policy says the sign-off is pulled at once if a student is excommunicated, disfellowshipped, or resigns. Losing it costs a great deal. Good Honor Code standing. The right to stay enrolled. A job on campus. A room on campus. Even the degree itself, if the course work is done. So a student who stops believing in the middle of a degree faces being thrown out, or years of hiding it. Students who were never members may attend, at a higher fee. A member who leaves is therefore treated worse than someone who was never baptized. FreeBYU took the matter to the accrediting bodies and lost. A narrow appeal route was added in 2015 and 2016.

sources.name: BYU Honor Code Office: Withdrawn or denied ecclesiastical endorsements (official policy)
BYU Student Standing Policy
KSL: 'BYU adjusts honor code policies for students who leave LDS Church' (2016)
The Daily Universe: 'Ex-Mormon BYU alumni group seeks to force honor code change' (FreeBYU)

response:
BYU says it is a private religious school, paid for in large part by tithing. Latter-day Saint students pay a much lower fee, and the faith community makes up the rest.

The deal is stated up front. Stay in good standing with the church that funds you. Students agree to it when they enrol.

BYU notes that the accrediting bodies and the American Bar Association have upheld its right to set religious terms. An appeal route now exists for students who resign. And every student needs the yearly sign-off, including those who are not members. They just do not need to be members.

responseSource.name: BYU Honor Code Office: Ecclesiastical endorsements and resources

rationale:
The policy is set out word for word in BYU's own papers. Leaving the church pulls the sign-off, and pulling the sign-off ends the right to stay enrolled. So the facts come from the school itself.

What is really in dispute is what to call it. A private school setting religious terms, or a penalty for changing your mind.

Ask it as a question, not as a charge.

plain.d: BYU asks every student for a yearly sign-off from a church leader. It calls that an ecclesiastical endorsement. BYU's own written policy says the sign-off is pulled at once if a student is cut off from the church, put under formal discipline, or simply resigns.
Good standing under the Honor Code. The right to stay enrolled. A job on campus. A room on campus. And the degree itself, even if all the course work is done.

A student who stops believing halfway through a degree faces being thrown out. Or years of hiding it. A student who was never a member may attend, at a higher fee. So a member who leaves is treated worse than someone never baptised. FreeBYU took the matter to the accrediting bodies and lost. A narrow appeal route was added in 2015 and 2016.

BYU is a private religious school, paid for in large part by tithing. Latter-day Saint students pay a much lower fee, and the faith community makes up the rest. The deal is stated up front. Stay in good standing with the church that funds you. Students agree to that when they enrol. BYU notes that the accrediting bodies and the American Bar Association have upheld its right to set religious terms. An appeal route now exists for a student who resigns. And every student needs the yearly sign-off, member or not.

They admit this themselves; the rule is in BYU's own papers. So do not argue about the facts. The real question is what to call it. A private school setting religious terms, or a penalty for changing your mind. Ask it as a question, not as a charge.
"What happens to a BYU student who stops believing in their third year?"

titleLong: BYU students who formally leave the church lose enrollment eligibility
responseLead: A private school may set its own terms, and tithing pays most of the cost.
rationaleLead: They admit this: the rule is in BYU's own papers, so argue about the name.

title: Leaving costs family, friends and community
claim: People who leave often report strain in a marriage, being cut off by family, losing their community, and being pushed to the edge. Those patterns are set out in reporting at NPR and HuffPost, and in thousands of gathered accounts. Two things drive them. First, Latter-day Saint teaching: a family split by faith loses the hope of being sealed for ever. Second, the word 'apostate' carries heavy weight. Boyd K. Packer's 1993 talk named 'so-called scholars,' feminists and gays as the church's three dangers, and that shaped the mood. Note one thing. Unlike the Jehovah's Witnesses, this church has no formal rule to shun. So the costs are social and family ones, not ones the church orders.

sources.name: NPR: 'Shunned ex-Mormons form own communities' (2005)
HuffPost: 'Do Mormons Shun?'
Faith After Mormonism: 'Feeling shunned after leaving Mormonism' (collected experiences)

response:
Church leaders have spoken against cutting off family who leave, more than once and by name. Elder D. Todd Christofferson said in public that he 'would not cut that child out of family life'.

Official teaching tells members to keep loving and including family who go. There is no teaching, handbook rule, or discipline that tells a member to shun.

The church would add that broken ties follow a change of faith in many traditions. That is how families behave, rather than what the church asks.

responseSource.name: Compiled Holland/Christofferson statements on members who leave

rationale:
The costs themselves are well attested, in reporting at NPR and HuffPost and in a great mass of first-hand accounts.

The harder claim is that the church causes them, and that one is genuinely argued. The written policy tells members not to shun. The teaching and the rhetoric can still push people apart. Boyd K. Packer's 1993 talk, naming 'so-called scholars', feminists and gays as dangers, shaped the mood.

Both things are true at once. The harm is real, and there is no order to shun.

plain.d: Strain in a marriage. Being cut off by family. Losing the community. Being pushed to the edge of a world that was everything. NPR and HuffPost have reported these patterns, and thousands of first-hand accounts say the same.

Part of it is teaching. A family split by faith loses the hope of being sealed for ever. And the word apostate carries real weight. Boyd K. Packer's 1993 talk named "so-called scholars," feminists and gays as dangers, and that shaped the mood.

There is no formal shunning here. Unlike the Jehovah's Witnesses, this church has no rule that tells a member to cut anyone off. No teaching, no handbook line, no discipline. Say that plainly, because it is true.

Church leaders have spoken against it, more than once and by name. Elder D. Todd Christofferson said in public that he "would not cut that child out of family life." Official teaching tells members to keep loving family who go. And broken ties follow a change of faith in many traditions. That is how families behave, not what the church asks.

Genuinely arguable, and both halves are true at once. The harm is well attested. So is the lack of any order to shun. What is argued is whether the church drives it. The written rule tells people not to pull away. The teaching and the mood can still reward it.
"What would change at home if you stopped going?"

titleLong: Leaving carries documented family and social costs — though the church formally discourages shunning
responseLead: There is no rule to shun, and Christofferson said he would not cut a child off.
rationaleLead: Arguable, and both halves are true: real harm, but no order to shun.

title: Alyssa Grenfell on what leaving cost her
claim: Alyssa Grenfell went to BYU. She now writes and posts as an ex-Mormon, with about 570,000 subscribers on YouTube. Her 2023 book is 'How to Leave the Mormon Church: An Exmormon's Guide to Rebuilding After Religion.' In it, and on her channel, she sets out three things. Members who step away keep being contacted and visited by ward representatives. Wearing the garment each day works as a check on the body, so giving it up is a signal others can see, and it costs you. And pulling a faith apart costs you your sense of self, your family and your friends. Her book is one person's testimony. Its central facts are backed up elsewhere. Contact after leaving matches what the resignation cases show, and garment rules are set out in the church's own General Handbook at 38.5.

sources.name: Alyssa Grenfell (background and reception)
Grenfell, How to Leave the Mormon Church (2023)
Mormonish podcast interview with Grenfell
General Handbook 38.5: Temple garment expectations (corroborating policy)

response:
The church does not answer memoirs by former members. Its standing position is that a member who steps away is still loved and still welcome.

Ministering visits are freely given care, and they stop when a person asks, or resigns. The garment is a sacred private covenant, taken freely in the temple. It is not a way of watching anyone.

Apologists would add two things. A paid ex-Mormon media career has its own pull. And one life should not stand in for a church of 17 million.

responseSource.name: General Handbook (ministering, garments, and record removal provisions)

rationale:
Her main claims hold up at the level of pattern. Contact after leaving, garment rules at General Handbook 38.5, and the social cost of going are all backed by church papers and by outside reporting.

The book itself is one person's word on particular events, and it is badged that way here.

It belongs on the site as a voice for a pattern that is documented. It does not stand as proof on its own.

plain.d: Alyssa Grenfell. A BYU graduate, now an ex-Mormon writer with a YouTube channel of about 570,000 subscribers. Her book is How to Leave the Mormon Church: An Exmormon's Guide to Rebuilding After Religion, from 2023.

Three things. That ward representatives keep contacting and visiting after a member has stepped away. That wearing the garment every day works as a kind of bodily check, so stopping is a visible and costly signal. And that deconstruction costs you identity, family and friends.

plain.t: How much of it is checkable
plain.d: The pattern is. Continued contact after leaving matches what the resignation and QuitMormon cases document. Garment expectations are set out in the church's own General Handbook, at 38.5. Specific incidents in a memoir are one person's testimony, and should be labelled that way.

The church does not reply to individual memoirs. Its standing position is that members who step away are still loved and welcome. Ministering visits are voluntary pastoral care, and they stop when a person asks or resigns. The garment is a sacred private covenant freely taken in the temple, not surveillance. Apologists would add that a monetised ex-Mormon media career has its own incentives, and that one story should not stand for a church of 17 million.

Genuinely arguable, and use it carefully. Her core claims are corroborated at the level of pattern, by church policy documents and independent reporting. The individual incidents are not independently verified. Treat her as a representative voice, not as proof.
"Have you heard how people describe the first year after leaving?"

titleLong: Alyssa Grenfell's exit testimony: post-departure contact, garments, and the cost of deconstruction
responseLead: The church does not answer memoirs; visits are care, and the garment is a private covenant.
rationaleLead: Use with care: the pattern is documented, but one memoir is not proof.

title: The CES Letter, and 13 essays conceding the facts
claim: Jeremy Runnells' CES Letter of 2013 compiled a list of historical problems and sent it to a Church Educational System director, who never answered. It became the most widely circulated exit document in modern Mormonism. Runnells was summoned to a disciplinary council and resigned in 2016. In the same period the church published 13 Gospel Topics Essays, between 2013 and 2015, conceding many long-denied historical facts — multiple First Vision accounts, seer-stone translation, and Joseph Smith's polygamy. They were released with no announcement, unsigned, and buried in the website's topics database. Church Historian Elder Steven E. Snow acknowledged the deliberate 'soft roll out.' In some cases, members teaching from the essays were rebuked by local leaders.

sources.name: CES Letter (the primary document)
Gospel Topics Essays (official landing page)
Mormon Stories: Elder Steven E. Snow explains the quiet rollout (recording)
Salt Lake Tribune: 'Mormon leaders spread word about controversial essays'

response: The church did the thing critics had long demanded. It published frank, scholar-checked essays on its hardest topics, on its own website. It later folded that history into the official Saints volumes and the curriculum. No church had done that before. Elder Snow's account of the quiet rollout was pastoral, not secretive. Most members were not troubled by these issues. The essays were placed where a searching member would find them, without alarming those who were not asking. FAIR argues that the CES Letter is a shotgun list of recycled claims. Most of them, it says, are answered in the essays and in the apologetic literature.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Response to the CES Letter

rationale:
The timeline is settled. Elder Snow himself described the quiet rollout, and it is on the record.

Was that guarding people, or holding back? That is a judgement call, and the church did put the material out in the end. It counts for something.

Runnells was put on trial for a list of questions. That is on record too, and it sits badly beside the claim of openness.

plain.d: In 2013 Jeremy Runnells compiled a list of historical problems and sent it to a director in the Church Educational System. He never got an answer. The document became the most widely circulated exit letter in modern Mormonism. Runnells was summoned to a disciplinary council and resigned in 2016.

plain.t: What the church published at the same time
plain.d: Thirteen Gospel Topics Essays, between 2013 and 2015. They concede facts that had long been denied. Multiple First Vision accounts. Translation by seer stone. Joseph Smith's polygamy.

With no announcement. Unsigned. Buried in the topics database of the website. Elder Steven E. Snow, then Church Historian, acknowledged the deliberate "soft roll out." In some wards, members who taught from the essays were rebuked by local leaders.

The church did the thing critics had asked for. It published frank, scholar-checked essays on its hardest topics, on its own site, and later folded that history into the Saints volumes and the curriculum. Snow's explanation of the quiet release was pastoral rather than secretive. Most members were not troubled by these issues, and the essays were placed where a searching member would find them. FAIR argues the CES Letter is a shotgun list of recycled claims, most of which the essays and apologetic work answer.

Genuinely arguable. The timeline is established, including Snow's own recorded explanation. Whether it was information control or pastoral prudence is a judgement call. The church did publish the material, and that counts. Runnells being disciplined for compiling questions sits awkwardly beside the transparency claim.
"When did you first read the Gospel Topics Essays? How did you come across them?"

titleLong: Information control: the CES Letter phenomenon and the quiet rollout of the Gospel Topics Essays
responseLead: The church did what critics asked, publishing frank essays on its hardest topics.
rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. The essays are real, but they still put Runnells on trial.

title: Six scholars and feminists, disciplined in one month
claim: In September 1993, six Mormon scholars and feminists were cut off or disfellowshipped within weeks of each other. They were Lavina Fielding Anderson, Avraham Gileadi, Maxine Hanks, D. Michael Quinn, Paul Toscano and Lynne Kanavel Whitesides. What they had done was publish history and theology that leaders did not want. Quinn had written on plural marriage after 1890. Others had written on Heavenly Mother, or argued for women. Months before, the apostle Boyd K. Packer had named the church's three great dangers in public: 'the gay-lesbian movement, the feminist movement, and the so-called scholars or intellectuals.' The discipline was local on paper, but the evidence points to apostles taking part. Mormon studies went quiet for a generation.

sources.name: September Six (survey with primary citations)
The Conversation: 'How September 1993 continues to trouble the church' (Sara Patterson, 2023)
Dialogue: 'The September Six and the lost generation of Mormon studies'

response:
FAIR and the church hold that discipline is run locally, by stake presidents. It is for conduct such as speaking out against the church and its leaders. That is apostasy as the handbook sets it out, and it is not scholarship as such.

They note that many working historians publish critical work and are never disciplined. The church does not run these councils from the centre.

The church also points to what came after, as a sign that it can take rigorous history. The Joseph Smith Papers. The Gospel Topics Essays. And Maxine Hanks being rebaptised in 2012.

responseSource.name: FAIR: History scholars and Church discipline

rationale:
The six actions, their timing, and Packer's speech about three dangers are all on the record. No one disputes them.

What is argued is only how much was run from the centre.

As a claim about how the church met dissent, it stands.

title: $32 billion hidden behind 13 shell companies
claim: On 21 February 2023 the Securities and Exchange Commission charged the church and its investment arm, Ensign Peak Advisors. The charge was failing to disclose. From 1997 to 2019, Ensign Peak hid a portfolio of listed shares behind 13 shell LLCs with named-only 'managers.' It filed Forms 13F that were wrong, so that the church's holdings would not show. The portfolio grew to about $32 billion. Per the SEC order, this was done with the knowledge and approval of the church's First Presidency, out of concern about bad press. Ensign Peak paid $4 million and the church paid $1 million to settle. This is a legal finding about candour. It is not a claim about whether any doctrine is true.

sources.name: SEC press release 2023-35 (with link to the administrative order)
CNBC: 'Mormon church, affiliated nonprofit to pay $5 million to settle SEC charges'
2023 SEC charges against the LDS Church and Ensign Peak (survey)

response:
The church's official statement says it took legal advice on how to meet the 13F rules while keeping the portfolio private. It cites scripture on keeping sacred gifts quiet and on avoiding show. It says it regrets the mistakes made.

When the SEC first raised a concern in 2019, Ensign Peak changed its filings at once. It now files a single form for the whole fund.

The church stresses what the settlement did not allege. No misuse of funds. No fraud against investors. No harm to members. It was a breach about forms, and the money is still set aside for the church's religious and charitable work.

responseSource.name: Church Newsroom: Church issues statement on SEC settlement

rationale:
The facts are fixed by the SEC order, and by the church's own settlement and public statement owning the mistakes.

The 13 shell companies, the $32 billion, and the wish to avoid bad press are all in the order itself. So is the finding that the First Presidency knew and approved.

All that is left to argue is what to call it. Poor legal advice, or a choice to hide.

plain.d: On 21 February 2023 the Securities and Exchange Commission charged the church and its investment arm, Ensign Peak Advisors. The charge was failing to disclose. From 1997 to 2019, Ensign Peak hid a portfolio of listed shares behind 13 shell companies. Each had a manager in name only. The forms it filed, called Forms 13F, were wrong. The portfolio grew to about $32 billion.
To avoid revealing the church's holdings. The SEC order says this was done with the knowledge and approval of the First Presidency, out of concern about negative publicity.
Ensign Peak paid $4 million. The church paid $1 million. Note what this is and is not. It is a legal finding about candour. It says nothing about whether any doctrine is true.

The church says it took legal advice on how to meet the rules while keeping the portfolio private. It cites scripture on keeping sacred gifts quiet, and on not making a show. It says it regrets the mistakes made. When the SEC first raised a concern in 2019, Ensign Peak changed its filings at once. It now files one form for the whole fund. And note what the settlement did not allege. No misuse of funds. No fraud against investors. No harm to members.

They admit this themselves. The facts are fixed by the SEC order, and by the church's own statement owning the mistakes. The shell companies and the wish to avoid bad press are in the order. All that is left to argue is what to call it.
"Why thirteen shell companies? The order says it was about publicity."

titleLong: 2023 SEC settlement: $5M fine for two decades of concealed holdings via shell LLCs
responseLead: The church took legal advice, fixed the filings in 2019, and regrets the mistakes.
rationaleLead: They admit this: the SEC order fixes the facts, so only the name is argued.

title: Nephite priests from the wrong tribe
claim: The Book of Mormon says the Nephites kept the law of Moses strictly (2 Nephi 5:10; 25:24) and offered burnt sacrifices (1 Nephi 5:9; Mosiah 2:3). Yet Nephi — of the tribe of Joseph through Manasseh (Alma 10:3) — consecrates his brothers Jacob and Joseph as priests (2 Nephi 5:26; Jacob 1:18). The Mosaic law restricted the priesthood and sacrificial service to Aaron's line within Levi (Numbers 3:9-12; 16:39-40; Deuteronomy 33:8-11), and Hebrews 7:13-14 states plainly that of a non-Levite tribe 'no man gave attendance at the altar.' 2 Chronicles 26:16-21 shows the penalty. Critics argue that a genuinely law-observant Israelite colony could not run a non-Levitical sacrificial priesthood while claiming to keep the law of Moses.

sources.name: Institute for Religious Research — Contradictions Between Book of Mormon and Bible
Book of Mormon (2 Nephi 5), primary text
FAIR — Temples in the Book of Mormon

response:
Apologists argue the Nephites held the higher Melchizedek priesthood. Jacob was ordained 'after the manner of his holy order' at 2 Nephi 6:2, and Alma 13 develops the idea. In the Bible that order comes before Levi and stands above it. See Genesis 14, Psalm 110, and Hebrews 7:4-10. So the rules about Levi did not bind them.

They add three things. The Book of Mormon never claims Levite authority for these priests. No Levites travelled with Lehi's party. And Jewish communities of exactly Lehi's era ran altars outside the Jerusalem system, at Elephantine and at Arad.

FAIR concludes the practice was not unthinkable for Israelites far from home.

responseSource.name: FAIR — Temples in the Book of Mormon / Nephite priesthood

rationale:
The Melchizedek reading has a base in the text itself, at Alma 13. And Elephantine gives real historical precedent for irregular practice far from home.

But Hebrews 7 treats a priesthood outside Levi as at odds with the law of Moses. And the Nephites claim to be keeping that law in all things.

So the tension between strict law-keeping and a non-Aaronic altar is not resolved.

plain.d: The Nephites kept the law of Moses strictly. See 2 Nephi 5:10 and 25:24. They offered burnt sacrifices too, at 1 Nephi 5:9 and Mosiah 2:3. Yet Nephi was of the tribe of Joseph, through Manasseh (Alma 10:3). And at 2 Nephi 5:26 he makes his brothers Jacob and Joseph priests.

The law of Moses restricted priesthood and sacrifice to Aaron's line inside Levi. See Numbers 3:9-12 and 16:39-40. Hebrews 7:13-14 says plainly that of another tribe "no man gave attendance at the altar." 2 Chronicles 26:16-21 shows what happened when a king tried.

That the Nephites held the higher Melchizedek priesthood. Jacob was ordained "after the manner of his holy order" at 2 Nephi 6:2, and Alma 13 develops it. That order predates Levi in the Bible itself — Genesis 14, Psalm 110, Hebrews 7:4-10. They add three things. The book never claims Levitical authority. No Levites came with Lehi. And real Jewish communities of that era ran altars outside Jerusalem, at Elephantine and Arad.

Genuinely arguable, and this is a small case. Alma 13 gives them a textual base, and Elephantine is real history. The tension is that Hebrews 7 treats a non-Levitical priesthood as incompatible with the law the Nephites claim to keep in all things.
"How does a man from Joseph's tribe offer sacrifice under Moses' law?"

refwhy.Numbers 3:9-12: The Levites given to Aaron, and 'the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death.'
refwhy.Numbers 16:39-40: After Korah, no one 'which is not of the seed of Aaron' may offer incense. The rule, with a warning attached.
refwhy.Deuteronomy 33:8-11: Levi's blessing. It gives him the incense and the 'whole burnt sacrifice upon thine altar.'
refwhy.Hebrews 7:13-14: The plainest verse. Of another tribe, 'no man gave attendance at the altar.'
refwhy.2 Chronicles 26:16-21: King Uzziah burns incense and is struck with leprosy. What happened when a non-priest tried it.
refwhy.2 Nephi 5:10: The Nephites keep the law 'in all things.' That phrase is what makes the priesthood problem sharp.
refwhy.2 Nephi 5:26: Nephi consecrates Jacob and Joseph as 'priests and teachers.' A man of Joseph's tribe appointing priests.
refwhy.2 Nephi 25:24: 'We keep the law of Moses,' said again later in the book. So it is not a passing remark.
refwhy.1 Nephi 5:9: They 'offer sacrifice and burnt offerings.' Sacrifice, which the law hands to Aaron's line alone.
refwhy.Mosiah 2:3: Burnt offerings 'according to the law of Moses,' centuries later. The practice keeps going.
refwhy.Jacob 1:18: Jacob's own words. He and Joseph were 'consecrated priests… by the hand of Nephi.'
refwhy.Alma 10:3: The family line that creates the problem. Lehi comes from Manasseh, not from Levi.

titleLong: Nephite priests and sacrifices without Levitical lineage
responseLead: The Nephites held the Melchizedek priesthood, which the Bible puts before Levi.
rationaleLead: Small case: Alma 13 gives them a base, but Hebrews 7 keeps the tension alive.

title: Nephite temples, where the law allowed one
claim: Nephi builds a temple 'after the manner of the temple of Solomon' (2 Nephi 5:16), and the Book of Mormon later describes temples in multiple cities (Alma 16:13; 26:29; Helaman 3:9, 14). Deuteronomy 12:5-14 confines sacrificial worship to 'the place which the LORD your God shall choose,' understood after Solomon as the Jerusalem temple alone (1 Kings 8:29). Josiah's reform, within living memory of Lehi's departure, had specifically destroyed rival sanctuaries (2 Kings 23:4-20). A colony professing strict Mosaic observance while multiplying temples runs against the law's command to worship in one place.

sources.name: Institute for Religious Research — Contradictions Between Book of Mormon and Bible
FAIR — Temples in the Book of Mormon
Book of Mormon (2 Nephi 5:16), primary text

response:
FAIR points to Jewish temples outside Jerusalem, from Lehi's own time or soon after. There was a temple with sacrifice at Elephantine in Egypt. There was a sanctuary at Arad. Leontopolis came later. So Jews far from Jerusalem did in fact build temples.

FAIR argues that the one-place rule of Deuteronomy 12 applied inside the land of Israel. It did not bind a group cut off from that land across an ocean.

On that reading Nephi's temple is what a devout but permanently separated colony would do.

responseSource.name: FAIR — Temples in the Book of Mormon

rationale:
Elephantine and Arad are real sites, dug up and dated. They blunt the claim that this was unthinkable.

But scholars judge those altars irregular against the law of Deuteronomy. The Book of Mormon presents Nephite temples as fully proper.

So the clash with Deuteronomy 12 stands as a matter of law, even though the practice has precedent in history.

plain.d: Nephi builds a temple "after the manner of the temple of Solomon" at 2 Nephi 5:16. Later there are temples in several cities — Alma 16:13, Alma 26:29, Helaman 3:9 and 3:14.

Deuteronomy 12:5-14 confines sacrifice to "the place which the LORD your God shall choose." After Solomon that meant Jerusalem alone, as 1 Kings 8:29 assumes. And Josiah's reform, within living memory of Lehi leaving, had destroyed the rival sanctuaries — 2 Kings 23:4-20.

FAIR points to real Jewish temples outside Jerusalem. The sacrificial temple at Elephantine in Egypt. The sanctuary at Arad. Leontopolis later. So Jews far from Jerusalem did build temples. FAIR argues the centralisation command applied inside the land of Israel, not to a colony cut off across an ocean.

Genuinely arguable, and this is a minor one. Elephantine and Arad are archaeological facts and they blunt the word unthinkable. The remaining point is narrow. Those sites are judged irregular against the law. The Book of Mormon presents its temples as fully legitimate.
"Deuteronomy 12 says one place. How did Nephi read that?"

refwhy.Deuteronomy 12:5-14: The one-place law. Offer only 'in the place which the LORD shall choose,' not 'in every place that thou seest.'
refwhy.1 Kings 8:29: Solomon's prayer, which fixes that place at the Jerusalem temple.
refwhy.2 Kings 23:4-20: Josiah tearing down the rival altars, just before Lehi left. It shows how hard the rule was pressed.

responseLead: Jews did build temples far from Jerusalem. Elephantine and Arad were dug up.
rationaleLead: A minor one: the digs are real, but those altars were judged irregular.

title: Acts 3:21 does not rule out the Nephite visit
claim: The Book of Mormon's centerpiece is the resurrected Christ descending to minister bodily to the Nephites for days (3 Nephi 11:8-17; 26:13). Critics set this against Peter's statement that Jesus is one 'whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things' (Acts 3:20-21; cf. Acts 1:9-11). The argument is that the New Testament expects Christ to remain in heaven between the ascension and the last days, leaving no room for an extended post-ascension earthly ministry in the Americas.

sources.name: Institute for Religious Research — Contradictions Between Book of Mormon and Bible
Book of Mormon (3 Nephi 11), primary text

response:
Apologists reply that the New Testament itself records Christ appearing after the ascension. He appeared to Stephen at Acts 7:55-56. He appeared to Paul on the Damascus road at Acts 9:3-6 and 1 Corinthians 15:8. He appeared to John on Patmos at Revelation 1:12-18.

So Acts 3:21 cannot mean Christ never appears before the restitution. It describes where he resides, not a ban on visits.

The Nephite ministry is claimed to be the same kind of appearance at larger scale. And 'other sheep I have' at John 10:16 is read as Jesus expecting it.

responseSource.name: FAIR — Jesus Christ's visit to the Americas

rationale:
The strong reading of Acts 3:21, that Christ makes no earthly appearance until the end, is defeated by the New Testament itself. He appeared to Stephen, to Paul and to John.

Whatever other problems 3 Nephi has, and they are covered elsewhere, this verse does not rule out an appearance.

Christians should drop it.

plain.d: 3 Nephi 11-28 has the risen Christ come down and minister to the Nephites in the body for days. Against that, Acts 3:20-21 calls Jesus one "whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things." So, the argument goes, he cannot have been in America.

The New Testament records him appearing after the ascension more than once. To Stephen in Acts 7:55-56. To Paul on the Damascus road in Acts 9:3-6 and 1 Corinthians 15:8. To John on Patmos in Revelation 1:12-18.

plain.t: So what does the verse mean
