FAIR gives exactly those three appearances and says the Nephite visit is the same kind of thing on a larger scale. They also read "other sheep I have" in John 10:16 as Jesus anticipating it.
Do not use this one. There are real problems with 3 Nephi and they are covered elsewhere. Acts 3:21 is not one of them, and using it will cost you your credibility on the cases that do work.
Nothing. If someone else raises it, say plainly that you don't think it holds.

refwhy.Acts 3:20-21: The verse the argument uses. It does not prove what people think, since Jesus did appear after this.
refwhy.Acts 1:9-11: The ascension, and the promise that he will come back the same way. It rules out nothing in between.
refwhy.3 Nephi 11:8-17: The descent itself. 'Behold, I am Jesus Christ.' The heart of the book, and what this argument aims at.
refwhy.3 Nephi 26:13: He taught them 'for the space of three days,' then came often. The length is what troubles people.

titleLong: Christ's Nephite visit vs. Acts 3:21 'heaven must receive him'
responseLead: Christ appeared after the ascension to Stephen, Paul and John, so the verse permits it.
rationaleLead: Do not use this one: their reply is simply correct, and it will cost you.

title: A temple 'in this generation', promised in 1832
claim: D&C 84:2-5, given in September 1832, declares that a temple 'shall be reared in this generation' on the dedicated lot in Independence, Missouri — 'verily this generation shall not all pass away until an house shall be built unto the Lord.' No temple was ever built there, and every member of that generation is long dead. Critics apply Deuteronomy 18:20-22: a prophet whose predicted thing 'follow not, nor come to pass' has spoken presumptuously. Jeremiah 28:9 and Ezekiel 33:33 are used the same way. Related cases include D&C 114:1, where David W. Patten is called to a mission 'next spring' though he was killed months earlier, and the 1835 statement about the Second Coming in fifty-six years.

sources.name: Pastor Unlikely — 41 Authentic Bible Verses to Contradict Mormonism
Institute for Religious Research — Joseph Smith's Missouri Temple Prophecy
Doctrine and Covenants 84, primary text
FAIR — Alleged false prophecies of Joseph Smith

response:
FAIR argues that prophecy in the Bible is often conditional without saying so. Jonah announced flatly that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown. It was not, and Jonah was no false prophet.

D&C 124:49-51, from 1841, puts that principle into their own canon. When enemies stop a commanded work, God 'requires that work no more'. The Saints were violently driven out of Jackson County in 1833, which made the temple impossible.

Other readings take 'an house' in verse 5 as fulfilled by the Kirtland temple in 1836. Or they treat the words as an order rather than a flat forecast.

responseSource.name: FAIR — The temple in Independence, Missouri

rationale:
The non-fulfilment is not in dispute. And the formula 'this generation shall not all pass away' reads like a flat, dated oracle. Later leaders such as Orson Pratt kept restating it as one.

Yet the Jonah precedent is real, and the conditional clause at D&C 124:49 sits inside their own canon.

So this turns on how you read prophecy, not on a disputed fact.

plain.d: D&C 84:2-5, given in September 1832. A temple "shall be reared in this generation" on the dedicated lot at Independence, Missouri. And "verily this generation shall not all pass away until an house shall be built unto the Lord."

No temple was ever built there. Every member of that generation is long dead. Two related cases sit beside it. D&C 114:1 called David W. Patten on a mission "next spring"; he was killed months before it. And there is the 1835 statement about the Second Coming in fifty-six years.
Deuteronomy 18:20-22. A prophet whose word "follow not, nor come to pass" has spoken presumptuously. Jeremiah 28:9 and Ezekiel 33:33 are used the same way.

FAIR says biblical prophecy is often conditional without saying so. Jonah announced flatly that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown. It was not, and Jonah was no false prophet. And D&C 124:49-51, from 1841, canonises that principle: when enemies stop a commanded work, God "requires that work no more." The Saints were driven out of Jackson County in 1833. Others read "an house" as the Kirtland temple of 1836.

Genuinely arguable. The non-fulfilment is not in dispute, and the wording reads like a dated, unconditional oracle — Orson Pratt kept reaffirming it as one. But the Jonah precedent is real, and the conditionality clause is inside their own canon. This turns on how you read prophecy, not on a disputed fact.
"How do you tell a conditional prophecy from one that just failed?"

refwhy.Deuteronomy 18:20-22: The test being applied. If the thing 'follow not, nor come to pass,' the LORD did not speak it.
refwhy.Ezekiel 33:33: Fulfilment as the mark of a true prophet. Weaker than Deuteronomy 18, so do not lead with it.
refwhy.Jeremiah 28:9: The same test, but narrowed to prophecies of peace. Note that limit before you quote it.
refwhy.D&C 84:2-5: The prophecy. A temple 'shall be reared in this generation,' and 'this generation shall not all pass away' first.
refwhy.D&C 114:1: David Patten sent on a mission 'next spring.' He was killed months before the spring came.
refwhy.D&C 124:49-51: Their answer, inside their own canon. When enemies stop a commanded work, God 'requires that work no more.'

titleLong: Joseph Smith's predictive prophecies vs. the Deuteronomy 18 test
responseLead: Jonah said forty days and Nineveh stood. A word from God can carry a condition.
rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. It reads like a dated oracle, but D&C 124:49 sets a condition.

title: Coffee can keep a member out of the temple
claim: D&C 89, from 1833, counsels against wine, strong drink, tobacco and 'hot drinks,' later defined as coffee and tea. Its own preamble says it is sent 'not by commandment or constraint' (D&C 89:2). For decades observance was uneven. Under Heber J. Grant, abstinence became a fixed requirement for a temple recommend, formalized by 1921. So a person who drinks coffee or wine cannot enter the temple today, and therefore, in Latter-day Saint teaching, cannot receive the ordinances required for exaltation. Critics set this against the New Testament's explicit release from rules about food and drink. Jesus 'declared all foods clean' (Mark 7:18-19). Paul forbids judging believers 'in meat, or in drink,' and calls 'touch not; taste not; handle not' rules of no value (Colossians 2:16-23). He warns that 'commanding to abstain from meats' marks latter-day apostasy (1 Timothy 4:1-5). And he makes dietary practice a matter of conscience (Romans 14:14-17; cf. Matthew 11:19).

sources.name: Church History Topics — Word of Wisdom (D&C 89)
FAIR — Word of Wisdom: History and implementation
MRM — The Word of Wisdom: Food Restrictions & False Prophets
Doctrine and Covenants 89, primary text

response:
The strongest form of their position is this. The Word of Wisdom is not a purity law. It does not claim that certain substances defile the soul. It is a revealed health code and a covenant standard, resting on the body as a temple of God at 1 Corinthians 6:19-20.

Any covenant community may set such a standard as a condition of its own ordinances. The Bible has precedents. The Nazirite vow. Daniel's abstention. The Rechabites. All are commended.

The shift from counsel to commandment is explained as prophets applying it over time, by common consent, 'adapted to the capacity of the weak' at D&C 89:3. That is the same living authority they believe governed food rules in both Testaments.

responseSource.name: FAIR — Word of Wisdom: History and implementation

rationale:
The history is not disputed, and church sources concede it. It was given 'not by commandment', and it later hardened into a gate for the temple, fixed under Heber J. Grant by 1921.

Whether that clashes with Scripture is argued. The health-code framing is coherent.

But Colossians 2:20-23 and 1 Timothy 4:3 take aim at exactly this: making abstinence rules a measure of standing. And here a rule about drink is tied to the ordinances held to be required for exaltation.

plain.d: D&C 89, given in 1833. It counsels against wine, strong drink, tobacco and "hot drinks" — later defined as coffee and tea. Its own second verse says it is sent "not by commandment or constraint."
Under Heber J. Grant, keeping it became a fixed requirement for a temple recommend, formalised by about 1921. So a cup of coffee can now keep a member out of the temple, and out of a child's wedding.
That it is a health code and a covenant standard, not a purity law — the body as a temple, as in 1 Corinthians 6:19-20. A church may raise a standard over time without contradicting itself.
Arguable both ways. The real question is not coffee. It is what happens when advice given expressly not as a commandment becomes a test of worthiness. That is close to what Jesus rebuked in Mark 7.
"D&C 89:2 says it isn't a commandment. When did that change, and who changed it?"

refwhy.Mark 7:18-19: Jesus says what enters a man 'cannot defile him.' The verse behind the claim that food rules were set aside.
refwhy.Colossians 2:16-23: 'Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink,' and 'touch not; taste not; handle not.' The closest fit.
refwhy.1 Timothy 4:1-5: Warns that 'commanding to abstain from meats' marks a falling away. Strong wording, though it names food, not drink.
refwhy.Romans 14:14-17: 'The kingdom of God is not meat and drink.' Paul makes it a matter of conscience, not of standing.
refwhy.Matthew 11:19: Jesus was called 'a winebibber' by his critics. Cited because he drank wine, which D&C 89 counsels against.
refwhy.D&C 89:1-9: The revelation itself. Verse 2 says it is sent 'not by commandment or constraint' — the line this case turns on.

titleLong: The Word of Wisdom: coffee, tea, and temple worthiness
responseLead: It is a health code and a covenant standard, and any church may set one.
rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. The real question is advice that turns into a test of worthiness.

title: Sacred underwear, worn day and night for life
claim: Endowed Latter-day Saints covenant to wear the temple garment — a prescribed white underclothing bearing sacred marks. The General Handbook, at 38.5, instructs that it should be worn 'day and night throughout your life,' and never altered. Since 2024 the temple-recommend interview includes a standardized statement on garment wearing, to which members respond, making the practice a recurring worthiness checkpoint. Critics note that the New Testament nowhere prescribes ritual clothing for believers. The claimed biblical analogue is the tzitzit fringes of Numbers 15:38-39 and Deuteronomy 22:12, which were a visible outer sign commanded specifically to Israel under the Mosaic law. And Colossians 2:16-23 warns against measuring Christian standing by outward observance, as do Matthew 23:5 and 1 Samuel 16:7.

sources.name: General Handbook 38.5 — Temple Garment
Church — Temple Garment FAQ
Salt Lake Tribune — LDS leaders alter temple recommend questions (2024)

response:
The church presents the garment as a private, personal reminder of covenants made in the temple. It offers the parallel of the nun's habit, the priest's cassock, the Jewish prayer shawl, and the Muslim skullcap. All are 'part of a rich tapestry of human devotion to God'.

The church notes that the tzitzit has the same stated purpose. Numbers 15:39 says the fringes are there 'that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD'.

Wearing it is framed as keeping a covenant freely made, not as a claim that clothing saves. And the statement in the recommend interview is read as being answerable for a covenant, not as legalism.

responseSource.name: Church Newsroom — Temple Garment FAQ

rationale:
The practice, and the 2024 statement in the recommend interview, are documented from the church's own handbook at 38.5. Whether it clashes with Scripture is a question of judgement.

The tzitzit parallel is real in function. Both are a sign for remembering. But the tzitzit belongs to the Mosaic covenant, which Christians hold to be fulfilled.

And the Bible neither commands nor forbids such a practice for the church. So the criticism rests on inference, not on a direct clash. Treat the practice itself with respect.

plain.d: Endowed members covenant to wear the temple garment — prescribed white underclothing bearing sacred marks. The General Handbook instructs that it be worn "day and night throughout your life" and never altered. Since 2024 the recommend interview includes a standard statement about it.
Do not mock it. "Magic underwear" is the single fastest way to end the conversation, and it deserves to end. This is sacred to the person in front of you and it is personal.
That it is a private reminder of covenants made in the temple — no stranger than a nun's habit, a priest's collar, a Jewish prayer shawl or a Muslim skullcap. That comparison is fair.
Not whether clothing can be sacred — plainly it can. Whether daily clothing should be a condition of standing before God, and where Scripture prescribes that for ordinary believers.
"I'm not going to make fun of it. Can I ask what it means to you?"

refwhy.Numbers 15:38-39: The fringes, worn so 'ye may look upon it, and remember.' The church cites the same purpose, so this helps their case.
refwhy.Deuteronomy 22:12: The fringe command again. Note that it is outer clothing, given to Israel under the law of Moses.
refwhy.Colossians 2:16-23: Warns against measuring Christian standing by outward keeping. The question is the checkpoint, not the cloth.
refwhy.Matthew 23:5: Jesus on those who 'make broad their phylacteries.' That is about display, so it fits private clothing badly.
refwhy.1 Samuel 16:7: God 'looketh on the heart,' not the outward appearance. The general rule being appealed to.

titleLong: Temple garments: prescribed sacred underclothing and its enforcement
responseLead: It reminds them of covenants, much as a habit, a collar or a prayer shawl would.
rationaleLead: A minor case: the practice deserves respect, so ask about the checkpoint, not the cloth.

title: Becoming gods, still affirmed in a 2014 essay
claim: Latter-day Saint scripture teaches that the faithful sealed in celestial marriage 'shall pass by the angels, and the gods… Then shall they be gods, because they have no end… because they have all power' (D&C 132:19-20; cf. 132:37, Abraham 3:22-26). Joseph Smith's King Follett discourse of 1844 taught that God 'was once a man like us' and that the Saints must learn 'how to be gods yourselves.' Lorenzo Snow crystallized it: as man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may be. The church's 2014 essay 'Becoming Like God' complains that this is reduced in media to a cartoonish image of people receiving their own planets — yet reaffirms the substance, exaltation to godhood with divine creative capacity. Critics set this against Yahweh's own words: 'before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me' (Isaiah 43:10; cf. 44:6-8, 45:5, Psalm 90:2). They note that the first promise of godhood in Scripture came from the serpent — 'ye shall be as gods' (Genesis 3:5).

sources.name: Gospel Topics Essay — Becoming Like God
King Follett Sermon (Ensign reprint)
Doctrine and Covenants 132, primary text
Pastor Unlikely — 41 Authentic Bible Verses to Contradict Mormonism

response:
The essay's strongest case is that this language runs through early Christianity. Psalm 82:6 says 'Ye are gods', and Jesus quotes it at John 10:34. 2 Peter 1:4 speaks of 'partakers of the divine nature'. Romans 8:17 speaks of being joint-heirs with Christ.

Church fathers from Irenaeus to Clement of Alexandria taught it. Clement wrote that the Word of God became man 'that thou mayest learn from man how man may become God'.

On that reading, exaltation restores an ancient doctrine of theosis rather than inventing many gods. Isaiah's denials are read as aimed at idols and rival gods, not at God's own children inheriting his nature. Exalted beings stay forever under the Father. And the essay stresses how little has been revealed about the first half of Lorenzo Snow's couplet.

responseSource.name: Gospel Topics Essay — Becoming Like God

rationale: The teaching is established from their own canon and from the 2014 essay Becoming Like God. That essay rejects the planet cartoon while restating the substance: godhood, with the power to create. The theosis case does not close the gap. Deification in the fathers always kept the line between Creator and creature. It never taught that God was once a man. And it never made the deified gods in the sense D&C 132:19-20 describes. Isaiah 43:10 is left in direct tension. 'Before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.'

plain.d: D&C 132:19-20 says the faithful sealed in celestial marriage "shall pass by the angels, and the gods." Then "shall they be gods, because they have no end… because they have all power." Joseph Smith's King Follett sermon of 1844 taught that God "was once a man like us," and that the Saints must learn "how to be gods yourselves." Lorenzo Snow put it in a couplet: as man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may be.

The 2014 essay Becoming Like God complains that this gets reduced to a cartoon about people getting their own planets. Fair enough. But read on. The essay reaffirms the substance — exaltation to godhood, with the power to create.

Isaiah 43:10 has God say "before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me." Isaiah 44:6-8 and 45:5 say the same. And notice who first offered godhood in Scripture. The serpent, in Genesis 3:5: "ye shall be as gods."

And it is serious. Deification language runs through early Christianity. Psalm 82:6, quoted by Jesus in John 10:34: "Ye are gods." 2 Peter 1:4 on being "partakers of the divine nature." Romans 8:17 on being joint-heirs with Christ. Irenaeus taught it, and Clement of Alexandria wrote that the Word became man so that man might learn how to become God. On this reading the church restores theosis, not polytheism. Isaiah's denials are aimed at idols. And exalted beings stay forever subordinate to the Father.

Strong for you, but you must handle theosis honestly or you will lose. Early Christian deification always kept the line between Creator and creature. It never taught that God was once a man, and never made the deified gods in the sense D&C 132 describes. Isaiah 43:10 is about existence, and it is still standing.
"Isaiah 43:10 says no God will be formed after him. How do you read that?"

refwhy.Isaiah 43:10: The verse to press. 'Before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.'
refwhy.Isaiah 44:6-8: 'Is there a God beside me? yea, there is no God; I know not any.' God saying he knows of no others.
refwhy.Isaiah 45:5: 'There is none else, there is no God beside me.' The same denial a third time, which is why all three are quoted.
refwhy.Genesis 3:5: The serpent's offer: 'ye shall be as gods.' The first promise of godhood in the Bible, and who made it.
refwhy.Psalm 90:2: 'From everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.' There was no time when God was not God.
refwhy.D&C 132:19-20: The core text. 'Then shall they be gods, because they have no end… because they have all power.'
refwhy.D&C 132:37: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob 'are not angels but are gods.' Named men, said to be there already.
refwhy.Abraham 3:22-26: The council before this life, and 'we will go down… and we will make an earth.' Where the creating role comes from.

titleLong: Exaltation: humans becoming gods vs. Isaiah's exclusive monotheism
responseLead: Early Christians taught theosis, and Jesus quoted 'Ye are gods' at John 10:34.
rationaleLead: Strong for you, but handle theosis honestly: it always kept Creator and creature apart.

title: 126 years of barring Black members, 1852–1978
claim: From Brigham Young's announcements in 1852 until Official Declaration 2 in June 1978, the church barred members of Black African descent. Men could not be ordained to the priesthood. Men and women could not receive the temple endowment or be sealed. In the church's own soteriology, that meant exclusion from the ordinances required for exaltation, for 126 years. A 1949 First Presidency statement defended the ban as divinely instituted, grounding it in premortal conduct and in the curse of Cain. The church's 2013 essay 'Race and the Priesthood' now disavows 'the theories advanced in the past.' It situates the ban's origin in the racial culture of 1850s America, and claims no founding revelation. Critics set the policy against Peter's revelation that 'God is no respecter of persons' (Acts 10:34-35), and Paul's 'there is neither Jew nor Greek… ye are all one in Christ Jesus' (Galatians 3:28). Acts 17:26, Colossians 3:11 and Revelation 7:9 point the same way.

sources.name: Gospel Topics Essay — Race and the Priesthood
Official Declaration 2 (1978), primary text
FAIR — Blacks and the priesthood

response:
Their strongest case leans on the 2013 essay itself, and it is honest work.

Joseph Smith ordained Black men. Elijah Able and Q. Walker Lewis are the named cases. The restriction arose under Brigham Young, amid the racial culture of 1850s America, with no recorded founding revelation. It was ended by genuine revelation to Spencer W. Kimball in 1978. And the church has since repudiated every reason it once gave.

Apologists draw a parallel from Acts. The gospel was withheld from Gentiles until Peter's vision. God lifts restrictions on his own timetable, through living prophets. And a church able to disavow its leaders' errors is showing revelation at work, not disproving it.

responseSource.name: Gospel Topics Essay — Race and the Priesthood

rationale:
The history is fully documented, and the church's own essay concedes it. From 1852 to 1978 is 126 years. Six generations of real people carried it.

The Acts 10 parallel cuts against them. Peter's vision ended ethnic exclusion at the very start of the church. Here the ban came in after an open start. Prophets then defended it as doctrine for over a century. Its stated reasons are now disavowed.

That leaves the question about prophets standing.

plain.d: From Brigham Young's announcements in 1852 until June 1978, the church barred members of Black African descent. Men could not be ordained to the priesthood. Men and women could not receive the temple endowment or be sealed. In the church's own teaching, those are the ordinances required for exaltation. It lasted 126 years.

plain.t: How it was defended at the time

It leans on that essay, and it is honest work. Joseph Smith ordained Black men — Elijah Able and Q. Walker Lewis. The restriction began under Young, without a recorded revelation. It was ended by revelation to Spencer W. Kimball in 1978. Every theological justification has been repudiated. Apologists add a parallel from Acts: the gospel was withheld from Gentiles until Peter's vision. God lifts restrictions on his own timetable, through living prophets. And a church willing to disavow its leaders' errors is showing revelation at work, not disproving it.

The Acts parallel cuts the other way. Peter's revelation ended ethnic exclusion at the very start of the church. Here the ban was brought in after an inclusive start. Prophets then defended it as doctrine for over a century. And its reasons are now officially disavowed. Real people carried that for six generations. The question about prophetic reliability is still there.
"Acts 10:34 says God is no respecter of persons. How do you hold that with 1852 to 1978?"

title: Seven weeks from Masonic initiation to the endowment
claim: Joseph Smith was initiated into Freemasonry in Nauvoo on 15 and 16 March 1842. He rose to Master Mason in a single day. Seven weeks later, on 4 May 1842, he introduced the temple endowment. The first nine men to receive it were all Masons. The church's own history essay acknowledges these facts. The two rites shared documented elements. Tokens, which are grips. Signs. Key words. Ritual penalties miming throat-cutting and disembowelment. The five points of fellowship. And the compass-and-square symbols. The penalty oaths and the five points were removed from the ceremony in April 1990. Critics contrast the covenant of non-disclosure with Jesus's 'in secret have I said nothing' (John 18:20; cf. Matthew 10:26-27, Ephesians 5:11-13). They argue that a restored ancient ordinance should not track eighteenth-century Masonic ritual in datable detail.

sources.name: Church History Topics — Masonry
MRM — Masonry and the Mormon Temple Endowment Ceremony
CES Letter — Temples & Freemasonry
FAIR — The temple endowment and Freemasonry

response:
The church and FAIR grant the parallels, but separate form from substance. Masonry served as a catalyst. It gave Joseph a ritual language his hearers knew, in which to teach covenants that were truly revealed.

The content of the endowment has no match in Masonry. Creation. Fall. Redemption. And covenants of consecration. Unlike Masonry, it was given to women, and to 'even the weakest of the Saints'.

FAIR argues that the rite is the vehicle, not the endowment itself. So changing it, in 1990 and in 2019, is revelation going on rather than damage control.

And the temple is sacred, not secret. Its teachings are in print. Only certain signs and tokens are held back by covenant. Jesus too held some things back from the crowd, at Mark 4:34 and John 16:12.

responseSource.name: Church History Topics — Masonry

rationale:
The facts are documented, and the church's own essay effectively concedes them. Masonic initiation on 15 and 16 March 1842. The endowment seven weeks later, on 4 May. The shared elements. And the removal of the penalty oaths and the five points in April 1990.

The catalyst framing interprets those facts rather than rebutting them.

Note one thing more. The older defence, that the endowment was preserved from Solomon's temple, has quietly been dropped.

plain.d: Joseph Smith was initiated into Freemasonry at Nauvoo on 15 and 16 March 1842. He rose to Master Mason in a single day. Seven weeks later, on 4 May 1842, he introduced the temple endowment. The first nine men to receive it were all Masons. The church's own history essay acknowledges this.

Tokens, which are grips. Signs. Key words. Ritual penalties miming the cutting of the throat and the opening of the body. The five points of fellowship. And the compass and square. The penalty oaths and the five points were removed from the ceremony in April 1990.
This is sacred to the person you are talking to. Do not smirk about it, and do not ask them to describe what they covenanted not to describe. Ask about the history, which is public.

The church and FAIR grant the parallels and separate form from substance. Masonry was a catalyst for revelation — a familiar ritual language Joseph used to teach covenants that were genuinely revealed. The content has no Masonic counterpart: creation, fall, redemption, and covenants of consecration. Unlike Masonry it was given to women, and to the weakest of the Saints. The ritual is the vehicle, not the endowment itself, so revising it in 1990 and 2019 is continuing revelation rather than damage control. And the temple is sacred, not secret. The teachings are published; only certain signs and tokens are withheld, as Jesus held some things back in Mark 4:34 and John 16:12.

They admit the facts, and the catalyst reading is a fair theological move. It interprets those facts; it does not deny them. Notice one thing. The older apologetic — that the endowment was preserved from Solomon's temple — has quietly been dropped. Set the dates beside John 18:20, where Jesus says "in secret have I said nothing."
"He became a Mason in March and gave the endowment in May. How do you read those dates?"

refwhy.Matthew 10:26-27: 'What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light.' The gospel as public by design.
refwhy.Ephesians 5:11-13: Fits badly. Paul is writing about shameful deeds done in secret, not about reverent ritual.

titleLong: The temple endowment: Masonic parallels, penalty oaths, and secrecy
responseLead: Masonry was a catalyst. It gave him a ritual language for covenants God had given.
rationaleLead: They admit the dates: the catalyst reading reads those facts, it does not deny them.

title: A Heavenly Mother members may not pray to
claim: The church's 2015 essay 'Mother in Heaven' affirms as 'cherished and distinctive' doctrine that all human spirits are children of a Heavenly Father and a Heavenly Mother. Silence in the Bible is not denial. Latter-day Saints do not hold the Bible to be complete on doctrine.

And prayer still goes to the Father alone, in Christ's name, as Jesus taught. So she is honoured, not worshipped.

The argument from consequence is coherent inside Latter-day Saint premises.

But it supplies no scripture. And scripture is the thing at issue.

title: Jesus 'attained the rank of Godhood', says Talmage
claim: Official Latter-day Saint doctrine teaches that Jesus is the firstborn spirit child of Heavenly Father and heavenly parents — 'the firstborn of the spirit children of our Heavenly Father,' in Gospel Principles chapters 2 and 3. That makes him the literal elder brother of all humans, of the same kind as us, who progressed to divinity in the premortal world. James Talmage's Jesus the Christ says Christ 'attained the rank of Godhood' premortally. The Bible teaches that Christ is the eternal, uncreated Creator. 'All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made' (John 1:3) — a scope that excludes Christ himself from the category of things that came to be. He 'is before all things' (Colossians 1:17). His goings forth are 'from of old, from everlasting' (Micah 5:2). He is 'the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever' (Hebrews 13:8), and says 'before Abraham was, I am' (John 8:58). A being begotten as one spirit child among billions, who then attains godhood, is a different kind of being from one who eternally is God.

sources.name: Gospel Principles, ch. 2 'Our Heavenly Family' (churchofjesuschrist.org)
Guide to the Scriptures: 'Firstborn'
The Living Christ: The Testimony of the Apostles (First Presidency/Twelve, 2000)
MRM: The Relationship Between Jesus and Lucifer in a Mormon Context

response: Apologists reply that Jesus did not become divine late, or out of nothing that matters. He is Jehovah, the God of the Old Testament. The Living Christ of 2000 says so directly. He was fully divine before creation. He created 'worlds without number' under the Father's direction at Moses 1:33. And D&C 93:21 calls him 'the Firstborn' who was 'in the beginning with the Father'. On Colossians 1:15 they note that Paul himself calls Christ 'the firstborn of every creature'. FAIR argues that the Greek at Colossians 1:16 means organising material that already exists, not making from nothing. So 'all things were made by him' need not take in eternal spirit-matter, or Christ's own spirit. Firstborn status, they argue, means first place and heirship, as at Psalm 89:27. Latter-day Saint theology affirms that to the full.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Does Colossians 1:16 teach that Jesus created all things out of nothing?

rationale:
The doctrine is documented from current official sources, and the clash is structural rather than a fight over one verse.

Grant that Christ as Jehovah was divine before the world was. This theology still makes him a begotten spirit brother of humanity whose divinity was attained. That is one of us who rose, rather than the eternal Creator who came down.

John 1:3 sweeps everything in. Colossians 1:17 says 'he is before all things'. Neither leaves a class of self-existing spirit-stuff, or sibling spirits, that Christ did not make. The Latter-day Saint reading has to carve out exactly what the text shuts off.

And the 'firstborn of every creature' point fails against verse 16's own reason: 'for by him were all things created'. He is first over creation because he made it.

plain.d: That Jesus is the firstborn spirit child of Heavenly Father and heavenly parents. Gospel Principles, chapters 2 and 3, says so. That makes him the literal elder brother of every human, of the same kind as us. James Talmage's Jesus the Christ says he "attained the rank of Godhood" before this life.

John 1:3 — "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made." That scope leaves Christ outside the category of made things. Colossians 1:17 says "he is before all things." Micah 5:2 says his goings forth are "from everlasting." Hebrews 13:8 says he is the same yesterday, today and forever. John 8:58 has him say "before Abraham was, I am."

He did not become divine late. He is Jehovah, the God of the Old Testament — The Living Christ, 2000, says so directly. D&C 93:21 calls him the Firstborn who was in the beginning with the Father, and Moses 1:33 has him creating worlds without number. On Colossians 1:15 they note Paul himself calls Christ "the firstborn of every creature." And FAIR argues the Greek at Colossians 1:16 means organising existing material, not making something from nothing.

Colossians 1:16 explains its own firstborn line: "for by him were all things created." He is first over creation because he made it. And the deeper problem is not a proof text. Even granting that Christ was Jehovah before the world, this makes him a begotten spirit sibling whose divinity was attained. That is a different kind of being from the eternal Creator who came down.
Strong for you. But say the strong half of their case first — the Jehovah identification is real and most Christians do not know they teach it. Then ask about John 1:3.
"Was there ever a time when Jesus was not God?"

rationaleLead: Strong for you, but give the Jehovah half first, then ask about John 1:3.

title: Jesus and Lucifer as spirit brothers
claim: Latter-day Saint scripture and manuals teach that Lucifer was 'a spirit son of God.' In the premortal council he offered a rival plan of redemption — 'Behold, here am I, send me, I will be thy son… wherefore give me thine honor' (Moses 4:1-4) — competing with the premortal Jesus before the world was made (Abraham 3:27-28; D&C 76:25-27; Gospel Principles chapter 3). Since all beings are spirit children of the same Heavenly Father, Jesus and Lucifer are, in that taxonomy, elder and younger spirit brothers. The church's own Newsroom statement of December 2007, answering Mike Huckabee, acknowledged the underlying doctrine while rejecting the framing: all beings 'were created by God and are his spirit children,' while 'Satan… is a fallen angel.' Biblically, Christ is the Creator of all spiritual beings — 'by him were all things created… whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers' (Colossians 1:16). Satan is therefore a creature Christ made, of a different order from his Maker; Ezekiel 28:13-15 says 'thou wast created.' John 1:3, Hebrews 1:4-6 and Nehemiah 9:6 say the same.

sources.name: Gospel Principles, ch. 3 'Jesus Christ, Our Chosen Leader and Savior'

response:
FAIR concedes the taxonomy is 'technically accurate' but calls the framing misleading without context.

A shared spirit-parentage implies no parity. Cain and Abel were brothers, and nobody calls them equals. FAIR notes that the Bible itself calls Satan one of the 'sons of God', at Job 1:6 and 2:1.

Jesus is uniquely the first and greatest Son. He is the Creator of this world, and the Only Begotten in the flesh. Satan squandered what he had and became the eternal enemy of God.

The 2007 Newsroom statement takes the same line. Christ and Satan are 'diametrically opposite' in every attribute.

Their reply rebuts the crude version, that Mormons think Jesus and the devil are alike. Nobody serious says that. It does not touch the real conflict, which is about what kind of being each one is.

In biblical Christology, Satan belongs to the class of made 'principalities and powers' that Christ himself made. Creator and fallen creature can no more be brothers of one species than a potter and his pot. And Job 1:6's 'sons of God' names angels in Yahweh's court, not begotten siblings of Yahweh.

So the moral-contrast defence answers a charge nobody serious is making.

title: God the Father has flesh and bones
claim: Joseph Smith taught canonically that 'The Father has a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's' (D&C 130:22; see also 131:7-8). In the King Follett discourse of 1844 he preached that 'God himself was once as we are now, and is an exalted man.' The church's current essay 'Becoming Like God' still quotes that approvingly, alongside Lorenzo Snow's couplet, and affirms Smith's rejection of creation from nothing: God 'organized the universe out of existing elements' (Abraham 3:22-24; 4:1). The trajectory reached its extreme in Brigham Young's Adam-God doctrine — 'Adam is our father and our God, and the only God with whom we have to do' (Journal of Discourses 1:50-51, 1852), incorporated into the 1877 temple lecture at the veil. President Spencer W. Kimball officially repudiated it in October 1976: 'We denounce that theory… false doctrine.' The Bible teaches the opposite at every point. 'God is a Spirit' (John 4:24). 'God is not a man' (Numbers 23:19; Hosea 11:9). 'From everlasting to everlasting, thou art God' (Psalm 90:2). 'Before me there was no God formed' (Isaiah 43:10; cf. 45:5, Malachi 3:6). And the worlds were framed by the word of God (Hebrews 11:3).

sources.name: Doctrine and Covenants 130:22

response:
FAIR argues that 'God is a Spirit' at John 4:24 states mode and character, not anatomy. It runs parallel to 'God is light' at 1 John 1:5 and 'a consuming fire' at Deuteronomy 4:24. Nobody takes those as the whole story.

Spirit and body are not opposites in any case. Risen beings have flesh and bone at Luke 24:39. FAIR marshals the appearances of God at Exodus 33:11 and 33:23. And David Paulsen of BYU argues that the earliest Christians thought of God in bodily terms, before Greek philosophy displaced that view.

On Adam-God, FAIR holds that Young's remarks were poorly recorded, speculative, or misunderstood. They were never canonised. And the church rejecting them shows living prophets correcting course, rather than prophecy failing.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Mormonism and the nature of God/God is a Spirit

rationale:
Every element is documented from canon or from current church publications. D&C 130:22 is canon. The 2014 essay confirms that the church still teaches the exalted-man doctrine.

The FAIR reading of John 4:24 has some force on its own. But the conflict rests on the verses taken together. A God who 'was once as we are now' cannot be God 'from everlasting to everlasting', or unchanging as Malachi 3:6 says. A God who rose inside an eternal frame of matter and law is not the Bible's Maker of all that is.

The Adam-God episode is on its own damaging to the self-correction reply. Young taught it plainly, again and again, over 25 years, including inside the temple. Kimball's 1976 denunciation means one prophet branded another prophet's pulpit teaching about God 'false doctrine'.

And David Paulsen of BYU argues the earliest Christians thought of God in bodily terms, before Greek philosophy displaced it. One prophet formally called another prophet's pulpit teaching about God false doctrine.
"Psalm 90:2 says from everlasting to everlasting. Was there a time he was not God?"

title: Hinckley in 1998: not 'the traditional Christ'
claim: Asked whether Latter-day Saints believe in 'the traditional Christ,' church president Gordon B. Hinckley said in 1998: 'No, I don't. The traditional Christ of whom they speak is not the Christ of whom I speak. For the Christ of whom I speak has been revealed in this the Dispensation of the Fulness of Times.' It is in the Church News of 20 June 1998. That is the sitting prophet conceding, in his own words, the substance of the evangelical claim. The Latter-day Saint Christ — firstborn spirit child, elder brother of Lucifer and of humanity, one of three separate Gods — differs from the Christ of historic Christianity. Paul warns against those who preach 'another Jesus, whom we have not preached' with 'another gospel' (2 Corinthians 11:3-4; Galatians 1:6-9; cf. Matthew 24:23-24, 1 John 4:1-3). The church's essay 'Are Mormons Christian?' responds not by claiming doctrinal agreement but by contesting the definition of 'Christian.'

sources.name: Church News: 'Crown of gospel is upon our heads' (June 20, 1998)
Gospel Topics Essay: Are 'Mormons' Christian?
MRM: Quotes That Didn't Make the Cut — Hinckley

response: FAIR argues the quote is real but misused. In context Hinckley was marking off the Latter-day Saint Christ from the creedal Christ. That is the being of Nicaea and Chalcedon, without body and beyond grasp. He was not marking him off from the Jesus of the New Testament. Latter-day Saints insist they worship that Jesus as divine Son of God, Saviour and Redeemer. The Living Christ of 2000 says exactly that. The essay Are Mormons Christian? adds that the earliest Christian view of God 'changed dramatically over the course of centuries' under Greek thought. So holding to fourth-century creeds cannot be the test of who follows Jesus. They claim restored Christianity, not reformed Christianity. And on 2 Corinthians 11:4 they note that Paul's target was a different gospel message, not an exam on metaphysics.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Jesus Christ/Biblical

rationale:
The quotation is real. It is in the church's own Church News of 20 June 1998, and Hinckley plainly affirms a real difference. That much is not in dispute, and the doctrinal entries back it up.

What this entry tests is the further step: that the sentence admits 'another Jesus' in Paul's sense. That is genuinely argued.

FAIR's point about context has real merit. 'Traditional Christ' most naturally means the creeds. And Latter-day Saint sources steadily identify their Christ with the Jesus of the New Testament: the same person, a different metaphysics.

Whether that counts as another Jesus should be argued from the doctrinal cases, not settled by this quote.

The traditional Christ of whom they speak is not the Christ of whom I speak. For the Christ of whom I speak has been revealed in this the Dispensation of the Fulness of Times." It is in the Church News of 20 June 1998.
Because it is the sitting prophet naming the difference himself. Paul warns about "another Jesus, whom we have not preached" in 2 Corinthians 11:4, and another gospel in Galatians 1:8.

title: Every human a spirit child of Heavenly Parents
claim: Latter-day Saint doctrine teaches that every human lived before birth as a literal spirit child begotten by Heavenly Parents. The Gospel Topics essay 'Mother in Heaven' says that 'all human beings, male and female, are beloved spirit children of heavenly parents.' A First Presidency statement of 1909, quoted in Gospel Principles chapter 2, says that man as a spirit 'was begotten and born of heavenly parents, and reared to maturity in the eternal mansions of the Father.' Abraham 3:22-23 describes premortal 'intelligences that were organized before the world was'; see also D&C 93:29 and Moses 3:5. The Bible teaches the reverse order and origin. 'That was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual' (1 Corinthians 15:46-47). The LORD 'formeth the spirit of man within him' (Zechariah 12:1). And man became a living soul when God breathed into formed dust (Genesis 2:7; cf. Isaiah 44:24).

response:
FAIR assembles a biblical case for life before birth. God knew Jeremiah 'before I formed thee in the belly', at Jeremiah 1:5. The 'sons of God shouted for joy' when the earth was founded, at Job 38:4-7.

At death 'the spirit shall return unto God who gave it', at Ecclesiastes 12:7. To return is to have been there. Hebrews 12:9 calls God 'the Father of spirits'. And the disciples' question about the man born blind, at John 9:2, seems to allow for choices made before birth.

FAIR adds that souls existing before bodies was a live view in early Christianity. Origen held it, and it was condemned only in the sixth century. On 1 Corinthians 15:46 they answer that Paul's subject is resurrection bodies, not where spirits come from.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Biblical support for a pre-mortal existence

rationale:
The teaching is documented from current official sources, and the core conflict stands. No biblical text says human spirits were begotten by Heavenly Parents before the world. Zechariah 12:1 puts the forming of a man's spirit 'within him'.

The proof-texts thin out in context. Jeremiah 1:5 is the language of choosing and foreknowing, as at Romans 8:29. The 'sons of God' at Job 38:7 are angels, and God's point to Job is that Job was not there. 'Return' at Ecclesiastes 12:7 pairs with dust going back to earth.

FAIR is right about 1 Corinthians 15:46, so do not lean on it. And Origen shows the idea was thinkable early, though his version had no Heavenly Mother and no spirit birth.

The distinctive claim, that human spirits were literally born to heavenly parents, has no biblical support at all.

plain.d: That every human lived before birth as a literal spirit child of Heavenly Parents. The essay Mother in Heaven says all human beings "are beloved spirit children of heavenly parents." Abraham 3:22-23 describes intelligences organised before the world. See also D&C 93:29 and Moses 3:5.

FAIR builds a real biblical case. God knew Jeremiah "before I formed thee in the belly" at Jeremiah 1:5. The sons of God "shouted for joy" when the earth was founded, in Job 38:4-7. At death the spirit "shall return unto God who gave it," in Ecclesiastes 12:7 — and return implies having been there. Hebrews 12:9 calls God "the Father of spirits." The disciples' question in John 9:2 seems to allow for it. Origen held that souls existed before bodies, before the church condemned it in the sixth century. And on 1 Corinthians 15:46 they say Paul is talking about resurrection bodies.

Strong for you, and give them one point. FAIR is right that 1 Corinthians 15:46 is about resurrection bodies, so do not lean on it. The rest dissolves in context. Jeremiah 1:5 is about God choosing, as in Romans 8:29. The sons of God in Job 38:7 are angels, and God's whole point is that Job was not there. Ecclesiastes 12:7 pairs with dust going back to earth. And Origen taught nothing like heavenly parents giving birth to spirits. That specific claim has no biblical support at all.

title: The Trinity, or three Gods with one purpose
claim: Official Latter-day Saint doctrine holds that the Father, Son and Holy Ghost are 'three separate beings,' with the Father and Son having tangible bodies, who are 'one in purpose' but not one Being (Gospel Topics: 'Godhead'; D&C 130:22). Joseph Smith's First Vision account has God declaring all existing creeds 'an abomination in his sight' (Joseph Smith—History 1:19), and the Book of Abraham narrates creation by 'the Gods' (Abraham 4:1). Smith preached a plurality of gods explicitly in the Sermon in the Grove of June 1844. The Bible's monotheism is exclusive and about being, not merely about purpose. 'The LORD our God is one LORD' (Deuteronomy 6:4). 'I am the LORD that maketh all things; that stretcheth forth the heavens alone; that spreadeth abroad the earth by myself' (Isaiah 44:24) — no council of gods at creation. 'There is none other God but one' (1 Corinthians 8:4-6; cf. Isaiah 43:10, 45:5-6). Notably, the Book of Mormon itself reads monotheistically: Alma 11:28-29 asks 'Is there more than one God?' and answers no. So does 2 Nephi 31:21.

sources.name: Gospel Topics: Godhead (churchofjesuschrist.org)
Church Newsroom: Godhead
BYU Religious Studies Center: 'God' (Latter-day Saint Essentials)
MRM: Godhead (Defined)

response: The strongest case runs on four fronts. First, Jesus prays that believers 'may be one, even as we are one', at John 17:20-23. Believers cannot merge into one substance. So the oneness of Father and Son in the same sentence reads most naturally as relational. That is the 'one in purpose' reading. Second, Jesus is visibly distinct from the Father all through the New Testament. At his baptism. In Gethsemane. In Stephen's vision at Acts 7:55-56. And 1 Corinthians 8:6 marks off 'one God, the Father' from 'one Lord, Jesus Christ'. Third, respected Christian philosophers model the Trinity as three centres of mind united in essence and will. Cornelius Plantinga Jr., Richard Swinburne and William Lane Craig all do. BYU scholars argue that this lands close to Joseph Smith's Godhead. The quarrel, they say, is with Greek metaphysics added later, not with the Bible. Fourth, Hebrew work on the divine council in Psalm 82 shows plural elohim language native to the Old Testament.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Mormonism and the nature of God/Nicene creed

rationale:
The doctrine is documented, and a real conflict exists. But their case has real merit at exactly the point this entry tests. The John 17 reading is defensible. Social trinitarianism is a live position among Christian thinkers.

The clash gets sharp where this doctrine goes further. Those thinkers still hold one uncreated divine essence. Here there are three separate beings. Two have bodies. At least one attained divinity. And exaltation hands godhood to others. Isaiah 44:24 and Isaiah 43:10 shut that out.

Note the strain inside their own canon. The Book of Mormon reads as strict monotheism at Alma 11:28-29, against Smith's later Nauvoo teaching.

It is graded contested because the John 17 argument works on its own ground.

plain.d: That the Father, Son and Holy Ghost are three separate beings, one in purpose but not one being. The Father and the Son have tangible bodies; see D&C 130:22 and the Gospel Topics page on the Godhead. Joseph Smith—History 1:19 has God call all existing creeds "an abomination in his sight." Abraham 4:1 has creation carried out by "the Gods." And Smith preached a plurality of gods openly in the Sermon in the Grove, in June 1844.

Deuteronomy 6:4 — "The LORD our God is one LORD." Isaiah 44:24 is sharper still. God stretches out the heavens "alone" and spreads the earth "by myself." No council of gods. 1 Corinthians 8:4 says "there is none other God but one."
The Book of Mormon reads like the Bible here. Alma 11:28-29 asks whether there is more than one God, and answers no. 2 Nephi 31:21 says the same.

And this is the strongest set they have. First, John 17:22: Jesus prays that believers "may be one, even as we are one." Believers do not merge into one substance. So the oneness in that same sentence reads as relational. Second, Jesus is visibly distinct from the Father all through the New Testament. At his baptism. In Gethsemane. In Stephen's vision at Acts 7:55-56. And 1 Corinthians 8:6 distinguishes one God the Father from one Lord Jesus Christ. Third, respected Christian philosophers model the Trinity as three centres of mind in one essence and will. Cornelius Plantinga Jr., Richard Swinburne and William Lane Craig all do. BYU scholars argue that lands near the Godhead. Fourth, Psalm 82 has plural elohim language native to the Old Testament.

Genuinely arguable, and the John 17 reading is fair. Do not pretend otherwise. The difference shows where the doctrine goes further. Those philosophers still hold one uncreated divine essence. Here there are three independent beings, two with bodies, at least one of whom became divine — and exaltation hands godhood to others. Isaiah 44:24 and 43:10 exclude that.
"Isaiah 44:24 says he made everything alone. Who else was there?"

title: Brigham Young: some sins need the sinner's blood
claim: Brigham Young taught from the Tabernacle pulpit that some sins exceed the atoning power of Christ's blood and require the sinner's own. 'There are sins that men commit for which they cannot receive forgiveness in this world, or in that which is to come, and if they had their eyes open to see their true condition, they would be perfectly willing to have their blood spilt upon the ground, that the smoke thereof might ascend to heaven as an offering for their sins.' That is Journal of Discourses 4:53-54, from 1856; see also 4:219-220, from 1857. In June 2010 the church formally stated that 'so-called blood atonement… is not a doctrine of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.' Scripture teaches the total sufficiency of Christ's one sacrifice: 'by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified' (Hebrews 10:12-14); 'the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin' (1 John 1:7); 'It is finished' (John 19:30). Hebrews 9:26, Isaiah 53:5-6 and 1 Timothy 2:5-6 say the same.

sources.name: Brigham Young sermon, JD 4:215–221 (full text, Utah Lighthouse Ministry scan)
Deseret News: Mormon church statement on blood atonement (June 18, 2010)
Mormonr: Blood Atonement and Capital Punishment (documents both sermons and disavowals)

response:
FAIR and Mormonr answer on four fronts.

The blood-atonement language belongs to the heated preaching of the Mormon Reformation, in 1856 and 1857. It was overstatement, meant to stir people to repent.

It was framed as a free choice, and tied to a view of the death penalty for capital crimes, echoing Genesis 9:6. It was not tied to mob action. There is no evidence the church ever set up any system of killing sinners to save them.

It was never made canon. D&C 42:18 and 42:79 call for church trial and the civil courts, not ritual death.

And the church has since dropped it by name, in Bruce R. McConkie's 1978 letter and in the 2010 statement. It stands today as an abandoned guess from the 1800s.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Repudiated concepts/Blood atonement

rationale:
Both the teaching and its disavowal are documented beyond dispute. The sermons are word for word in the Journal of Discourses at 4:53-54 and 4:219-220. And the 2010 statement shows the church understands what was taught well enough to disavow it by name.

What Young preached, that certain sins lie beyond the reach of Christ's blood, flatly contradicts Hebrews 10:14 and 1 John 1:7.

The hyperbole reading strains against his own words. They read as sober counsel across several sermons and several years.

The grade is medium because the doctrine is genuinely repudiated and carries no weight in salvation now. Its lasting force is as a second clear case, beside Adam-God, of a prophet teaching from the pulpit what the church now calls false doctrine.

plain.d: That some sins go beyond what Christ's blood can reach, and need the sinner's own. From the Tabernacle pulpit in 1856 he said that such men, if their eyes were open, "would be perfectly willing to have their blood spilt upon the ground, that the smoke thereof might ascend to heaven as an offering for their sins." It is in the Journal of Discourses 4:53-54, and again at 4:219-220 in 1857.

Hebrews 10:14 — "by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified." 1 John 1:7 — the blood of Jesus Christ "cleanseth us from all sin." And John 19:30 — "It is finished." See also Hebrews 9:26 and 1 Timothy 2:5-6.
In June 2010 it stated formally that "so-called blood atonement… is not a doctrine of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints." Bruce R. McConkie had repudiated it in a letter in 1978.

FAIR and Mormonr make four points. The language belongs to the heated preaching of the Mormon Reformation in 1856 and 1857, and was meant to provoke repentance. It was framed as voluntary, and tied to capital punishment for capital crimes, echoing Genesis 9:6 — not to vigilante killing. It was never canonised; D&C 42:18 and 42:79 prescribe excommunication and the civil courts. And the church has repudiated it by name.

Strong for you, and use it gently. Both the sermons and the disavowal are documented. What Young preached — that some sins lie beyond the reach of Christ's blood — flatly contradicts Hebrews 10:14 and 1 John 1:7. The hyperbole reading strains against his own words, which are sober counsel across several sermons and years. The weight of this now is not the doctrine. It is that a prophet taught from the pulpit what the church now calls false.

title: Joseph Smith's 30 to 40 wives, one aged 14

title: D&C 132: obey polygamy, Emma, or be destroyed

title: 'I can only find one,' while sealed to thirty
claim: On 26 May 1844, a month before his death, Joseph Smith preached publicly: 'What a thing it is for a man to be accused of committing adultery, and having seven wives, when I can only find one.' It is recorded in History of the Church 6:411. By that date he had been sealed to more than 30 women. This capped years of institutional denials. The 1835 Article on Marriage, which stayed in the Doctrine and Covenants until 1876, declared one man and one wife. title: 120 emigrants killed under a white flag, 1857
claim: On 11 September 1857, Mormon militiamen of the Iron County brigade lured the surrendered Baker-Fancher wagon train out under a white flag and murdered about 120 men, women and children, sparing only the small children. The attack was planned and ordered by local church and militia leaders in the Cedar City area, including the stake president Isaac Haight and Bishop John D. Lee. The church's own sponsored history — Ronald Walker, Richard Turley and Glen Leonard, 'Massacre at Mountain Meadows,' Oxford 2008 — confirms local church leadership responsibility. In 2007, Elder Henry B. Eyring expressed 'profound regret' on behalf of the First Presidency. Only John D. Lee was ever executed, in 1877. Exodus 20:13, Matthew 5:44 and Romans 12:19 are the texts at issue.

sources.name: Walker, Turley & Leonard, Massacre at Mountain Meadows (Oxford, church-sponsored)
LDS Church History Topics: Mountain Meadows Massacre
Church Newsroom: 150th Anniversary statement (Eyring, 2007)

response:

The setting was the Utah War. A federal army was on its way. The burnings in Missouri and at Nauvoo were fresh in mind, and wartime talk was everywhere.

The history the church paid for finds that Brigham Young did not order it. His letter, telling them to let the train pass, came two days late. Local leaders acted against that counsel. The cover-up was local first. Those who took part were later cut off from the church.

The church has built memorials. It has worked with the families of the dead. And it published the fullest account itself.

title: Mayor Joseph Smith ordered a newspaper's press destroyed
claim: On 10 June 1844, Joseph Smith as mayor and the Nauvoo city council ordered the destruction of the Nauvoo Expositor's press, after its single issue of 7 June. That issue's core reporting — on Smith's secret plural marriage and on his plurality-of-gods teaching — was substantively accurate. The destruction triggered riot charges, Smith's surrender at Carthage, and the mob attack of 27 June. At Carthage, Smith fired a smuggled six-shot pepperbox pistol into the mob, wounding three men. That is John Taylor's own account, in History of the Church 7:102-103, and it was long omitted from devotional retellings of the 'martyrdom.' 1 Peter 2:23, Matthew 26:52 and Proverbs 10:9 are the texts at issue.

sources.name: LDS Church History Topics: Nauvoo Expositor
Joseph Smith Papers: Order to Destroy Nauvoo Expositor Press
FAIR: Joseph Smith fired a gun at Carthage Jail

response: Dallin H. Oaks published a legal analysis in the Utah Law Review in 1965. Before the Fourteenth Amendment, the First Amendment did not bind city governments. So abating the newspaper as a nuisance had some legal footing under the Nauvoo Charter. Oaks concedes that destroying the press itself likely went beyond that. The council feared the paper would bring a mob down on the city. The mob came anyway. On Carthage, defending yourself against a lynch mob with painted faces does not make an unjust killing just. Smith was in state custody under the governor's pledged protection. The pistol is recorded by the eyewitness John Taylor himself, and the church has published the fact, including in Saints. Martyrdom in the broad sense means being killed for your religion, not dying passively.

responseSource.name: Dallin H. Oaks, 'The Suppression of the Nauvoo Expositor,' Utah Law Review 9 (1965); FAIR

rationale:

Apologetics contests the framing, martyr against man in a gunfight, and softens the legal question.

But the killing on 27 June was plainly murder outside the law. And the suppression of a truthful press was what set it off. Both things are true. Neither is refuted.

plain.d: Joseph Smith was mayor of Nauvoo. He and the city council ordered the press of the Nauvoo Expositor destroyed. The paper had printed one issue, on 7 June. Riot charges. Smith's surrender at Carthage. And the mob attack of 27 June in which he and Hyrum were killed.

They admit the facts, and so should you. Both things are true at once. The killing at Carthage was extrajudicial murder. And the trigger for it was the suppression of a newspaper that was telling the truth. Do not use the pistol to sneer; use it to ask what the word martyr is doing.

title: Temple oath: avenge the prophets' blood upon this nation

title: The Danites, and two Missouri towns burned in 1838
claim: In Missouri in 1838, a secret Mormon paramilitary band called the Danites was organized under Sampson Avard. It intimidated and expelled church dissenters; the Danite Manifesto threatened Oliver Cowdery, the Whitmers and others. During the conflict of October 1838, Mormon forces including Danites raided and burned the non-Mormon settlements of Gallatin and Millport. The contested question is how much Joseph Smith knew and authorized. Avard testified that Smith was the mastermind. Stephen LeSueur argues that Smith endorsed the Danites and benefited from them. Church-aligned scholars argue that Avard ran his own criminal program. Romans 12:17-19 and 2 Corinthians 10:3-4 are the texts at issue.

Stephen C. LeSueur, The 1838 Mormon War in Missouri (overview)

response:
Avard was a self-aggrandising opportunist who turned state's witness to save himself. That makes his 'Smith was the mastermind' testimony as self-serving as testimony gets. He was excommunicated in 1839.

Leland Gentry and Alexander Baugh trace three phases. It began as legitimate community defence. Avard then corrupted it into secret oaths and plunder, without Smith's authorisation.

The 1838 setting was a fight for survival. Mormons were being burned out. Governor Boggs's Extermination Order and the Haun's Mill massacre followed within weeks. Mormon violence, while real, was a fraction of what was done to them.

And the church's own history topics acknowledge the Danite excesses.

responseSource.name: Gentry & Baugh scholarship, summarized at FAIR

rationale:
The Danites existed. Dissenters were driven out. Gallatin and Millport were raided and burned. None of that is disputed.

The load-bearing claim is that Smith told them to. That rests largely on Avard's tainted word, and serious historians divide. Stephen LeSueur on one side. Gentry and Baugh on the other.

Smith praised Danite leaders in public and rode the wave. Command of the operation is not shown. Contested is the honest grade.

In the fighting of October 1838, Mormon forces raided and burned two towns that were not Mormon. Gallatin and Millport. Danites rode with them.

How much Joseph Smith knew, and how much he told them to do. Avard testified that Smith was the mastermind. Stephen LeSueur argues that Smith backed the Danites and gained by them. Scholars close to the church argue that Avard ran his own show.

Avard was a self-serving opportunist who turned state's witness to save himself, and was excommunicated in 1839. That makes his testimony the least reliable kind. Leland Gentry and Alexander Baugh trace three phases: a legitimate community defence that Avard corrupted into secret oaths and plunder, without Smith's authorisation. And the context was existential. Mormons were being burned out. Governor Boggs's Extermination Order and the Haun's Mill massacre followed within weeks. Mormon violence was real, and it was a fraction of what was done to them.
