The interview asks: "Are you a full-tithe payer?" And once a year members declare their status to the bishop. That meeting was called tithing settlement; since 2019 it is tithing declaration.
D&C 64:23 is canon: "he that is tithed shall not be burned at his coming." D&C 119:3-4 sets the standard. Leaders have taught paying tithing before feeding your family.
James Huntsman sued over how tithing was used. The full Ninth Circuit dismissed it 11 to 0 in January 2025. Do not repeat the fraud claim. It has been answered in court.

There is no paid local clergy. Bishops, teachers and leaders all serve free. Tithing pays for chapels, temples, education, operations and a large welfare and humanitarian programme. Members widely testify that paying it is a blessing rather than a burden. Tithing long predates this church; Malachi 3:8-10 calls withholding it robbing God, so gating on it has a biblical case. And the declaration is self-reported. Nobody audits your income.

They admit the structure, and none of it is contested. It is all in current church publications. The core point is simply a description: ordinances tied to salvation are conditioned on a financial contribution. Set that beside 2 Corinthians 9:7 — give "not grudgingly, or of necessity."
"What happens at the recommend interview if you say you haven't paid?"

refwhy.2 Corinthians 9:7: Give 'not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.' The verse against a required sum.
refwhy.Matthew 23:23: Jesus on tithing mint and cummin while missing 'judgment, mercy, and faith.' Note that he does not abolish tithing.
refwhy.Mark 12:41-44: The widow's two mites, praised for giving 'all her living.' Cuts both ways, since it commends costly giving.
refwhy.D&C 64:23: 'He that is tithed shall not be burned at his coming.' Canon, and the source of the fire language.
refwhy.D&C 119:3-4: Sets the amount. 'One-tenth of all their interest annually,' and it is called a standing law for ever.

titleLong: Tithing enforcement: temple access gated on payment
responseLead: There is no paid clergy here, and Malachi 3:8-10 calls withholding it robbing God.
rationaleLead: They admit the structure, and the fraud claim was thrown out 11 to 0.

title: Missionaries pay $500 a month to serve
claim: Latter-day Saint missionaries go out young. Men at 18 for 24 months, women at 19 for 18 months. They work full-time and unpaid, and they pay to do it. The flat sum has been $500 a month since 2020, and families usually find it. Missionaries hand over control of the day to mission rules and a mission president. That covers the schedule, what they may read and watch, and a companion at all times. Until February 2019, contact with family was weekly email and two phone calls a year, on Mother's Day and at Christmas. The pull to serve, from family and from culture, is strong. So is the stigma of coming home early. Members write about both at length.

sources.name: Church News: First Presidency announces increase in missionary contribution (2019)
NBC News: Mormons allow missionaries to call home weekly (2019)

response:
Service is freely chosen, and it is framed as consecrated service rather than work.

The flat payment levels it out. A missionary in Tokyo pays what one in Peru pays, and ward funds cover those who cannot.

Huge numbers of returned missionaries call it the making of them. A language learned. A habit of discipline. A life turned toward service.

The rules exist for safety and focus, as they do in monastic and military life. And the 2019 changes, with weekly calls and looser schedules, show the church listening to how missionaries fare.

responseSource.name: Church News / Newsroom announcements, 2019

rationale:
Every element comes from the church's own publications. The $500 a month since 2020. The rules. And the two calls a year before February 2019.

Their case is real too. It is freely chosen, and the benefits people report are genuine. Calling it unpaid labour understates how much people want to go.

But the claim describes facts the church itself confirms. The practice is open, and consented to.

plain.d: Men go at 18 for 24 months. Women go at 19 for 18 months. They work full-time and unpaid, and they pay to do it — a flat $500 a month since 2020, usually funded by the family.

Mission rules and a mission president set the schedule, the media allowed, and the rule that a companion is always present. Until February 2019, contact with family was weekly email plus two phone calls a year: Mother's Day and Christmas.
Cultural and family expectation to serve is strong. So is the stigma of coming home early. That is widely described by members themselves.

Service is voluntary, and it is framed as consecration rather than labour. The flat payment equalises it: a missionary in Tokyo pays what one in Peru pays, and ward funds cover those who cannot. Enormous numbers of returned missionaries call it the formative experience of their lives — a language, a discipline, a habit of service. The structure exists for safety and focus, as in monastic and military life. And the 2019 changes, with weekly calls and more flexible days, show the institution listening.

They admit all of it; every element comes from the church's own publications. The steelman is real too. It is voluntary, and the benefits people report are genuine. Calling it unpaid labour understates how much people choose it. This one is low stakes — mention it, do not press it.
"How often could you call home on your mission?"

titleLong: The missionary program: unpaid, family-funded, controlled contact
responseLead: Service is freely chosen, and the flat $500 keeps Tokyo and Peru the same.
rationaleLead: They admit it all, and it is low stakes: mention it, do not press it.

title: Dropped teachings, and 'never lead the church astray'
claim: Latter-day Saint prophets have taught, from prophetic platforms, doctrines the church later abandoned or disavowed. Brigham Young affirmed that the moon and the sun are inhabited (Journal of Discourses 13:271, 1870), and taught Adam-God in general conference, later denounced as 'false doctrine' by Spencer W. Kimball. Bruce R. McConkie's 'Mormon Doctrine' of 1958 required over 1,000 corrections identified by apostolic review, yet sold for decades before being pulled in 2010. Meanwhile Wilford Woodruff's declaration is printed with Official Declaration 1 in the canon: 'The Lord will never permit me or any other man who stands as President of this Church to lead you astray.' That creates an unfalsifiable loop. Whatever prophets teach is prophetic until it isn't, and the errors retroactively become 'opinion.' Deuteronomy 18:21-22, Matthew 7:15-20 and 1 Thessalonians 5:21 are the tests applied.

sources.name: Journal of Discourses 13:268–274, Brigham Young, July 24, 1870 (full text)
Official Declaration 1 with Woodruff excerpts (current LDS canon)
MRM: Early Mormon Leaders on the Inhabitants of the Sun and Moon
FAIR: Brigham Young on science and education

response: The church expressly teaches that prophets are fallible men. Joseph Smith said that 'a prophet is only a prophet when acting as such'. Not every sermon is revelation. Young's musing about the moon and sun was flagged as opinion. He said 'I rather think it is'. And it matched mainstream science of his century, since William Herschel believed the sun inhabited. It was never canonised or made a test of faith. Mormon Doctrine was a private book McConkie published without approval. Its correction and its withdrawal show the system correcting itself rather than failing. And Woodruff's statement, in context, answered a specific fear that the Manifesto was apostasy. It promises that God would remove a president who tried to lead the church fundamentally astray. It does not promise that presidents never err.

responseSource.name: FAIR, 'Brigham Young on science and education' and prophetic-fallibility materials

rationale: The quotations are real and can be checked. But the force of the claim depends on whether these were held out as prophetic, and their case has real substance. Young flagged the moon and sun remark as opinion. Mormon Doctrine was never official, though it needed over 1,000 corrections and still sold for decades before being pulled in 2010. Adam-God is the strong example. It was taught in conference as doctrine and later disavowed, and it keeps the tension live. The unfalsifiability point against Woodruff's line is fair philosophy. As a claim of failed prophecy, this is genuinely contested ground.

plain.t: What prophets have taught and the church later dropped
plain.d: Brigham Young said the moon and the sun are inhabited. That is Journal of Discourses 13:271, from 1870. He also taught Adam-God in general conference, which Spencer W. Kimball later denounced as false doctrine. And Bruce R. McConkie's Mormon Doctrine, from 1958, needed more than 1,000 corrections after apostles reviewed it. It sold for decades, and was pulled in 2010.
Wilford Woodruff's declaration sits with Official Declaration 1 in the canon. "The Lord will never permit me or any other man who stands as President of this Church to lead you astray."
It makes a loop that nothing can test. Whatever a prophet teaches is prophetic, until it is not. Then it becomes opinion, after the fact.

And much of it lands. The church teaches openly that prophets are fallible men. Joseph Smith said a prophet is only a prophet when acting as such, and not every sermon is revelation. Young flagged the moon and sun remark as speculation — "I rather think it is" — and it matched the science of his day; William Herschel thought the sun inhabited. It was never canonised. Mormon Doctrine was a private book McConkie published without permission, so its correction shows the system working. And Woodruff was answering a specific fear, that the Manifesto was apostasy.

Genuinely arguable, and pick your example carefully. The moon quote and Mormon Doctrine are weak, and you will be corrected on both. Adam-God is the strong one, because it was taught in conference and later disavowed. The unfalsifiable-loop point is fair philosophy. It is not a failed prophecy.
"How would you tell the difference between a prophet's revelation and his opinion?"

refwhy.Deuteronomy 18:21-22: The fulfilment test. It covers predictions, not a prophet's wrong opinion, so use it carefully here.
refwhy.Matthew 7:15-20: 'By their fruits ye shall know them.' A test of character and outcome, not of doctrinal detail.
refwhy.1 Thessalonians 5:21: 'Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.' It makes checking a duty, not disloyalty.
refwhy.Official Declaration 1: Where Woodruff's promise is printed. God 'will never permit' a president 'to lead you astray.' In their canon.

titleLong: Failed prophetic teachings vs. 'never lead the church astray'
responseLead: They teach that prophets are men. Not every sermon is a word from God.
rationaleLead: Pick Adam-God. The moon quote and Mormon Doctrine are weak, and you will be corrected.

title: Abuse reports routed to lawyers: the Bisbee case
claim: A 2022 Associated Press investigation, drawing on about 12,000 pages of sealed records, reported that the church's abuse help line routes bishops' reports of child sexual abuse to church lawyers at Kirton McConkie rather than to police. In the Bisbee, Arizona case, Paul Adams confessed abuse of his daughter to two bishops beginning in 2011. Church counsel advised that Arizona's clergy-penitent privilege barred reporting. The abuse continued for roughly seven more years, and came to include a second daughter, an infant, until Adams was independently caught in 2017. Critics allege that the help line functions to manage legal risk ahead of child protection. Mark 9:42, Luke 8:17 and James 1:27 are the texts they cite.

sources.name: AP investigation: 'Seven years of sex abuse: How Mormon officials let it happen'
Salt Lake Tribune: Sex abuse and the LDS Church 'help line' — 4 takeaways
Church Newsroom: Church Provides Further Details about the Arizona Abuse Case

response:
The church calls the AP framing egregiously wrong.

The bishop repeatedly urged Adams and his wife to report, and tried to intervene. Arizona law made the confession privileged. He legally could not pass on what he learned in it without consent. Arizona's courts agreed. In 2023 the state supreme court upheld the privilege and dismissed the claims against the church.

The help line exists so that untrained lay bishops reach professionals at once. Those professionals instruct them to comply with reporting laws, which vary by state. The church says its first priority is protecting victims.

And others knew. The mother knew, and so did people who saw what Adams posted online. They did not report either.

responseSource.name: Church Newsroom, 'Church Provides Further Details about the Arizona Abuse Case' (Aug 2022)

rationale:
The core timeline is established by court records and is not disputed. A confession in 2011. No report. Seven more years of abuse, coming to include a second daughter, an infant, until Adams was caught independently in 2017.

The claim about cause is genuinely argued. Did the help line exist to shield the institution ahead of children? The legal advice tracked Arizona's actual privilege statute, the courts sided with the church, and the bishops' bind was real.

What remains is that the system's design produced a catastrophic outcome, and that these calls route through defence counsel. Whether that is malice, negligence or compliance is the contested question.

plain.d: In 2022 the Associated Press published an investigation drawing on about 12,000 pages of sealed records. It reported that the church's abuse help line routes a bishop's report of child sexual abuse to church lawyers, the firm Kirton McConkie, rather than to police.

Paul Adams confessed to two bishops, beginning in 2011, that he was abusing his daughter. Church counsel advised that Arizona's clergy-penitent privilege barred reporting. The abuse went on for about seven more years. It came to include a second daughter, an infant. Adams was caught independently in 2017.

The church calls the AP framing egregiously wrong, and its case is not weak. The bishop repeatedly urged Adams and his wife to report it, and tried to intervene. Arizona law made the confession privileged. He could not legally pass on what he learned in it without consent. Arizona's courts agreed. In 2023 the state supreme court upheld the privilege and dismissed the claims. The help line exists so that untrained lay bishops reach professionals at once. Those professionals tell them how to comply with reporting law, which differs in every state. Others knew too — the mother, and people who saw what Adams posted online — and they did not report either.

Genuinely arguable, and this one needs care. The timeline is not disputed: a confession in 2011, no report, and seven more years. A child was harmed in that gap. What is contested is why. The legal advice tracked the actual Arizona statute, and the courts sided with the church. What no answer removes is that the system produced this outcome, and that these calls run through defence counsel.
"When a bishop calls that line, who is on the other end?"

refwhy.Mark 9:42: 'Whosoever shall offend one of these little ones… a millstone.' Jesus's own weight on harming a child.
refwhy.Luke 8:17: 'Nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest.' Aimed at a system that kept the report inside.
refwhy.James 1:27: 'Pure religion' is to visit 'the fatherless and widows in their affliction.' Care for the weak as the test.

titleLong: The abuse help line and the Bisbee, Arizona case
responseLead: By Arizona law that confession was private. The state's high court agreed in 2023.
rationaleLead: Arguable, and handle with care: the timeline is fixed, the cause is not.

title: The bank Ohio refused, opened anyway on revelation
claim: In November 1836 Joseph Smith co-founded the Kirtland Safety Society bank. When the Ohio legislature denied a charter, it reorganized in January 1837 as the 'Kirtland Safety Society Anti-Banking Company' and issued notes anyway. On 6 January 1837, Wilford Woodruff recorded in his journal that Smith declared he had 'receieved that morning the word of the Lord upon the subject of the Kirtland Safety Society' — not only 'the voice of the spirit… but even an audaible voice' — and that if the commandments were heeded 'all would be well.' Warren Parrish, an officer of the bank who later left the church, claimed Smith prophesied it would 'like Aaron's rod… swallow up all other banks… and survive when all others should be laid in ruins.' The bank was massively undercapitalized, and its notes lost most of their value within weeks. On 24 October 1837, Smith and Sidney Rigdon were each fined $1,000 plus costs for illegal banking, in Rounds qui tam v. Smith, under Ohio's 1816 statute. Smith fled Kirtland on the night of 12 January 1838. Historians estimate that 200 to 300 members left the church in the fallout — roughly 10 to 15% of Kirtland membership, including about a third of the general leadership. Heber C. Kimball later said that at the time, for every member who stood by Joseph Smith as prophet, 'there were twenty who did not.'

sources.name: Wilford Woodruff journal, 6 Jan 1837 (Wilford Woodruff Papers)
Transcript of Proceedings, Rounds qui tam v. Rigdon/Smith, Oct 1837 (Joseph Smith Papers)
Introduction to the Kirtland Safety Society (Joseph Smith Papers)
Church History Topics: Kirtland Safety Society (LDS Church)
Warren Parrish letter, Painesville Republican, 15 Feb 1838 (repr. UTLM)
Heber C. Kimball discourse, 23 Aug 1857, Journal of Discourses 5:171-181
Walker, 'The Kirtland Safety Society and the Fraud of Grandison Newell' (BYU Studies)

response:
FAIR and church historians argue five things.

The 1830s were the age of unregulated wildcat banking. Hundreds of banks, many of them chartered, failed in the national Panic of 1837. So the collapse reflects the economy rather than fraud.

The charter was refused for Ohio party reasons. Hard-money Democrats turned down nearly every new charter that session, and anti-Mormon feeling may have added to it. Operating as a joint-stock anti-banking company followed legal advice under law that was genuinely unsettled.

Joseph Smith put in more of his own money than almost anyone, and lost heavily. That is not the profile of a swindler. He resigned in June 1837 and warned the Saints against the notes before the worst of it.

And Woodruff's journal does not record what the revelation said. The grand line about swallowing up all banks comes only from Warren Parrish, by then a hostile ex-member with his own alleged part in the failure.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Creation of the Kirtland Safety Society

rationale:
The load-bearing facts are conceded in the church's own publications. The Joseph Smith Papers and the Church History Topics essay grant it all. The refused charter. The choice to operate anyway. The October 1837 fines for illegal banking. Smith's flight. And that leaders bore blame.

The revelation claim rests on a faithful source, not a hostile one. Wilford Woodruff wrote it in his own journal on 6 January 1837. The church-affiliated Woodruff Papers Project published it. Smith attached the word of the Lord, and an audible voice, to a venture that failed within months. It was ruled illegal. And 200 to 300 members left.

Their case genuinely softens the question of intent. Fraud is not shown. The Panic of 1837 was real, and Parrish deserves discounting.

It does not touch the core problem under Deuteronomy 18:21-22. A promise that all would be well was falsified by events.

plain.d: In November 1836 Joseph Smith helped found a bank. It was called the Kirtland Safety Society. Ohio refused it a charter. So in January 1837 it changed its name, to the Kirtland Safety Society Anti-Banking Company. Then it issued its notes anyway.

On 6 January 1837, Wilford Woodruff wrote in his journal that Smith had "receieved that morning the word of the Lord upon the subject of the Kirtland Safety Society." Not only by the spirit, he wrote, "but even an audaible voice." If the commandments were heeded, all would be well. Warren Parrish, an officer who later left, claimed Smith prophesied it would swallow up all other banks like Aaron's rod.

The bank had far too little capital behind it. Its notes lost most of their value within weeks. On 24 October 1837 Smith and Sidney Rigdon were each fined $1,000 and costs for illegal banking, under an Ohio statute of 1816. Smith fled Kirtland on the night of 12 January 1838.

Historians put the loss at 200 to 300 members. That is roughly 10 to 15% of Kirtland. It took about a third of the top leaders with it. Heber C. Kimball later said that for every member who stood by Joseph Smith as prophet, "there were twenty who did not."

FAIR and church historians make five points. The 1830s was the age of wild, unwatched banking. Hundreds of banks went down in the Panic of 1837. The charter was refused partly for Ohio party reasons; hard-money Democrats turned down nearly every new charter that year. Smith put in more of his own money than almost anyone, and lost it — not what a swindler does. He resigned in June 1837, and warned the Saints about the notes. And Woodruff never wrote down what the revelation said. The grand line about swallowing up all banks comes only from Parrish, who by then had left and was hostile.
"Woodruff wrote that he heard an audible voice about the bank. What do you make of that?"

refwhy.Deuteronomy 18:21-22: The test. A word given in the LORD's name that does not come to pass was not from him.
refwhy.Proverbs 12:22: 'Lying lips are abomination to the LORD.' A weak fit here, since fraud was never established.
refwhy.Jeremiah 23:21: 'I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran.' The charge of speaking without being sent.

titleLong: The Kirtland Safety Society: An Illegal Bank Backed by Claimed Revelation
responseLead: Hundreds of banks fell in the Panic of 1837, and Smith lost his own money.
rationaleLead: They admit the facts: 'all would be well' was falsified within months.

title: 262 new plural marriages after the 1890 Manifesto
claim: The 1890 Manifesto, now Official Declaration 1, publicly announced the end of plural marriage. Church leaders repeatedly denied any new plural marriages thereafter. In fact apostles and members of the First Presidency secretly authorized or performed roughly 262 new plural marriages between 1890 and 1904. That is B. Carmon Hardy's count in the appendix to Solemn Covenant. D. Michael Quinn's lower estimate, published in Dialogue 18:1 in 1985, put the figure at roughly 250. Many took place in Mexico, in Canada, or at sea. By some estimates, nine or ten General Authorities themselves took new plural wives. The Reed Smoot Senate hearings of 1904 to 1907 exposed the practice. In March 1904, church president Joseph F. Smith testified under oath that he had continued to cohabit with his five plural wives, and had fathered eleven children with them since 1890, in acknowledged violation of the law. Weeks later he issued the 1904 Second Manifesto. It asserted that no post-1890 marriages had occurred 'with the sanction, consent or knowledge of the Church' — a claim contradicted by the documented participation of his own counselors and apostles. Apostles John W. Taylor and Matthias F. Cowley were forced from the Quorum of the Twelve over the affair. This repeats the Nauvoo pattern of 1841 to 1844, making it the second sustained episode of public institutional denial of a privately continued practice.

sources.name: D. Michael Quinn, 'LDS Church Authority and New Plural Marriages, 1890-1904,' Dialogue 18:1 (1985): 9-105
Reed Smoot hearings, testimony of Joseph F. Smith (Proceedings, U.S. Senate Committee on Privileges and Elections, 1904, vol. 1; transcript excerpts)
Gospel Topics essay: 'The Manifesto and the End of Plural Marriage' (LDS Church)
B. Carmon Hardy, Solemn Covenant: The Mormon Polygamous Passage (Univ. of Illinois Press, 1992) — BYU Studies review
1904 Second Manifesto statement (BYU-Idaho archives)
Church History Topics: Reed Smoot Hearings (LDS Church)

response:
The church's own Gospel Topics essay makes the case, and concedes most of the record.

After October 1890, plural marriages 'continued to be quietly performed' in Mexico and Canada. The Manifesto stated President Woodruff's intention to obey the laws of the United States. It 'said nothing about the laws of other nations'.

Leaders in good faith read it as a legal document. They did not read it as a ban on the principle everywhere. 'Many Church leaders believed the Manifesto merely suspended plural marriage for an indefinite time.'

Husbands already married kept living with their plural wives, and fathered children well into the next century. They did not cast off covenant families. Only in 1904, with the Second Manifesto, were members put on notice. Taylor and Cowley were then dropped from the quorum.

Apologists add three points. Turning away from what leaders believed God had commanded was wrenching. It happened while the federal government hunted them. And muddle, not plotting, explains the fifteen-year lag.

responseSource.name: Gospel Topics essay: The Manifesto and the End of Plural Marriage

rationale:
This is the rare case where the church's own essay concedes nearly every element. Marriages quietly performed with leader involvement. Cohabitation and children. The Manifesto's limited legal scope. Two apostles removed.

And Joseph F. Smith's sworn Smoot testimony of March 1904 is a first-person admission by a church president. Five plural wives, and eleven children by them since 1890.

What their case reframes is sincere confusion against duplicity. It cannot erase that leaders publicly and repeatedly denied what they privately authorised. The Second Manifesto's 'sanction, consent or knowledge' claim is falsified by Hardy's 262 and Quinn's lower estimate of roughly 250.

Nor can it erase that this replays the Nauvoo pattern. Measured by Proverbs 12:22, Ephesians 4:25 and Numbers 30:2, the pattern stands conceded in substance and argued only in motive.

plain.d: The 1890 Manifesto, now Official Declaration 1, publicly ended plural marriage. Leaders then repeatedly denied that any new plural marriages were taking place.

Apostles and members of the First Presidency secretly authorised or performed roughly 262 new plural marriages between 1890 and 1904. That is B. Carmon Hardy's count in Solemn Covenant. D. Michael Quinn's lower estimate, published in Dialogue in 1985, put the figure at roughly 250. Many took place in Mexico, in Canada, or at sea. By some estimates, nine or ten General Authorities took new plural wives themselves.

The Reed Smoot Senate hearings, from 1904 to 1907. In March 1904 the church president Joseph F. Smith testified under oath. He had gone on living with his five plural wives, and had fathered eleven children by them since 1890, against the law. Weeks later he issued the Second Manifesto. Apostles John W. Taylor and Matthias F. Cowley were forced out of the Quorum of the Twelve.

The church's own essay concedes most of it. Marriages "continued to be quietly performed" in Mexico and Canada. The Manifesto was about the laws of the United States, and "said nothing about the laws of other nations," so leaders read it as limited. Many believed it only suspended the practice for a time. Existing husbands kept their covenant families rather than abandon them. Only in 1904 were members "put on notice." The transition away from something leaders believed God had commanded was wrenching, and it happened under federal persecution.

They admit almost all of it, in their own essay. Joseph F. Smith's sworn testimony is a church president admitting it himself. What is argued is motive — sincere confusion rather than duplicity. But the Second Manifesto said no marriages had happened with the "sanction, consent or knowledge of the Church," and Quinn and Hardy document that they had. And this is the second time, after Nauvoo.
"What did Joseph F. Smith tell the Senate in 1904?"

refwhy.Proverbs 12:22: 'Lying lips are abomination to the LORD.' The measure applied to fifteen years of public denials.
refwhy.Matthew 5:33-37: 'Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay.' Against careful wording meant to mislead.
refwhy.Ephesians 4:25: 'Speak every man truth with his neighbour.' The plain rule for what leaders told members.
refwhy.Numbers 30:2: A man who swears an oath 'shall not break his word.' Set beside the sworn Smoot testimony.
refwhy.Jacob 2:24-30: Their own book calls many wives 'abominable,' with the one exception clause. It frames the whole question.
refwhy.D&C Official Declaration 1: The 1890 Manifesto itself, in their canon. Read the wording and see how narrow the promise is.

titleLong: Post-Manifesto Polygamy (1890-1904): Public Denial, Private Practice — the Second Time
responseLead: The Manifesto spoke of United States law. It said nothing about other nations.
rationaleLead: They admit nearly all of it, and a church president admitted it under oath.

title: Facsimile 1: Abraham, or a funeral scene
claim: Joseph Smith published Facsimile 1 as Abraham 'fastened upon an altar,' with 'the idolatrous priest of Elkenah attempting to offer up Abraham as a sacrifice' (Facsimile 1 Explanation, figures 2 and 3; cf. Abraham 1:12-15). Egyptology identifies the original as a standard funerary lion-couch vignette: the jackal-headed god Anubis attending the deceased Osiris-Hor. It survives as Papyrus Joseph Smith I. That is part of the Book of Breathings made for the Theban priest Hor, in the Ptolemaic era, around the second or first century BC. That is more than 1,500 years after Abraham. The papyrus has a lacuna, a missing section, exactly where the priest's head and alleged knife appear in the 1842 published version. The woodcut restoration shows a bald human head and a drawn knife. Robert Ritner and others note ink traces of a headdress at the shoulder, indicating a jackal-headed Anubis, and no parallel vignette shows a knife. Smith's other identifications do not match any accepted Egyptological reading either: the bird as 'Angel of the Lord,' the canopic jars as idolatrous gods of foreign nations, the crocodile as 'idolatrous god of Pharaoh.'

sources.name: Robert K. Ritner, The Joseph Smith Egyptian Papyri: A Complete Edition (2013); 'The Breathing Permit of Hor' (JNES 62, 2003) — summarized with translations
Gospel Topics essay: 'Translation and Historicity of the Book of Abraham' (LDS Church)
FAIR: Book of Abraham facsimiles — missing portions of Facsimile 1
Pearl of Great Price Central: 'The Idolatrous Priest (Facsimile 1, Figure 3)'
Book of Abraham Facsimile 1 analysis (4witness)

response:
John Gee, Kerry Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central argue four things.

First, the hole means nobody knows what the original showed. Some hold that the papyrus was already torn in 1835. A knife and a human head could have stood there. They add that this scene is odd for its type. The figure on the couch looks alive and clothed, with both hands perhaps raised.

Second, Egyptian temple texts do show enemies ritually killed. So a sacrifice reading is not absurd.

Third, Jews living in Egypt plainly reused Egyptian pictures and gave them new meanings. So this scene could have gone with an Abraham text, whatever it was first drawn for.

Fourth, on the catalyst view the papyri were only a prompt. That makes the explanations inspired comment, not Egyptology.

responseSource.name: Pearl of Great Price Central: The Idolatrous Priest (Facsimile 1, Figure 3)

rationale:
Unlike Facsimiles 2 and 3, this one has a real gap in the evidence. The hole covers exactly the disputed parts. So the restoration case runs on parallels and ink traces, not on a surviving original.

The scholarly reading is far better supported. Anubis, in a routine embalming scene from Hor's Breathing Permit. Ink traces of a headdress at the shoulder. Hundreds of parallel scenes. And no parallel at all with a knife in it. The church's own essay grants that Egyptologists read it differently.

But they dispute what filled the hole, not the Egyptology. And the scene does have odd features. So this figure is scored contested.

Note the labels around it, though. The jars as gods of foreign nations, and the crocodile as Pharaoh's god, have no support at all.

plain.t: What Joseph Smith said it shows
plain.d: Abraham "fastened upon an altar." Over him, "the idolatrous priest of Elkenah attempting to offer up Abraham as a sacrifice." That is his own printed explanation, figures 2 and 3. Abraham 1:12-15 tells the story.

A standard funeral scene. The original survives as Papyrus Joseph Smith I. It is part of the Book of Breathings made for a Theban priest named Hor, around the second or first century BC. That is more than 1,500 years after Abraham. The scene shows the jackal-headed god Anubis tending the dead man on a lion couch.

The papyrus has a hole. It sits exactly where the priest's head and the knife appear in the 1842 woodcut. The woodcut shows a bald human head and a raised knife. Robert Ritner and others note ink traces of a headdress at the shoulder, which points to Anubis. And no other scene of this kind has a knife in it.

John Gee, Kerry Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central make four points. Nobody knows what filled the hole, so a human head and a knife could have been there. This scene is unusual: the figure on the couch looks alive and clothed, with both hands perhaps raised. Egyptian temple texts do show ritual killing of enemies, so a sacrifice reading is not absurd. Jews living in Egypt did reuse Egyptian pictures for their own stories. And the catalyst view says the papyri only prompted revelation, so the explanations are inspired comment rather than translation.

Genuinely arguable, unlike the other two facsimiles. The hole covers the very things in dispute, so the case runs on parallels and ink traces. The Egyptological reading is far better supported, and the church's own essay grants that Egyptologists read it differently. But note the rest. The canopic jars as gods of foreign nations, and the crocodile as the god of Pharaoh, have no support at all.
"What do you make of the missing piece? That's where the whole argument sits."

title: Facsimile 2: a fertility god called God enthroned
claim: Facsimile 2 is a hypocephalus: a funerary amulet placed under a mummy's head, from Book of the Dead spell 162, made for a man named Sheshonq. It is a well-understood class of object, meant to keep the deceased warm and to aid resurrection. Joseph Smith's explanations instead present it as cosmology. Figure 1 is 'Kolob, signifying the first creation, nearest to the celestial, or the residence of God.' Figure 5 is the sun receiving light 'through the medium of Kae-e-vanrash.' Abraham 3:2-4 and 3:9 go with them. Most starkly, there is figure 7. Egyptologists uniformly identify it as Min, an ithyphallic fertility god, shown seated with an erect phallus and upraised flail, approached by a serpent. Smith labelled it 'God sitting upon his throne, revealing through the heavens the grand Key-words of the Priesthood; as, also, the sign of the Holy Ghost unto Abraham, in the form of a dove.' Even the Latter-day Saint scholar Michael Rhodes's translation of the rim and panels yields standard funerary formulae for Sheshonq, not Abrahamic cosmology. Portions of the original were missing and were filled in for the 1842 publication with characters copied from other papyri, including lines from the Hor Book of Breathings.
bom: Book of Abraham, Facsimile 2 Explanation, Figs. 1, 5, 7

sources.name: Ritner, The Joseph Smith Egyptian Papyri: A Complete Edition (2013) — hypocephalus translation; summarized with images

response:
Latter-day Saint scholarship concedes that figure 7 depicts a form of Min. Rhodes, Gee, Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central all grant it. They then argue three things.

First, Min was for Egyptians a supreme creator god. He stood for the power that makes life. So 'God sitting upon his throne' may catch the figure's role in Egyptian religion, even if the image shocks a modern reader.

Second, hypocephali are esoteric objects. They encode cosmic geography and rebirth. A cosmological reading is therefore not alien to the genre. A few of Smith's labels are argued to land near Egyptian ideas, such as figure 1 as the creative force at the centre, and figure 4 as the firmament.

Third, under the Semitic-adaptation and catalyst frameworks, the explanations were never meant as decipherment. They were inspired reuse, in the way Egyptian Jews reused pagan imagery.

responseSource.name: Pearl of Great Price Central: God Sitting Upon His Throne (Facsimile 2, Figure 7)

rationale:
There is no dispute about what figure 7 is. Their own sources name it as Min, shown with an erect phallus.

The dispute is only whether Smith's label can be rescued. Can 'God sitting upon his throne, revealing the grand Key-words of the Priesthood' be read as a fair gloss on a fertility god approached by a serpent? No Egyptologist reads one of these amulets as teaching Kolob, key-words, or the Holy Ghost.

Michael Rhodes is a Latter-day Saint scholar. His own reading of the rim and panels gives ordinary funeral prayers for Sheshonq.

Their case does not meet the translation evidence. It moves the explanations outside translation, which gives the point away.

Deuteronomy 18:21-22 and 1 Thessalonians 5:21 set the test. Smith said he translated by the gift and power of God. The checkable claims fail checking, and no rival translation has answered them.

plain.d: A hypocephalus. That is a round funeral amulet, laid under the head of a mummy. It comes from spell 162 of the Book of the Dead, and this one was made for a man named Sheshonq. Its purpose was to keep the dead warm and help them rise.

plain.t: What Joseph Smith said it means

Egyptologists all identify it as Min, a fertility god. He is shown seated, with an erect phallus and a raised flail, approached by a serpent. His explanation goes on: "as, also, the sign of the Holy Ghost unto Abraham, in the form of a dove."

Michael Rhodes is a Latter-day Saint scholar. His own translation of the rim and panels gives ordinary funeral prayers for Sheshonq. Parts of the original were missing in 1842 and were filled in with characters copied from other papyri, including lines from Hor's Book of Breathings.

Rhodes, John Gee, Kerry Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central grant that figure 7 is a form of Min. They argue three things. To Egyptians, Min was a supreme creator god. He stood for the power that makes life. So "God sitting upon his throne" may catch his role, even if the image startles us. Second, hypocephali are esoteric objects about cosmic geography and rebirth. A cosmological reading is not alien to that genre. Some argue that figure 4, as the firmament, lands near an Egyptian idea. Third, under the catalyst view, the explanations were never meant as decipherment at all.
"Even the church's own scholars say figure 7 is Min. What do you do with that?"

title: Facsimile 3: a goddess labelled 'King Pharaoh'
claim: Facsimile 3 is a standard presentation vignette from the Book of Breathings of the priest Hor. The deceased Hor, led by Maat and Anubis, is presented before the enthroned Osiris, with Isis behind him. Unlike Facsimile 1, the hieroglyphic captions beside each figure survive in the published woodcut and name the figures, and Egyptologists can read them. Robert Ritner's translations run as follows. Figure 2, which Smith labelled 'King Pharaoh, whose name is given in the characters above his head,' is captioned 'Isis the great, the god's mother' — a goddess. Figure 4, which Smith called 'Prince of Pharaoh, King of Egypt, as written above the hand,' is 'Maat, mistress of the gods' — also a goddess. Figure 1, Smith's 'Abraham sitting upon Pharaoh's throne,' is the god Osiris. Figure 5, Smith's 'Shulem, one of the king's principal waiters,' is captioned 'The Osiris Hor, justified forever' — the papyrus owner himself. Figure 6, Smith's 'Olimlah, a slave belonging to the prince,' is the god Anubis. Smith thus rendered two female goddesses as male royalty, and claimed their names were given in the characters above — characters that, once read, name Isis and Maat. Earlier Egyptologists shown the facsimiles reached the same conclusions independently: Théodule Devéria in 1860, and the 1912 panel that included Flinders Petrie and James Breasted.

sources.name: Ritner, The Joseph Smith Egyptian Papyri: A Complete Edition (2013) — Facsimile 3 caption translations; quoted in FAIR's treatment
FAIR: responses to Joseph Smith's interpretations of Facsimile 3 (quotes Ritner, Parker, Baer readings)
Pearl of Great Price Central: 'Isis the Pharaoh (Facsimile 3, Figure 2)'
Gospel Topics essay: 'Translation and Historicity of the Book of Abraham' (LDS Church)

response:
The strongest case comes from Gee, Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central. It offers no rival reading of the captions. It accepts them, and argues that the figures were relabelled.

First, in Egyptian thought Pharaoh stood for Osiris on earth. Isis could be tied to the throne itself, and even to the king. So Isis as Pharaoh has some precedent.

Second, Jews in Egypt plainly took Egyptian scenes and used them for their own figures. Abraham turns up in later Egyptian magic texts. So an old Jewish editor could have relabelled this as Abraham at court.

Third, scenes of this kind do dress one figure in another's imagery. So crossing gender in a label is not unknown.

Fourth, some of the glyphs are copied badly in the woodcut. The Isis name group is one. That clouds what stood on the original.

responseSource.name: Pearl of Great Price Central: Isis the Pharaoh (Facsimile 3, Figure 2)

rationale:
This is the hardest facsimile case for their side. Smith staked his labels on the characters themselves: 'whose name is given in the characters above his head'. Those characters can now be read. They say Isis and Maat. Not a Pharaoh. Not a prince. Where Smith saw 'Shulem the waiter', they name Hor, who owned the papyrus.

No source on their side offers a rival reading. Théodule Devéria reached the same result in 1860. So did the 1912 panel that included Flinders Petrie and James Breasted.

Their answer accepts the Egyptology and posits an old relabelling that no document shows. Not on this papyrus.

The church's own essay grants that Egyptologists read it differently from Smith. It stops short of granting error. So the verdict is unrefuted rather than admitted.

This was a checkable claim made in the name of the gift and power of God. On the evidence as it stands, it fails the test of 1 Thessalonians 5:21 and Deuteronomy 18.

Robert Ritner translated them. Figure 2, which Smith called "King Pharaoh, whose name is given in the characters above his head," is captioned "Isis the great, the god's mother." A goddess. Figure 4, which Smith called "Prince of Pharaoh, King of Egypt," is "Maat, mistress of the gods." Also a goddess. Figure 1, Smith's Abraham on the throne, is Osiris. Figure 5, Smith's "Shulem, one of the king's principal waiters," is "The Osiris Hor, justified forever" — the owner of the papyrus. Figure 6, Smith's slave Olimlah, is Anubis.
Théodule Devéria reached the same conclusions in 1860. So did the 1912 panel of Egyptologists, which included Flinders Petrie and James Breasted. They worked independently.

It does not offer a rival translation. Gee, Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central accept the readings and argue for relabelling. Jews in Egypt did adapt Egyptian scenes for their own figures, and Abraham turns up in later Egyptian magical texts. Presentation scenes do dress figures in one another's imagery. And some caption glyphs are poorly copied in the woodcut.
"He said the name is written above the head. It's written. It says Isis."

title: Brigham Young taught that Adam is God
claim: On 9 April 1852, Brigham Young taught in general conference that Adam 'is our Father and our God, and the only God with whom we have to do' (Journal of Discourses 1:50-51). He repeated the teaching for over two decades, declaring in 1873 that 'Adam is my father' was doctrine God had revealed to him. In 1877 he had it incorporated into the temple lecture at the veil in the St George Temple, as recorded in L. John Nuttall's journal for 7 February 1877. The teaching contradicts Genesis, where Adam is a creature formed by God (Genesis 2:7), the Bible's insistence that God is not a man (Hosea 11:9; Isaiah 43:10; 1 Corinthians 15:45), and canonized Latter-day Saint scripture itself, which identifies Adam as the archangel Michael, subordinate to God (D&C 27:11; 107:53-55). In 1976, President Spencer W. Kimball told general conference: 'the Adam-God theory… We denounce that theory and hope that everyone will be cautioned against this and other kinds of false doctrine.' Either a prophet taught false doctrine over the pulpit and in the temple for 25 years, or the church now denounces true doctrine.

Mormonr: Adam-God Theory (primary documents)

response:
FAIR argues that Young's sermons survive only in rough transcripts. It argues that he taught other things that do not fit a strong Adam-God reading. And it notes that the teaching was never made canon by common consent.

On that account it was one man's private speculation. It was not church doctrine.

Kimball's 1976 denunciation is presented as the system working. The living church corrects itself. Doctrine is set by scripture and by the united voice of the First Presidency. It is not set by every pulpit remark of a past president.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Brigham Young and Adam-God theory

rationale:
Kimball's 1976 denunciation concedes the substance. Something Young taught as doctrine is now officially 'false doctrine'.

The misreporting defence fails against several independent records. The Journal of Discourses. Young's own reaffirmation in 1873. Wilford Woodruff's journal. And the St George temple lecture minutes of 7 February 1877.

The remaining move, that it was never canonised, rescues the church's doctrinal process only by conceding the evangelistic point. A president of the church, speaking as prophet, taught for 25 years, including inside the temple, something the church now denounces.

That collapses 'the prophet will never lead the church astray' as a working guarantee.

title: No account of the angelic ordination until 1834
claim: The church teaches that John the Baptist restored the Aaronic priesthood in May 1829. See D&C 13 and Joseph Smith—History 1:68-72. Peter, James and John are said to have restored the Melchizedek priesthood soon after. Yet no publication or record describes these angelic ordinations until Oliver Cowdery's account of October 1834, in the Messenger and Advocate. That is five years later. Joseph's 1832 history does not narrate them. The 1833 Book of Commandments revelations contain none of the passages. And the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants added the relevant text retroactively. What is now D&C 27:5-13 grew from a short 1830 revelation into one naming John the Baptist and Peter, James and John. Compare Book of Commandments 28. David Whitmer told interviewers he 'never heard that an Angel had ordained Joseph and Oliver to the Aaronic priesthood' until years after the church was organized in 1830, and William McLellin said the same. Critics conclude that the restoration narrative developed after 1830 and was written back into the founding revelations. Hebrews 7:23-24, 1 Peter 2:9 and Deuteronomy 4:2 are the texts at issue.

response:
FAIR and BYU scholars reply on four fronts.

Joseph's 1832 history does mention receiving 'the holy Priesthood by the ministring of Aangels'. And an 1829-era revelation, now D&C 27, points to authority from heavenly messengers.

Joseph and Oliver kept the details quiet because they were being hunted. Joseph said they were 'forced to keep secret the circumstances of having received the Priesthood'.

The 1835 additions are framed as a prophet making his own earlier words clearer, under the same inspiration.

And Whitmer and McLellin were hostile by then. They were recalling events forty or fifty years on.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Priesthood Restoration Concerns & Questions

rationale:
The documented facts favour the critics. The named-angel account appears nowhere before Oliver Cowdery's in October 1834, five years later. And the 1835 additions are visible in the church's own Joseph Smith Papers.

But their case is not empty. The 1832 history's 'ministring of Aangels' phrase is a genuine, if unclear, counter. So is the persecution-secrecy argument. And late hostile memories do deserve discounting.

What is beyond dispute is the retroactive growth of the text. What stays arguable is whether it records suppressed events or invents them.

That split is the definition of contested, though the pattern matches the First Vision's shifting accounts.

title: Revelations rewritten: a divining rod becomes Aaron's gift
claim: Revelations published in 1833 as the direct word of God were materially rewritten for the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants. There were hundreds of changes, including substantive additions and reversals, all verifiable in the church's own Joseph Smith Papers scans. Book of Commandments 4:2 says God 'will grant him no other gift' than translating the Book of Mormon; D&C 5:4 rewrites this to 'no other gift until it is finished,' opening the door to Joseph's later revelatory career. Book of Commandments 7 says Oliver Cowdery's gift is 'working with the rod,' the 'rod of nature'; D&C 8:6-9 renames the divining rod 'the gift of Aaron.' Book of Commandments 28, now D&C 27:5-13, grew from a short revelation into eighteen verses naming the priesthood-restoring angels. Deuteronomy 4:2 and Proverbs 30:5-6 forbid adding to God's words. A 'thus saith the Lord' text that must be re-engineered years later, to fit the movement's development, looks like an evolving human composition rather than delivered revelation.

response:
FAIR argues that Joseph Smith never claimed the words were dictated by God. Revelations came as impressions, put into his own imperfect language.

So the man who received them could revise them, expand them, and update them as the church grew. The additions to section 20 simply took in offices revealed after 1830.

The church prints every version openly in the Joseph Smith Papers. FAIR calls that the opposite of a cover-up.

And the revised texts were accepted by common consent at the 1835 conference.

rationale:
The changes are conceded and published by the church itself. The Joseph Smith Papers put both editions side by side, and FAIR's defence justifies the edits rather than denying them.

The remaining dispute is what to make of it. May a prophet revise God's words? And there their answer creates its own problem.

If revelations are Joseph's fallible paraphrases, open to later re-engineering, then the weight of any given 'thus saith the Lord' drops. That includes D&C 132.

The fact bites chiefly alongside the priesthood-restoration backdating.

plain.d: Revelations printed in 1833 as the word of God were rewritten for the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants. Hundreds of changes, some of them substantive. You can check every one in the church's own Joseph Smith Papers scans.

Book of Commandments 4:2 says God "will grant him no other gift." D&C 5:4 makes it "no other gift until it is finished." And Book of Commandments 28 grew into eighteen verses, now D&C 27. Those verses name the angels who restored the priesthood.

Deuteronomy 4:2 and Proverbs 30:5-6 forbid adding to God's words. Look at what these edits imply. A text says thus saith the Lord. Then it has to be re-engineered years later, to fit how the movement grew. That looks like a human draft.

They admit this themselves, and publish both editions side by side. The defence justifies the edits; it does not deny them. Notice the price. If revelations are fallible paraphrases that can be re-engineered later, then every thus saith the Lord weighs less — including D&C 132.
"Have you compared the 1833 and 1835 versions? They're both on the church's own site."

title: One Egyptian character, a whole paragraph of Abraham
claim: Alongside the Book of Abraham translation, Joseph Smith's circle produced the Kirtland Egyptian Papers. Among them is a bound 'Grammar and Alphabet of the Egyptian Language' from 1835, in the hands of W. W. Phelps and Warren Parrish, published in full by the Joseph Smith Papers. Joseph's own journal records him 'studying the Egyptian language,' and records that the group was 'engaged in translating an alphabet to the Book of Abraham, and arranging a grammar of the Egyptian language.' The system assigns single Egyptian characters paragraph-long English meanings that multiply through five 'degrees' — a scheme Egyptologists uniformly reject as bearing no relation to actual Egyptian. Three Book of Abraham manuscripts place characters copied sequentially from the recovered Hor Book of Breathings in the margins, beside the English text. Unlike the gold plates, here the working papers of a Joseph Smith translation project survive, and they show a method that was not translation. Abraham 1:1-3 is the text at issue, and Deuteronomy 18:21-22 and Jeremiah 23:16 the tests applied.

sources.name: Joseph Smith Papers: Grammar and Alphabet of the Egyptian Language (1835)
Wikipedia: Kirtland Egyptian papers
FAIR: What are the Kirtland Egyptian Papers and GAEL?
Pearl of Great Price Central: The Kirtland Egyptian Papers and the Book of Abraham

response:
Gee, Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central argue that the borrowing runs the other way.

On their view the scribes were working backwards. They had an English text already given, and tried to build Egyptian out of it. It was a study exercise Joseph allowed but did not write.

Most pages are in scribes' hands. The Grammar was never printed and never made canon. And they argue that the Abraham text came first, on the evidence of the manuscripts.

So the Kirtland Egyptian Papers show 1835 curiosity about Egyptian. They do not show how the Book of Abraham was made.

responseSource.name: Pearl of Great Price Central: The Kirtland Egyptian Papers and the Book of Abraham

rationale:
The narrow question is which came first: the English text, or the Alphabet documents. That is genuinely debated. Joseph Smith Papers editors call the documents intertwined, and scholars on both sides make textual arguments.

So the strongest critical framing, that the Grammar was the engine of translation, stays contested.

But the escape is expensive. Joseph's own journal says the group was 'arranging a grammar of the Egyptian language'. Either way, his circle produced an Egyptian system under his eye, and it is nonsense.

Set beside the papyri mismatch, this backs up the case rather than carrying it alone.

plain.d: The working papers. Alongside the Book of Abraham, Joseph Smith's circle produced the Kirtland Egyptian Papers. Among them is a bound volume, Grammar and Alphabet of the Egyptian Language, from 1835. It is in the hands of W. W. Phelps and Warren Parrish. The Joseph Smith Papers have published it in full.
That he was "studying the Egyptian language." And that the group was "engaged in translating an alphabet to the Book of Abraham, and arranging a grammar of the Egyptian language."

It gives a single Egyptian character a paragraph of English meaning. Those meanings then multiply through five degrees. Egyptologists reject it entirely. It bears no relation to Egyptian. And three Book of Abraham manuscripts have characters copied in order from the Hor papyrus down the margin, beside the English.

Gee, Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central argue the dependence runs the other way. The scribes were trying to work backwards from an English text already revealed. It was an exercise Joseph allowed but did not write. Most pages are in scribes' handwriting. The grammar was never published or canonised. And they argue the Abraham text came first, on textual grounds.

Genuinely arguable on the narrow question. Which came first is really debated, and the Joseph Smith Papers editors call the documents intertwined. But the escape is expensive. His own journal says he was arranging the grammar. Either way, his circle produced an Egyptian system, under his eye, that is nonsense. Use it to support the papyri case, not on its own.
"Have you seen the Egyptian alphabet they made in Kirtland? It's published."

refwhy.Jeremiah 23:16: Prophets who 'speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.' Heavy wording; use it with care.
refwhy.Abraham 1:1-3: The published English text. The Kirtland papers line it up against single Egyptian characters, one to a paragraph.

titleLong: The 'Grammar and Alphabet of the Egyptian Language': Joseph Smith's translation method on paper
responseLead: The scribes worked backwards from an English text already given, and never published it.
rationaleLead: Arguable on which came first, but his own journal says he arranged that grammar.

title: Zelph, the 'white Lamanite' in an Illinois mound
claim: On 3 June 1834, during Zion's Camp, Joseph Smith's men dug a skeleton with an arrowhead between its ribs from a burial mound near the Illinois River. The site is Naples-Russell Mound 8, a Hopewell-culture site in Pike County, Illinois. According to diaries kept by at least six participants — Wilford Woodruff, Heber C. Kimball, George A. Smith, Levi Hancock, Moses Martin and Reuben McBride — Joseph declared by vision that the bones belonged to 'Zelph,' a 'white Lamanite' warrior-chieftain under 'the great prophet Onandagus,' killed in battle. Several accounts say Onandagus was 'known from the Rocky Mountains to the eastern sea.' The story entered History of the Church 2:79-80. The episode shows Joseph exercising his revelatory gift on a checkable claim — a Hopewell burial unrelated to any Israelite civilization — and locating Book of Mormon peoples in North America, which limited Mesoamerican geography models must explain away. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 is the test applied.

sources.name: Kenneth Godfrey, 'The Zelph Story' (BYU Studies)
Wikipedia: Zelph
MormonThink: Zelph, ancient Mormon warrior
FAIR: Joseph Smith and Zelph

response:
FAIR, drawing on Kenneth Godfrey's source study, notes that Joseph himself wrote nothing about Zelph.

The six diary accounts disagree on key details. Which battle it was. Whether the Rocky Mountains phrase was original.

The History of the Church version is a later scribal blend that hardened a casual campfire comment into formal revelation.

And even taken at face value, apologists argue that Zelph could be a late-period Lamanite in the hinterlands, far from the Book of Mormon's core lands. So the story does not fix Book of Mormon geography.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Joseph Smith and Zelph

rationale:
The objections about sources are real. The accounts do differ on details, and the printed version is a blend. So the exact wording of Joseph's statement cannot be recovered. That keeps this out of unrefuted.

But all six diaries agree on the core. Joseph claimed a vision naming a specific skeleton as a white Lamanite under a prophet called Onandagus.

That core is either a false claim of revelation about a Hopewell burial, or it must be watered down to guesswork. That is the same untestable move seen elsewhere.

Contested on the details. Damaging on the pattern.

"Six men wrote down the Zelph story that week. What do you do with it?"

title: From a whole hemisphere to no official position
claim: For over a century the church taught a hemispheric Book of Mormon. Canonized revelations identify North American Indians as Lamanites (D&C 28:8; 32:2; 54:8). Joseph Smith endorsed ruins in Central America as Nephite, in the Times and Seasons of 1842. He endorsed North American sites too — the 'plains of the Nephites,' and Zelph. The New York hill where he got the plates was officially the Cumorah of the final battles (Mormon 6:6). Joseph Fielding Smith warned that a two-Cumorah theory would make members 'confused and disturbed in their faith.' Marion Romney affirmed the New York Cumorah in general conference in 1975. Under pressure from digging and from DNA, scholars retreated to limited-geography models. Two rival camps now argue. The Mesoamerican one, at FAIR and Scripture Central. The Heartland one, at Rod Meldrum's FIRM Foundation. Each publishes detailed refutations of the other. In 2019 the church's Gospel Topics statement said it 'does not take a position on the specific geographic locations,' and asked members not to teach any geography in church settings. No model reconciles the text, the founders' statements and the evidence.

sources.name: Gospel Topics: Book of Mormon Geography
Wikipedia: Proposed Book of Mormon geographical setting
FAIR: Heartland Model of Book of Mormon geography (apologists vs. apologists)
LDS Discussions: Book of Mormon Geography (annotated essay)
Scripture Central: Church Releases Statement on Book of Mormon Geography

response:
Apologists respond that the text itself never names a modern location. They add that the travel distances inside it actually require a limited geography.

So the hemispheric model was a cultural assumption early members laid over the text. Joseph among them, speaking as a man. It was not revelation.

Scripture Central argues that a Mesoamerican setting meets dozens of textual tests. Writing systems. Cities. Warfare. Population.

And the church's official neutrality is fitting humility on a question scripture leaves open. They compare it to unresolved questions in biblical geography.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Heartland Model of Book of Mormon geography

rationale:
The retreat is documented in the church's own 2019 statement. It 'does not take a position on the specific geographic locations'.

The defence that the text never names a place fails against canon. The Doctrine and Covenants is scripture, not speculation, and D&C 28:8, 32:2 and 54:8 name North American tribes as Lamanites. Prophets taught the New York Cumorah as doctrine.

The strongest sign that no answer works is the apologists themselves. FAIR and Scripture Central publish refutations of the Heartland model. Their arguments mirror the critics' case against Mesoamerica. The Heartland side returns the favour.

When every proposed place is convincingly refuted by fellow believers, the claim has become untestable by moving it.

plain.t: What was taught for a century

Under pressure from archaeology and DNA, scholars retreated to limited-geography models. Two camps now argue with each other. The Mesoamerican one, at FAIR and Scripture Central. And the Heartland one, at Rod Meldrum's FIRM Foundation. Each publishes detailed refutations of the other.
In 2019 a Gospel Topics statement said the church "does not take a position on the specific geographic locations." It asked members not to teach any geography in church settings.

Strong for you. This one leans on the digging and the DNA cases, so use it with them. Their answer is that the text never names a modern place. So the whole-hemisphere view was a habit of mind, not revelation. But the D&C is scripture, and it names North American tribes as Lamanites. Here is the telling part. Believers now take apart each other's maps, using the same arguments critics use.
"Where did it happen? Even the church says it takes no position."

refwhy.D&C 28:8: A mission 'unto the Lamanites' in New York state. Their canon places Lamanite peoples in North America.
refwhy.D&C 32:2: The same mission, into 'the wilderness among the Lamanites.' A second case in their canon.
refwhy.Mormon 6:6: The hill Cumorah of the last battle. For a century this was the New York hill, taught as doctrine.

title: An angel with a drawn sword, used in proposals
claim: The church's Gospel Topics essay 'Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo' concedes that Joseph Smith told women an angel appeared three times commanding polygamy. In the final appearance 'the angel came with a drawn sword, threatening Joseph with destruction unless he went forward.' He deployed this account in proposals. Zina Diantha Huntington was proposed to while courting Henry Jacobs, and was sealed to Joseph after being told of the angel; Henry later stood as a witness. Mary Elizabeth Rollins Lightner was already married. Lucy Walker was 16, living in his home after her mother's death; she was told to seek confirmation, and later described her anguish. Helen Mar Kimball, aged 14, recorded Joseph's promise: 'If you will take this step, it will ensure your eternal salvation and exaltation, and that of your father's household.' D&C 132 canonizes the pattern, since wives who refuse are 'destroyed' at verses 54 and 64. Scripture warns that even an angel preaching another gospel is accursed (Galatians 1:8), and that Satan appears as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14).

sources.name: Gospel Topics essay: Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo
Brian Hales: The Accounts of the Angel with a Drawn Sword
FAIR: Helen Mar Kimball — circumstances of her plural marriage
Christian Research Institute: Plural Marriage and Joseph Smith

response:
Brian Hales and FAIR argue that the angel accounts come from faithful participants, and that they show Joseph's reluctance. He delayed for years and acted only under divine compulsion. That is the opposite of a predator's eagerness.

They note that Helen Mar Kimball's sealing was likely unconsummated and dynastic. It linked families for the next life only.

They note that women such as Sarah Pratt and Cordelia Morley refused Joseph with no spiritual penalty. That shows real agency.

And they argue that marriage customs for young women in the mid-1800s were sharply different from ours. Modern categories of coercion do not map cleanly onto them.

responseSource.name: Brian Hales: The Accounts of the Angel with a Drawn Sword

rationale:
The essential facts are conceded in the church's own essay. The drawn-sword angel. Helen's marriage 'several months before her 15th birthday'. The sealings to already-married women. The salvation promise to Helen comes from her own faithful memoir.

The threats in D&C 132:54 and 64 are canon.

Their reframing disputes what it meant, not what happened. And 'an angel threatened him into it' is itself the admission. The proposals carried a promise from God and a threat from God at once.

Galatians 1:8 speaks to exactly the case of an angel authorising another gospel. 2 Corinthians 11:14 warns that Satan appears as an angel of light. This goes to character, and to the fruit test of Matthew 7:15-20.

plain.d: The essay Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo states that Joseph Smith told women an angel appeared three times commanding polygamy. On the last visit "the angel came with a drawn sword, threatening Joseph with destruction unless he went forward."

In proposals. To Zina Diantha Huntington, while she was courting Henry Jacobs. She was sealed to Joseph after being told of the angel, and Henry later stood as a witness. To Mary Elizabeth Rollins Lightner, who was already married. And to Lucy Walker, who was 16 and living in his home after her mother died. She was told to seek her own confirmation. She later wrote about her anguish.

She was 14. She wrote down what Joseph promised her: "If you will take this step, it will ensure your eternal salvation and exaltation, and that of your father's household." That is her own memoir, written as a faithful member of the church.

Brian Hales and FAIR say the angel accounts come from faithful participants, and that they show reluctance rather than appetite. He delayed for years, and moved only under compulsion from God. Helen's sealing was likely unconsummated and dynastic, linking families for the next life. Women did refuse — Sarah Pratt and Cordelia Morley both did, with no spiritual penalty. And marriage customs for young women in the 1840s were not ours.

They admit the facts. Look at what the answer itself says. An angel threatened him into it. So a proposal carried a promise from God and a threat from God at the same time. D&C 132:54 and 64 put the threat into scripture. Galatians 1:8 speaks to exactly this, and 2 Corinthians 11:14 warns that Satan appears as an angel of light.
"Helen was fourteen. What do you make of what she was promised?"

title: Anne Frank baptised by proxy at least nine times
claim: Latter-day Saint members performed proxy baptisms for hundreds of thousands of Holocaust victims. After Jewish organizations protested, the church signed a 1995 agreement to remove victims' names and stop the practice, except for direct ancestors of members. The researcher Helen Radkey then repeatedly documented violations across two decades. Anne Frank's name was submitted at least a dozen times, and the ordinance performed at least nine times, including in the Santo Domingo Temple in February 2012, which prompted a church condemnation. Simon Wiesenthal's parents were baptized by proxy in early 2012, drawing a formal church apology to the family. The church revised its database controls in 2010 and threatened discipline for violators. The episode exposes the doctrine underneath. D&C 128:15-18 declares that the dead 'cannot be made perfect' without our ordinances, and that vicarious work is 'essential to our salvation.' It rests on one disputed verse, 1 Corinthians 15:29, against the Bible's teaching that judgment follows death (Hebrews 9:27) and that a fixed gulf separates the dead (Luke 16:26) — a point the Book of Mormon itself makes at Alma 34:32-35.

sources.name: KSL: LDS Church issues statement after report of proxy baptism for Anne Frank
CBS News: Mormons apologize to Wiesenthal family for posthumous baptism
Fox 13: LDS Church condemns recent proxy baptism of Anne Frank
Mormonr: Holocaust Victims and Baptisms for the Dead

response:
The church and Mormonr reply that proxy baptism forces nobody. The teaching is that the dead may take it or refuse it. So it is an offer, not a conversion after death.

The church kept the 1995 agreement. Each case on record was one member acting against a stated rule.

And the church acted. It took names out. In 2010 it built blocks into the database for Holocaust victims. It said sorry to families. And it warned that anyone doing it again may lose temple access, or face a church court.

responseSource.name: Mormonr: Holocaust Victims and Baptisms for the Dead

rationale:
Every load-bearing fact is conceded by the church itself. The practice happened. The 1995 agreement existed. Violations went on for two decades. And the church publicly condemned and apologised for specific cases, including Anne Frank and the Wiesenthals.

The individual-members defence is fair as far as it goes. It also concedes the systemic point. A doctrine that makes ordinances for the dead 'essential to our salvation' creates a pressure that policy could not hold for twenty years.

The deeper use here is doctrinal. The whole temple-for-the-dead system hangs on one disputed verse, 1 Corinthians 15:29. Read it against Hebrews 9:27, Luke 16:26, and even Alma 34:32-35.

plain.d: Members performed proxy baptisms for hundreds of thousands of Holocaust victims. Jewish organisations protested. In 1995 the church signed an agreement to remove the names and stop, except for members' own direct ancestors.

The researcher Helen Radkey documented violations for two decades. Anne Frank's name was submitted at least a dozen times, and the ordinance performed at least nine times. One was at the Santo Domingo Temple in February 2012, and the church condemned it. Early in 2012, Simon Wiesenthal's parents were baptised by proxy. The church apologised formally to the family.

Against it stand Hebrews 9:27, where judgment follows death, and Luke 16:26, where a fixed gulf separates the dead. Alma 34:32-35 makes the same point.

That proxy baptism compels nobody. The teaching is that the dead may accept or reject it, so it is an offering rather than a conversion. The institution honoured the 1995 agreement, and each documented violation was an individual member acting against explicit policy. And the church acted: names removed, database blocks engineered in 2010, apologies made to families, and warnings that violators lose temple privileges or face discipline.

They admit this themselves. The practice, the agreement, the years of violations, and the apologies are all conceded. The individual-members defence is fair as far as it goes. It also concedes the systemic point. A doctrine that makes this work essential to salvation creates a pressure that policy could not hold for twenty years. Handle it gently; these are real families.
"Hebrews 9:27 says judgment comes after death. How do the temple ordinances fit that?"

title: Proposition 8: every pulpit, and $20 million
claim: In 2008 the First Presidency had a letter read from every California pulpit, on 29 June. It urged members to 'do all you can' — their 'means and time' — to pass Proposition 8, which stripped same-sex marriage from California law. Ward and stake structures were turned into a precinct operation: assigned donation targets, phone banks, and door-to-door canvassing. It was coordinated with the Protect Marriage coalition, which the church joined at Catholic Archbishop Niederauer's invitation. Members contributed an estimated $20 million, roughly half the Yes campaign's funds, while Latter-day Saints were about 2% of Californians. The church itself reported in-kind contributions, and was later fined by the California Fair Political Practices Commission for reporting them late. The same playbook had run in Hawaii in 1998, and on California's Proposition 22 in 2000. The church's canonized position reads differently: 'We do not believe it just to mingle religious influence with civil government' (D&C 134:9; cf. Matthew 22:21, John 18:36). For evangelism the point is institutional. A church claiming political neutrality directed member resources into civil law. Within a decade it reversed course culturally, supporting the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act.

sources.name: Church Newsroom: Same-Sex Marriage and Proposition 8
Thomas Jefferson School of Law: An Overview of LDS Involvement in Prop 8
George Washington Law Review: Proposition 8 and the Mormon Church — A Case Study in Donor Disclosure
Religion Dispatches: When Mormons Mobilize
FAIR: Mormonism and politics — California Proposition 8

response:
The church's Newsroom and FAIR respond that churches have always had the right, and a duty, to speak on moral questions. Marriage is a moral question, not partisan politics.

The church endorsed no candidate and no party. It joined a broad interfaith coalition rather than acting alone. Catholics, evangelicals, Orthodox Jews and Muslims were in it.

Direct institutional spending was a small, disclosed, in-kind amount. Members donated freely, as private citizens.

And D&C 134 also says governments should protect the free exercise of conscience. That, the church argues, is what it was doing.

responseSource.name: Church Newsroom: Same-Sex Marriage and Proposition 8

rationale:
The facts are documented and not denied. The First Presidency letter of 29 June 2008. The fundraising through church channels. The roughly $20 million from members, about half the Yes campaign's funds. And the FPPC fine for late reporting.

The defence justifies the involvement rather than disputing it, so the substance is admitted.

Whether religious political advocacy is wrong is a judgement Christians themselves divide over. So the force here is narrower. It lies in the mismatch with D&C 134:9. And it lies in the pattern of mobilise, then soften. Proposition 8, the 2015 exclusion policy, the 2019 reversal, then the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act.

Members gave an estimated $20 million, roughly half the funds of the Yes campaign. Latter-day Saints were about 2% of Californians. The church reported in-kind contributions, and was later fined by the California Fair Political Practices Commission for reporting them late. The same playbook had run in Hawaii in 1998, and on Proposition 22 in 2000.

That churches have always had the right, and a duty, to speak on moral questions. Marriage is a moral question, not a partisan one, and the church endorsed no candidate or party. It joined a broad interfaith coalition — Catholics, evangelicals, Orthodox Jews, Muslims — rather than acting alone. Direct institutional spending was small and disclosed. They admit the facts, and their answer justifies the involvement rather than denying it. Be careful here. D&C 134:9 says "we do not believe it just to mingle religious influence with civil government." And the pattern goes mobilise, then soften — Proposition 8, then the 2015 policy, then the 2019 reversal, then support for the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act.
"How do you read D&C 134:9 against what happened in 2008?"
