title: The City Creek tithing suit failed, 11–0
claim: In 2021 James Huntsman, of the prominent Huntsman family, sued the church for fraud, seeking the return of roughly $5 million in tithing. He cited President Hinckley's assurance in general conference in 2003 about the City Creek mall project: 'tithing funds have not and will not be used to acquire this property.' Against it he set the whistleblower David Nielsen's account that Ensign Peak Advisors, whose portfolio was built from surplus tithing, moved about $1.4 billion toward City Creek. A Ninth Circuit panel revived the claim in 2023. But on 31 January 2025 an 11-0 en banc court ruled for the church. Six judges held that no reasonable juror could find misrepresentation, because Hinckley in the same address said funds would come from 'commercial entities owned by the Church' and from 'earnings of invested reserve funds.' The remaining judges would have barred the suit under the church-autonomy doctrine. The case matters as the highest-profile legal test of the church's tithing representations, adjacent to the SEC's separate $5 million Ensign Peak settlement. D&C 119:3-4 and 2 Corinthians 8:20-21 are the texts at issue.

sources.name: Deseret News: Huntsman tithing lawsuit dismissed by unanimous 9th Circuit panel
Courthouse News: Church asks en banc Ninth Circuit to throw out fraud claims
Americans United: Huntsman v. Corporation of the President (case page)
Metropolitan News: Ninth Circuit judges disagree over why fraud suit fails
Sutherland Institute: Why the Ninth Circuit unanimously tossed the Huntsman lawsuit

response:
The church's defence, accepted by the full court, is that Hinckley's 2003 statement drew a line. It distinguished tithing itself from 'earnings of invested reserve funds' and from commercial-entity money.

City Creek was funded from the latter. So there was no misrepresentation, let alone fraud. Huntsman produced no evidence that tithing principal was spent.

The concurring judges added a second ground. The First Amendment's church-autonomy doctrine forbids civil courts from judging what a church tells members about sacred donations at all.

responseSource.name: Sutherland Institute: Why the Ninth Circuit unanimously tossed the Huntsman lawsuit

rationale:
After full argument on both sides, the fraud theory failed 11-0 on 31 January 2025. For a majority it failed on the merits, not on constitutional avoidance.

Hinckley's own wording at the time anticipated the distinction between earnings and principal.

So what is left is whether earnings on invested tithing are morally still tithing. That is a quarrel about words, not a proven deception. Honest grading calls this answered. The church won this one.

The broader transparency concern is real, but it belongs to the SEC and Ensign Peak case, which stands on its own.

What is left is whether earnings on invested tithing are still tithing, which is a quarrel about words. Cite this as proof of fraud and you will lose your credibility.
Nothing about this case. If money comes up, go to the SEC settlement, which is admitted fact.

title: Paul H. Dunn's war and baseball stories were invented

title: Moroni 10:4: a feeling as the test of truth

title: Alma 36's mirror pattern: evidence or coincidence
claim: This is the strongest literary argument for Book of Mormon antiquity. In 1969 John Welch identified extended chiasmus in the Book of Mormon. Chiasmus is inverted parallelism: A-B-C-C'-B'-A'. Alma 36 is the showpiece — a full-chapter structure pivoting on 'born of God,' argued to reflect an ancient Hebrew form Joseph Smith could not have known. The critical response is led by Earl Wunderli, in 'Critique of Alma 36 as an Extended Chiasm,' published in Dialogue in 2005. He shows that Welch's outline depends on selective labelling. Some repeated words are counted as structure, while others that break the pattern are not. Text in between is skipped. Loose matches are allowed. By Welch's own fifteen criteria, the chapter scores poorly. Chiasm-like patterns also appear where nobody claims Hebrew antiquity: in the Doctrine and Covenants, and in ordinary nineteenth-century prose. Chiasmus scholarship predated the Book of Mormon, such as John Jebb's 'Sacred Literature' of 1820, though Smith's access to it is undemonstrated. The physicists Boyd and Farrell Edwards countered statistically that Alma 36's chiastic ordering is unlikely by chance, and Wunderli rebutted their choice of elements. Genesis 9:6 and Amos 5:4-6 are biblical examples of the form.

sources.name: Earl Wunderli, 'Critique of Alma 36 as an Extended Chiasm' (Dialogue 38:4)
Boyd & Farrell Edwards, Response to Wunderli (Dialogue)
Wunderli, Response to the Edwardses (Dialogue)
Scholarly Publishing Collective: Critique of Alma 36 as an Extended Chiasm

response: Boyd and Farrell Edwards are physicists. They published a study of the odds. They estimate it is very unlikely that Alma 36's repeated elements would fall into that mirror order by chance. Their method, they argue, does not rest on Welch's or Wunderli's literary judgements. Apologists add that the shape fits the meaning. Conversion sits at the centre of a life told backwards. They argue that the candidates in the Doctrine and Covenants are plainly weaker. And they note that nothing puts John Jebb's Sacred Literature of 1820, or any work on chiasmus, in Joseph Smith's hands in rural New York before 1829.

responseSource.name: Boyd & Farrell Edwards, Response to Wunderli (Dialogue)

rationale:
This is a real two-sided exchange in peer-reviewed journals. Wunderli's point about picking and choosing lands. But the Edwardses' reply on the odds is a serious counter, and it survives his rebuttal in part.

Calling it contested, rather than dismissing it, is both true and good for your credibility.

The deeper point is this. Even grant a deliberate chiasm in Alma 36. The step to antiquity still fails. A writer soaked in King James parallels could produce a mirror shape, and modern texts have them.

A shape on the page cannot outweigh the anachronisms, the DNA and the textual evidence. Concede the pattern. Contest what follows.

plain.d: A shape in writing. Ideas run out and then back again in reverse — A, B, C, then C, B, A. It turns on a centre. Old Hebrew writers used it, and so does the Bible; Genesis 9:6 and Amos 5:4-6 are examples.

In 1969 John Welch found extended chiasmus in the Book of Mormon. Alma 36 is the showpiece. The whole chapter is laid out that way, turning on the words "born of God." Welch argues Joseph Smith could not have known the form.

Earl Wunderli published it in Dialogue in 2005. He says the outline depends on choosing. Some repeated words are counted as structure; others that break the pattern are not. Chunks of text are skipped. Loose matches are allowed. By Welch's own fifteen criteria, the chapter scores poorly. Chiasm-like shapes also turn up in the Doctrine and Covenants, and in ordinary writing of the 1800s.

Two physicists, Boyd and Farrell Edwards, replied with statistics. They estimate it is very unlikely that Alma 36's repeated elements would fall into that order by chance. Their method, they argue, does not rest on anyone's literary judgement. Apologists add that the shape fits the meaning, with conversion at the centre of an inverted life. They say the candidates in the D&C are weaker. And no evidence puts John Jebb's 1820 book on chiasmus, or any such work, in Joseph Smith's hands.

Genuinely arguable, and this is a real scholarly exchange in peer-reviewed journals. Concede the pattern; contest what follows from it. Even a deliberate chiasm does not prove antiquity. A writer soaked in King James parallelism could produce one, and modern texts contain them. Grant it gracefully and go back to the anachronisms and the DNA.
"I'll grant you the chiasm. Does a shape on the page make a book ancient?"

refwhy.Genesis 9:6: A short biblical chiasm — blood, man, man, blood. It shows the form is real and old.
refwhy.Amos 5:4-6: A longer example from the Bible. Nobody can say the form was invented to serve this argument.
refwhy.Alma 36:1-30: The showpiece chapter. Read it and watch the shape turn on 'born of God' at the centre.

titleLong: Chiasmus in Alma 36: apologetic evidence examined
responseLead: Two physicists ran the numbers. Alma 36's order is very unlikely by chance.
rationaleLead: Concede the pattern and contest what follows: a shape does not make a book old.

title: Nahom, and three altars found in Yemen
claim: This is the apologists' flagship archaeological evidence. 1 Nephi 16:34 says Ishmael was buried 'in the place which was called Nahom' — a name the party did not coin — after which the group turned 'nearly eastward' (1 Nephi 17:1). Three limestone altars excavated from the Bar'an temple near Marib, in Yemen, from 1988 onward, carry dedications by a donor of the NHM, or Nihm, tribe. They date to roughly the seventh or sixth century BC, which is Lehi's era, and the Nihm tribal region lies near where the frankincense trail bends east toward the coast. Warren Aston and Scripture Central present this as a precise external hit. Critics respond that the inscriptions are three consonants naming a tribe, not a place called Nahom; that the NHM root is common across Semitic names; that the eastward turn matches incense-trail geography generally; and that a form of the name, 'Nehhm,' appears on European maps from Carsten Niebuhr's expedition, in English by 1792. So the correlation is explainable by common naming plus coincidence. Non-Mormon archaeologists attach no significance to the parallel; Philip Jenkins wrote that 'there's no there there.' Proverbs 18:17 is the principle at stake.

Warren Aston and Scripture Central argue that NHM is rare as an Arabian place name. The altars independently tie the tribal name to precisely Lehi's period and region. That was unknowable from 1820s New York.

They note that no evidence connects Joseph Smith to Carsten Niebuhr's maps.

And they stress the chain of hits. A burial place bearing a Semitic root that carries the sense of mourning and consolation. Positioned exactly where the text turns the party east. Ending at plausible candidates for Bountiful on the Omani coast.

That chain, they argue, multiplies well beyond coincidence.

responseSource.name: Scripture Central: Book of Mormon Evidence — Nahom

rationale: Honesty requires ranking this as their best single datum. It is a real inscriptional match, correctly dated and plausibly located. It is also weaker than it is usually presented. A tribal name of three consonants. A root common in Semitic naming. A turn that follows the trade route everyone took. And a form of the name, Nehhm, on published European maps in English by 1792, decades before 1829. Archaeology outside Mormonism sees nothing evidentiary in it. Philip Jenkins wrote that 'there's no there there'. Both sides field serious arguments from real data, which is the definition of contested. Grant Nahom its full weight. Then note that one consonant cluster in Arabia cannot offset the total absence of Nephite evidence in the New World, where the story's thousand years unfold.

plain.d: 1 Nephi 16:34 says Ishmael was buried "in the place which was called Nahom." Note the wording. The party did not name it; they found it named. Then, at 1 Nephi 17:1, they turn "nearly eastward."

Three limestone altars from the Bar'an temple near Marib, in Yemen, found from 1988 onward. Each carries a dedication by a donor of the NHM tribe, the Nihm. They date to roughly the 600s or 500s BC — Lehi's era. And the Nihm region sits near where the frankincense trail bends east toward the coast.

Warren Aston and Scripture Central call this a precise external hit. NHM is rare as an Arabian place name. The altars anchor the tribal name to exactly Lehi's period and region. Nobody in 1820s New York could have known that. And they stress the chain. A burial place carrying a root that means mourning. Sitting exactly where the text turns east. Ending at plausible candidates for Bountiful on the Omani coast. Each link, they say, multiplies against coincidence.

The inscriptions give three consonants naming a tribe, not a place called Nahom. The NHM root is common in Semitic names. The eastward turn follows the trade route everyone used. And a form of the name, Nehhm, appears on European maps from Carsten Niebuhr's expedition, in English by 1792. Archaeologists outside the church see nothing in it; Philip Jenkins wrote that "there's no there there."

One consonant cluster in Arabia does not offset an empty New World, where a thousand years of the story take place.

title: The Smith family did not follow Brigham Young
claim: When Joseph Smith was killed in June 1844, he left no unambiguous succession plan, and the movement fractured among rival claimants. There was his counselor Sidney Rigdon; the Quorum of the Twelve under Brigham Young; and James Strang, who produced a letter of appointment dated June 1844, now at Yale's Beinecke Library and catalogued as 'attributed.' Strang then unearthed his own metal plates at Voree, Wisconsin, in 1845, before four witnesses, and there is no direct contemporaneous evidence that his witnesses ever recanted — a fact that complicates appeals to the Book of Mormon witnesses. Strikingly, the people who knew Joseph best did not go west. His widow Emma stayed in Nauvoo, married the non-Mormon Lewis Bidamon, and in her 1879 'Last Testimony' in the Saints' Herald of 1 October denied to her death that Joseph practised polygamy: 'He had no other wife but me.' His mother Lucy and brother William never gathered to Utah. His son Joseph Smith III became prophet of the rival RLDS church at Amboy, Illinois, in 1860. And none of the Three Witnesses went west in 1847. All were excommunicated by 1838. Oliver Cowdery was rebaptized in 1848 but died before reaching Utah. Martin Harris came only in 1870. David Whitmer never returned. D&C 28:2-7, D&C 43:3-4 and 3 Nephi 11:29 bear on it, as do 1 Corinthians 14:33, Matthew 7:15-20 and Deuteronomy 18:21-22.

response:
Apologists answer that succession did not depend on family. Joseph conferred the keys of the kingdom on the Quorum of the Twelve before his death. On 8 August 1844 the great majority of Nauvoo Saints sustained the Twelve over Rigdon.

Strang's letter of appointment is judged a forgery on handwriting and postal grounds. Apologists contend that several Voree witnesses later distanced themselves from Strang.

On Emma, FAIR argues that her denials are contradicted by heavy documentary evidence, including sealing records naming her participation in 1843. They explain them four ways. She wanted to protect her sons. She opposed polygamy. She was in property disputes with Brigham Young. And she was loyal to the movement her son led.

Family closeness, they note, is not the biblical test of truth.

responseSource.name: FAIR — Emma Smith and Brigham Young

rationale:
Every fact here is conceded on all sides. No written plan for succession was produced. Emma and the Smith family rejected Brigham Young. Joseph Smith III led the rival RLDS church from 1860. And Emma denied polygamy to the end, in her 1879 'Last Testimony'.

The keys-to-the-Twelve argument has real historical support. Most of Nauvoo did follow the Twelve.

But the defence costs more than its makers say. It requires holding that the prophet's own widow lied in public, steadily, for thirty-five years. Meanwhile friendly witnesses are treated as beyond question.

And the usual way of dismissing Strang's plates, and witnesses who never took it back, fits the Book of Mormon's own witnesses just as well.

The people who knew Joseph best. His widow Emma stayed in Nauvoo and married Lewis Bidamon, who was not a Mormon. His mother Lucy and his brother William never gathered to Utah. His son Joseph Smith III became prophet of the rival RLDS church at Amboy, Illinois, in 1860. And none of the Three Witnesses went west in 1847. All had been excommunicated by 1838. title: The Second Anointing: exaltation sealed in secret
claim: Beyond the endowment sits a higher ordinance most Latter-day Saints have never heard of: the second anointing, in which a couple's 'calling and election is made sure' and exaltation is sealed upon them. Compare D&C 131:5, 'the more sure word of prophecy,' and D&C 132:49. It has been administered since 28 September 1843, by invitation of the First Presidency only. David John Buerger's landmark study in Dialogue in 1983 documents thousands performed in the nineteenth century, then a sharp curtailment and near-total concealment in the twentieth; the church stopped publishing statistics by the 1930s. Even the apologetic site Mormonr confirms that the ordinance exists, is invitation-only, 'isn't generally taught in Church meetings or in Church publications,' and that teachers are instructed not to discuss it or answer questions about it. It came to broad public light in 2012, when Tom Phillips, a former stake president who received the rite from the apostle M. Russell Ballard, published a detailed firsthand account and told his story on Mormon Stories. Scripture offers assurance of salvation freely to every believer — 1 John 5:13, Romans 8:16, 2 Peter 1:10, Ephesians 2:8-9 — not as a secret rite reserved for elites.

title: 3,400 verses corrected, in a Bible never adopted
claim: From June 1830 to July 1833, Joseph Smith produced an 'inspired revision' of the entire Bible. He altered roughly 3,400 verses, with no manuscript support. And he declared it done: 'We this day finished the translating of the Scriptures' (History of the Church, 2 July 1833). Revelations had commanded that the work be finished (D&C 73:3-4) and published (D&C 124:89). Yet the church has never adopted it. Its official Bible remains the King James Version, with selected readings relegated to footnotes and an appendix. The rival RLDS church, now Community of Christ, published the full text as the Inspired Version in 1867. It held the manuscripts for 150 years. The church bought them in March 2024, with the marked Bible and the Kirtland Temple, in a deal worth $192.5 million. Stranger still, BYU's own scholars concede that the 1830 Book of Mormon was used as a source for some revisions to Isaiah. Yet many Book of Mormon variants were never carried into the revision, and some were changed yet again. So Joseph revised verses that his own earlier scripture quotes in their King James form. 1 Nephi 13:28, D&C 45:60-61 and Articles of Faith 1:8 bear on it, as do Deuteronomy 4:2, Proverbs 30:5-6, Isaiah 40:8 and 1 Peter 1:24-25.

response:
FAIR and BYU scholars respond that the July 1833 statement marked the end of a first pass. It was not a finished book. Joseph kept revising until his death in 1844, and never prepared a manuscript for the press.

The order to publish, at D&C 124:89, went unmet amid poverty and persecution. So the church inherited a working draft, not a finished Bible.

They add that the revision was never meant as one uniform restoring of lost words. It blends restoring, prophetic comment, harmonising and modernising. That explains the gaps against Book of Mormon readings.

And far from hiding it, the church put hundreds of its readings in the footnotes and appendix of its 1979 edition. The 2024 purchase shows reverence, not shame.

responseSource.name: FAIR — Joseph's Translation of the Bible (response to MormonThink)

rationale:
The core facts are undisputed. The revision was commanded. It was pronounced finished in Joseph's own record in 1833. It was commanded to be published in 1841. It was never canonised. And it was published instead by the rival denomination that rejected Brigham Young.

Their reply, that it was actually unfinished and mixed in genre, is a genuine scholarly position. Joseph did keep tinkering. That keeps this contested rather than unrefuted.

But the defence sits awkwardly with the sources. It must read 'we this day finished the translating of the Scriptures' as not meaning finished. And it concedes that the revelation commanding publication was never obeyed.

The category problem stays on any reading. A prophet corrected the Bible by revelation, and the church claiming his mantle still hands members the uncorrected King James.

title: Scripture for 86 years, then quietly removed
claim: In August 1835 a general assembly of the church voted to canonize the seven Lectures on Faith as the 'Doctrine' half of the Doctrine and Covenants. They are why the book is called Doctrine and Covenants, and they were printed as scripture for 86 years. In 1921 a committee removed them, with no revelation and no vote of common consent. The explanation was that they 'were never presented to nor accepted by the Church as being otherwise than theological lectures' — which contradicts the 1835 assembly minutes accepting the whole volume. The doctrinal driver is plain. Lecture 5 teaches that the Father is 'a personage of spirit,' which is irreconcilable with the later doctrine of D&C 130:22 that the Father has a body of flesh and bones. When the doctrine of God changed, the canon was edited to match. That is a de-canonization, in a church that claims its canon grows only by revelation. Jude 3, Isaiah 40:8 and Malachi 3:6 are the texts at issue.

On this view, 1921 was housecleaning rather than de-canonisation.

rationale:
The response concedes the key facts. The 1835 assembly voted to accept the entire book, lectures included, as 'the doctrine and covenants of their faith'. The claim that they were never accepted as more than lessons is contradicted by the 1835 record itself.

And 'incomplete on the Godhead' is a euphemism. Lecture 5's spirit-Father theology was superseded, and the canon was trimmed to match.

This pairs powerfully with D&C 132, which stays in the canon while being disavowed. The canon is edited by administrative decision, not by revelation.

It comes down to one question. What revelation removed them? There is none.

title: Zion's Camp: 900 miles, no land recovered
claim: In February 1834, D&C 103 promised the redemption of Zion — Jackson County — 'by power,' with the Lord's presence going before the armed expedition. 'The redemption of Zion must needs come by power… I will fight your battles,' and at 103:15-20 his angels would go up before them. Zion's Camp marched roughly 900 miles. Cholera killed about a dozen members. Missouri's governor declined to help. No land was recovered. In June 1834, D&C 105:9-13 called the whole thing off. The Saints must 'wait for a little season for the redemption of Zion,' with the failure attributed to the members' transgressions. Both the promise and its retraction sit in the canon today, alongside D&C 101:17-18. And 192 years later the 'little season' continues, since Jackson County was never redeemed. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 and Ezekiel 13:6-7 are the tests applied. Coordinate this with the general failed-prophecies entry, so the D&C 84 temple prophecy is not counted twice.

response:
Apologists read D&C 103 as conditional.

D&C 105 itself explains why. The Saints failed to consecrate, and they were not ready. So the Lord deferred the promise rather than broke it.

Zion's Camp is then reframed as a refining trial. Many future apostles and seventies were chosen from among its veterans. On that reading the march succeeded at its real purpose.

The conditions were announced after the failure, not before it. D&C 103 reads as a flat promise with divine backing behind it. 'Mine angels shall go up before you.' D&C 105 fits the conditions on once the march collapsed.

The unique value here is teaching value. Unlike disputed prophecy cases, the believer's own canon holds both the promise and the walk-back. No outside source is needed. And a 'little season' now entering its third century speaks for itself.

title: 'One mighty and strong': 18 men claimed it
claim: D&C 85:7-8 promises that God will send 'one mighty and strong, holding the scepter of power in his hand,' to 'set in order the house of God.' The verse is canonized and unfulfilled. So it has bred a steady stream of claimants. A Dialogue survey documents roughly eighteen main ones. By 1905 at least eight had already declared themselves. That forced a First Presidency statement, in the Deseret News in November 1905. It reinterpreted the verse as being about Edward Partridge and land matters in the 1830s. And it declared self-proclaimed candidates ignorant 'of God and the order of the Church.' Founders of fundamentalist sects have claimed the title, and so have violent figures, including the LeBaron clan. A vague canonized prophecy, plus prophetic authority, is a schism engine. And the institutional fix was to reinterpret the scripture by press release. Deuteronomy 18:20-22 and Matthew 24:24 are the tests applied.

title: 150 years of teaching, downplayed to Time magazine

title: Joseph Smith was not convicted in 1826
claim: The popular version says Joseph Smith was a convicted con man — that a court convicted him of fraud in 1826, right before he found the plates.

sources.name: Wikipedia: Joseph Smith and the criminal justice system
BYU Studies: 'Joseph Smith's 1826 Trial: The Legal Setting' (Madsen)
BYU Studies: 'Joseph Smith and the 1826 Trial: New Evidence and New Difficulties' (Hill)
Marquardt/UTLM: 'Joseph Smith's 1826 Trial — New Discoveries Prove Court Record Authentic'

response:
That is overclaimed.

The 1826 Bainbridge proceeding was real. Smith, aged 20, was charged as a 'disorderly person' over paid 'glass looking'. Justice Neely's own fee bill labels him 'The Glass Looker'.

But it was likely a preliminary examination. The surviving records are fragmentary and they contradict each other. The Pearsall account says 'guilty', while the fee bill and mittimus evidence point the other way.

Scholars dispute the outcome. Gordon Madsen reads an acquittal or discharge. Dan Vogel and Wesley Walters disagree. So 'convicted of fraud' states as fact what the documents cannot establish.

responseSource.name: FAIR: Joseph Smith's 1826 trial

rationale: Say 'convicted' and the apologist wins the exchange on the record's ambiguity. And that ambiguity is genuine, not spin. Here is the core that needs no conviction. By the church's own Gospel Topics admission, and by Richard Bushman in Rough Stone Rolling, Smith was a paid treasure-seer. He hunted buried valuables by staring at a stone in his hat. It was the same stone, in the same hat, that he then used to produce the Book of Mormon. The 1826 court documents back up that occupation whatever the verdict. Lead with the church-admitted seer-stone facts, and let the 1826 record confirm the timeline.

It was probably a preliminary examination, not a trial. The surviving records are fragmentary and they contradict each other. The Pearsall account says guilty. The fee bill and mittimus evidence point the other way. Scholars split — Gordon Madsen reads it as a discharge, while Dan Vogel and Wesley Walters disagree. Convicted states as fact what the documents cannot carry.
